Sports.title: Northampton chief lifts lid on Pollock contract negotiations with Hearn
Sports.content:
Northampton Saints director of rugby Phil Dowson believes more players could follow Henry Pollock and work with promoters like Eddie Hearn to grow their profile.

On Tuesday, Pollock put pen to paper on a multi-year extension with his boyhood club, with the England international agreeing a deal worth £400,000 per year.

At just 21, Pollock already has 13 England caps and made five appearances for the British & Irish Lions during last year's tour of Australia.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' James Cole explains the story of Pollock signing a new contract at Northampton Saints

Pollock's profile continues to grow, with the flanker becoming the first rugby union player to join Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency at the start of the year. Dowson revealed that the boxing promoter "drove as hard a bargain as he possibly could" during negotiations.

Reflecting on Pollock's decision to join Hearn's agency, Dowson said: "I think we'll see more of it.

"I think headlines and social media engagement, and all that, is positive for the game. Fundamentally, I talked to the coaches about this. We want more people watching the game, more people talking about the game and, ideally, most importantly, more people playing the game at loads of different age groups.

Image: Phil Dowson lauded Eddie Hearn for his role in Pollock's contract negotiations

"If Henry Pollock and Matchroom are getting some traction with the public, I think we should encourage that, but also take into account that we've got to continue to deliver that in the right way, and I think we have them."

Hearn told The Telegraph that he believes the 21-year-old is worth more than seven figures, predicting Pollock's value will "skyrocket" over the coming years while also arguing that the value of rugby will rise.

Dowson also lifted the lid on the boxing promoter's role in the negotiations, lauding him for helping him grow Pollock's profile, adding that part of the negotiations were handled by a "traditional rugby agent".

"Eddie's been excellent. He's raised the profile of the game," Dowson said.

"He's raised the profile of Henry and he's done what an agent's supposed to do. He's driven as hard a bargain as he possibly could.

"I've got a lot of respect for Eddie and how he goes about his work and some of the stuff he said in the media was really pertinent.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hearn believes that Pollock is the future of rugby and says by paying him what he deserves, he can grow the sport to another level

"I think there's elements of the contract which weren't done by Eddie, which were done by his traditional rugby agent.

"There are things from a marketing point of view and the extracurricular stuff that Eddie really looks after Pollock with, which we'll see more of.

"He wasn't necessarily doing every single negotiation from a rugby point of view."

Pollock has explained in the past that he had an open mind to the next steps of his career, but on Tuesday said he was "massively happy to re-sign with Saints".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hearn had previously said that Pollock was worth at least £1m

Some fans had questioned why the negotiations had taken so long to complete, with the flanker's loyalty coming under scrutiny, but Dowson said the process was made easier by Pollock's desire to stay.

"It's still his job, it's still his career. He needs to make sure he's getting the right deal for his aspirations and all those other elements that come with it," Dowson said. "I don't just mean from a financial point of view; I mean from a full, holistic perspective."

"Would there be loyalty in sport if he wasn't offered a contract? Would that be us not being loyal? I think we've got to be careful around that.

"He's playing really well. He's got lots of people talking about rugby. That's great. We wanted to keep him and he wanted to stay. That's a great position for us to start negotiations from, and that's the great thing about sport.

"People can have an opinion around it, but I don't think it was overly dragged out, to be honest, and I don't think it was ever done... there was no animosity in any way from my perspective."

Sports.title: Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands
Sports.content:
Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.

The prime minister, a committed Everton fan who still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.

The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, but police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.

Burnham has long opposed the ban, saying it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.

Asked by reporters on the plane to New York about lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.

“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.

The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.

A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.

“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”

A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”

Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.

Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.

Sports.title: Harry Kane admits England’s World Cup 2026 exit ‘hurt more than any other’
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has described England’s World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina as his most painful tournament exit because of how the team lost sight of who they were.

The captain is determined to move on as quickly as possible and is chasing a statement performance against Spain at Wembley on Saturday night in the Nations League. But he admits he is yet to get over the Argentina game and knows it is something he and his England teammates must work to process.

“It felt like it wasn’t us as a team,” Kane said, as he reflected on how England lost their way in the 2-1 defeat, barely touching the ball after they went ahead in the 55th minute. “It wasn’t the team that we wanted to be and said we’d be. When you maybe go against your beliefs and you lose, it feels 10 times worse than just losing in a way where … if we lose doing it our way you accept it, take it on the chin and move on. It’s tough and it will still be tough.

“I’m so passionate about England and especially because I’ve been on this journey … been to finals, semi‑finals and been so close. Each one hurts in a different way and this one hurt, for sure, more than any other one. I’d say even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar [in the 2-1 defeat by France in the 2022 World Cup quarter-finals] because of just the manner that it happened.”

It was put to Kane that it was a healing process. “It kind of is,” he replied. “But you have to heal while getting on with it. In football, you don’t have time. Before you know it’s the next one. It’s a hard balance because you’re trying to get over it and learn from it but also we play the world champions on Saturday and it’s a big, important game.”

Kane knows England must identify why they have repeatedly fallen short against the toughest teams when it matters most. “How can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more in those moments? Through qualifying campaigns and a lot of games in tournaments, we play with a certain intensity, we play in a good way. It’s something that we haven’t quite been able to do in latter stages of tournaments against the bigger and better nations.

“It may be a mixture of things. It may be personalities, mentality. It may be just the direction and how we want to play in those games. It’s conversations that we need to have as a group.”

Kane accepts it was not only against Argentina that England were not at their best. “Taking away the big loss at the end, there were still games at the World Cup where we didn’t quite reach our potential, the way that we train,” he said.

But the message – as articulated by Thomas Tuchel when he addressed the squad at St George’s Park on Tuesday – was of the need to fine-tune. “The general messaging is that we continue what we’ve been building,” Kane said. “Sometimes after a tournament, it’s easy to say it’s a new start but I don’t think it is that. It’s a continuation because we have done a lot of good things.”

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane asked: ‘How can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more?’ after England’s World Cup heartbreak. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

Tuchel has been rocked by the withdrawals of Declan Rice, Cole Palmer, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento for the upcoming Nations League fixtures; after Spain, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia. Rice’s absence has attracted attention because it is for load-management reasons rather than an injury that would immediately rule him out. Kane understands the move, given Rice’s well-documented problems with nerve pain in a hamstring.

“I spoke to Dec,” Kane said. “I know Dec goes far and beyond for the club and country. I know he’s been struggling for a while with his issues. Dec reached out to me, he voice-noted me. Everyone has to look after themselves and I trust all the boys.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is a seismic time for Kane. He is four caps shy of Peter Shilton’s all‑time England record of 125; he could be level with him by the end of this international window. Kane is also tipped to win the Ballon d’Or on 26 October and is poised to extend his contract at Bayern Munich. “We’re fairly close,” he said. “I’m happy there. It won’t be too long before there’s some sort of announcement.”

The 33-year-old allowed his thoughts to drift to the longer term and as he mused about his ambition to become an NFL kicker, there was a clear hint he saw himself finishing his football career in Major League Soccer.

“I take penalties and it [being an NFL kicker] is a very similar pressure and technique. If I was to do it, it is something I would take seriously. I would take six months to a year to try and practise before. Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that, it might be a thing where you could connect the two maybe with the seasons.”

Kane has previously said he would be interested in becoming a professional golfer. He loves to play and revealed he did not watch the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina because he went for a round of golf in New York.

“I watch golf and think: ‘I could be there.’ Then I go out and play and I am like: ‘There’s no way.’ I play off two. But I am a member at Wentworth and I shoot 10 over. Then I watch the pros, who played there last week, and 20 under wins it. I think I’ll stick to football.”

Sports.title: Kaptein fantastic strikes as Chelsea battle to WCL win over Austria Vienna
Sports.content:
Wieke Kaptein’s early goal gave Chelsea a winning start to their Champions League campaign proper against Austria Vienna, but it was a far from comfortable evening for them.

“Probably the performance is not the one we wanted to have,” Chelsea’s manager, Sonia Bompastor, said. “We could have controlled the game a little bit better in terms of scoring a second goal to kill the opposition’s hope, but sometimes you need to focus on what is most important and tonight that was to win and to take the three points from the game.”

A David v Goliath endeavour welcomed the visiting team at the Cherry Red Records Stadium and they rose to the challenge. The mammoth financial gulf between the two teams was highlighted in the buildup by the Austrian broadcaster ORF, which reported: “Chelsea Women’s personnel costs alone for the 2024-25 season, at a cool €17m, were higher than those of the entire Austria club (€14.9m) – including the men’s department, by far the largest item.” Meanwhile, Uefa noted that the manager, Stefan Kenesei, has a full-time job in state pensions insurance.

Ultimately, the gap in quality on the pitch looked far smaller than the finances suggested. Aware of that possibility, Bompastor did not take any risks and made only three changes to the team that secured a 2-0 win against Birmingham on Saturday, despite Arsenal up next on Sunday at Stamford Bridge.

It was a statement of intent from a team desperate to get their hands on the only club trophy to elude them and they were right to be cautious. As the Danish side HB Køge showed against Arsenal on Tuesday night, Champions League minnows can cause big problems.

“The physicality from those [lower-ranked] teams is good,” Bompastor said. “The players are able to match the intensity of the Champions League games from the beginning of the game until the end, as you could see tonight. I also think the coaches who are coaching those teams are good in terms of the tactical aspects. When they come into this game, they are really well prepared and they have a good game plan. So, nothing is easy.”

A moment of magic from the Dutch midfielder Kaptein gave the host side the breathing space of an early lead 11 minutes in. The 21-year-old was quickest to the loose ball after a slick sliding tackle from Katharina Schiechtl dispossessed Melvine Malard and she sent a rising strike in off the underside of the bar from 25 yards.

View image in fullscreen Sonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager, shouts instructions from the sidelines. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Austria Vienna responded rather than folding, threatening until the final whistle while supported vocally by the small block of travelling fans who appreciated the efforts of the underdogs. Set pieces and the forward Modesta Uka were their best outlets. Uka’s close control provided both an attacking threat and gave her teammates a reprieve from chasing.

The threat from Uka had been evident in the Austrian side’s qualifying campaign. The Kosovan scored in their 3-2 win against Hajduk Split and scored another two in their 5-0 victory against Farul Constanta in the second qualifying round, before grabbing a hat-trick in a 4-0 win against the Norwegian side Brann to overturn a 2-1 away defeat in the third round and secure their place in the league phase.

“She’s a great player and she deserves to play at this level, just as the whole team does,” Kenesei said. “She deserves to play in the Champions League and we’ve seen today how much potential there is.”

The longer the game went without Bompastor’s side building on their lead, the more confident the players in white became. Just shy of the 70th minute there was another tense moment for the host side, when pressure from the ever-bright Uka forced Veerle Buurman into an error. Katie McCabe looked to have clipped the Austria Vienna player, who seemed to have beaten her to the ball, but a pause after the ball went out of play did not lead to an intervention from the video assistant referee.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Frustrations boiled over a little at the close, when Almedina Sisic re‑entered the field without waiting a minute after receiving some treatment, with Bompastor forced to hold back her enraged assistant, Camille Abily, before giving the fourth official a piece of her mind.

Quick Guide Roundup: Lyon hit eight, Barça rally past Paris FC Show Marie-Antoinette Katoto [pictured] scored a hat-trick as Lyonnes thrashed Servette 8-0 in their opening league phase game of the Women’s Champions League. Katoto’s treble, Melchie Dumornay’s double and two own goals from the Swiss hosts saw Lyonnes go top of the early standings with a crushing display. The eight-times winners went ahead eight minutes in through Laia Balleste’s own goal before Katoto took control. The France striker bagged her first of the night in the 28th minute and added a second 12 minutes later. Dumornay’s chipped finish gave Lyon a four-goal advantage at the break and just two minutes after the restart, Katoto completed her treble from Lily Yohanes' backheeled pass. Dumornay added her second in the 54th minute and Laura Strik’s own goal piled more misery on Swiss champions Servette, who conceded again in the 89th minute when Ines Benyahia struck. In Wednesday's other early kick-off, Roma substitute Marta Pandini hit the post with a stoppage-time penalty as they were held to a 0-0 draw at OH Leuven. Ewa Pajor’s double helped holders Barcelona get off to a winning start as they came back from behind to beat Paris FC 5-2. Barça were handed an initial scare when Evelyne Viens put Paris in front only five minutes in, but Kerolin replied for the hosts with a tidy finish in the 18th minute. Clara Serrajordi put Barca ahead 10 minutes later, kicking off a destructive 15 minute-period for the hosts, which saw Pajor and Caroline Graham Hansen strike. Pajor struck again in the 70th minute, before the visitors pulled one back through Clara Mateo as Barça comfortably saw out the win. Lyonnes host Chelsea next Wednesday in their second league-phase game, while Barcelona visit Roma and Paris FC welcome Arsenal. PA Media Photograph: Pierre Albouy/REUTERS Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

In the end, it is a testament to the visiting team that they will leave London extremely disappointed not to have taken anything from a game that gave them opportunity after opportunity to do so.

“Yes, we’re proud,” Kenesei said. “We were brave as we’d planned, really, but to be honest I’m also disappointed that we didn’t get at least one point. We saw what you all saw today, that we performed at almost the same level as Chelsea.”

Chelsea can breathe easy, although Keira Walsh’s precautionary early withdrawal with a quad issue will be a concern, but they have a job to do to snuff out those chances before they face teams that will capitalise and punish them.

Sports.title: Netherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derby
Sports.content:
Before the latest instalment of a time-honoured international rivalry gearing up for two distinct new beginnings, Jürgen Klopp could not resist sprinkling a little of the old mischief. “The good thing is that we both have the exact same situation,” he said of Xavi Hernández, his counterpart when Germany visit the Netherlands on Thursday night. “We met on Monday and play on Thursday. And the coach knows the players from television. I actually know more of the Dutch players personally than Xavi does. Whether that’s an advantage, I don’t know, but it’s still a fact.”

In his public appearances Klopp has been on irrepressible form since taking the role in July. The task of whipping Germany back into shape has visibly and audibly topped up the energy levels that had drained by the time he departed Liverpool. Klopp, his wit sharp and appetite piqued, looks a far cry from the character who, to most trained eyes, was going through the motions upon his unveiling as Red Bull’s head of global soccer early last year.

Securing Klopp was a coup for the German football federation even if it came with a caveat, issued within seconds of his introduction to the media, that he would not be seen for dust if his family were hounded by the media. Xavi’s arrival in Amsterdam is no less fascinating even if, in the Dutch way, no bones were made by his employers about the fact Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot had been higher in their sights after Ronald Koeman’s departure. He is the Netherlands’ first foreign manager since Ernst Happel’s 10-month stint ended in 1978 but the fit is instinctively pleasing. Even if Guardiola was out of reach, they could land upon another product of the Johan Cruyff school that created modern-day Barcelona.

View image in fullscreen Xavi’s captain is Virgil van Dijk, who considered international retirement after the World Cup. Photograph: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP/Getty Images

If Xavi is to take the Netherlands, occasionally exciting but frequently unstable during a World Cup run that shuddered to a halt in the last 32, back to their roots it will require a measure of patience. The pool of players does not allow much else; the recall of Borussia Dortmund’s Joey Veerman, who has not played international football for more than two years, speaks of the need for a technically adept midfield fulcrum but otherwise Xavi has scant scope for surprises. Virgil van Dijk will continue as captain despite considering international retirement during the summer; the head coach’s options may feel more complete when Frenkie de Jong and Donyell Malen have returned from injury.

Xavi has resisted any temptation to engage in analysis of the Netherlands’ performance in the United States. “I don’t talk about the past,” is the standard line, ironically an easier one to roll out if the Nations League opener in Amsterdam brings a performance redolent of headier times. The revolution may have to be conducted with minimal effusive pronouncements from the coach. It is certainly a less dramatic shake-up than the one Klopp, acting like a man licensed to break a few moulds, has enacted before the next fortnight’s four-game baptism.

It raised eyebrows when Klopp named a squad of 44 players for the matches against the Netherlands, Serbia and, home and away, Greece. The expanded unit will be split into two: half will play on Thursday and in Germany’s next game, at home against the Greeks, and the remainder will be involved in the second two games. Only Finn Dahmen, the Augsburg goalkeeper, will be required across the set.

“I want to get to know as many players as possible,” Klopp said. “There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.”

View image in fullscreen The goalkeeper Finn Dahmen (centre) is the only player on call for all four Germany matches. Photograph: Federico Gambarini/DPA/AP

Club managers feeling squeamish at their players’ workloads during this expanded break will immediately have warmed to Klopp’s split selection. But the priority is to discover who best fits his vision for an intensely committed, front-footed, enthusiastic Nationalmannschaft that places round pegs, even unexpected ones, in round holes. Four players from Freiburg have made his sprawling selection; so has Felix Keidel from promoted Elversberg. Mika Baur of Celtic and the Hoffenheim winger Bambasé Conté were both stunned to receive first call-ups. The Brentford midfielder Vitaly Janelt joins his teammate Kevin Schade in the fray. Sixteen are uncapped.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Last weekend Klopp and his coaching staff convened at their headquarters in Herzogenaurach to watch as many of their charges’ domestic games as possible in one go. Freiburg’s Max Rosenfelder, one of the new brood, acknowledged the aura surrounding Klopp and described him as “a very, very special person”. Even if the mixed lineups prove to lack experience and cohesion, Klopp hopes his charges’ sheer thirst for the task will lift Germany from the doldrums of their most recent World Cup flop.

If he can unite 44 players, why not a whole country? Among Klopp’s many recent pronouncements was the timely intervention in favour of “positive patriotism” that followed an election victory by the anti‑immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party in Saxony‑Anhalt. If it is some time since Germany’s football team have been at their best, perhaps the same may be said for the nation too.

In the Dutch capital, two big‑name managers will take their first steps towards bringing the good times back. “It could be a bit wild, but I accept that, it just has to be lively,” Klopp said. That comes with something approaching a cast‑iron guarantee.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo vows to play on for Portugal and targets 1,000 career goals
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but confirmed he plans to play on for Portugal and hopes to reach 1,000 goals for club and country. Ronaldo, who is 21 goals shy of the milestone, accepted some critics are trying to “kill” him but is determined to carry on.

Ronaldo, who has won 233 caps for his country, captained Portugal in the summer at the World Cup, where they exited to Spain in the last 16. Asked if he considered walking away from international duty, he replied: “Yes, I did. Of course, I’m always thinking about my decisions, my future, the present also. I’m a thinker; you have to think. This is why you see me here now, it means I will continue.

“I had a conversation with our president [Pedro Proença], with our coach. I still believe that I’m able to help the national team to reach what they want. I think I can give the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football. There is a new young generation, but for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.

“Whenever they say they don’t want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go. When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave. The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … Just look at the numbers, I’m sure you can make some calculations, I’m still doing well. The day they don’t count on me, no problemo, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation.”

Jorge Jesus, the Portugal head coach who managed Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, said the 41-year-old would start in his first game in charge, against Wales in the Nations League on Thursday. Jesus, who has succeeded Roberto Martínez, also launched a passionate defence of Ronaldo, drawing applause from many in attendance at Portugal’s City of Football complex in Lisbon.

Quick Guide Bellamy remembers 'president' Ronaldo's arrival Show Craig Bellamy said Wales must enjoy facing “heavyweight” opposition in Portugal on Thursday and colourfully recalled being stuck at Lisbon airport because it was on lockdown to ensure Cristiano Ronaldo a “president-like” arrival. Bellamy (pictured) twice visited the city on pre-season camps with Burnley, where he worked as assistant to Vincent Kompany for two years. “He is beyond a superstar,” the Wales manager said of the Portugal captain, whom he shared a pitch with in the Premier League almost 18 years ago, when Ronaldo, who turns 42 in February, scored twice in a 2-0 win for Manchester United at home to West Ham. “There were rows of police cars everywhere,” Bellamy said of the moment he realised the airport was on lockdown. “We were like: ‘Something’s happened. We thought it was a security breach. We were stuck on the coach for about 10, 15 minutes. ‘When are we going to get off the coach?’ Suddenly this car turns up – I’ll be doing it a disservice but it was a Bentley or something like that – and parks in this parking slot, this guy walks out the front, goes to the boot, grabs this rucksack, and this other kid comes out the front, puts the rucksack on. Who is it? Ronaldo. “Even the police are like [trying to look at Ronaldo] but no one could bother him. It was the coolest walk I’ve ever watched. For a minute, we were on the coach just jaws dropped. ‘Everyone who is moaning? Shut up.’ We don’t mind. We’re watching this … it was like president stuff. How can you lock off a whole airport? I won’t even be able to get my computer through customs at Cardiff. What have I just seen?” Bellamy was effusive in his praise for Portugal’s all-time record goalscorer, who is closing on 1,000 goals for club and country. “Who gets 1,000 goals?” the 47-year-old said. “Seriously? It’s just silly, eh? I hope he gets it – but I hope he gets nothing on Thursday. We’re talking about one of the greatest players of all generations – his name will go down in history for hundreds and hundreds of years.” Ben Fisher Photograph: José Sena Goulão/LUSA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

“Cristiano is a symbol of Portugal and the national team,” said Jesus, sitting alongside Ronaldo at the Portugal federation’s campus. “If he will play the games, he is not entitled to that, it is up to the manager to decide.”

Ronaldo cut a relaxed figure on stage alongside Jesus. “For me the most important thing is I know what I am,” he said. “I know what I do to be here, I know what I have done to have the success that I have had. I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired … in 10 years.

“I’m happy with myself. It doesn’t matter if I play tomorrow, if I’m rested for the next game, for me the most important thing is that I feel good. The people around me, they trust in my work. Focus on the people who love Cristiano, not the people who criticise me, so I am a happy person.”

Asked directly about the criticism, Ronaldo triggered laughter from many in the room by replying: “I cannot be 100% honest, sometimes I have to be politically correct.” He added: “I do understand that some TV channels like to criticise me, they’ve tried to kill me – with a shotgun – but I can still move away from it. Anyway, I am used to it. I have been doing this for more than 20 years, I’m quite used to it. What I can control, I will. What I can’t, I won’t.”

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo attends a training session before the Nations League group stage match against Wales. Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/EPA

On Thursday Ronaldo will return to the Estadio José Alvalade, where he began his career with Sporting, before joining Manchester United in 2003. It is Portugal’s first game in Lisbon since beating the Republic of Ireland in a World Cup qualifier last October.

“It’s a special feeling because it was there where my beautiful history started,” Ronaldo said. “I’m very proud about that, to play for the national team after so many years, playing where I practically was opened to the world … It was a beautiful moment.

“It is always a pleasure to play for the national team, to wear the colours of Portugal. After so many years, it is [still always] like the first time. I will step on to the pitch with passion, emotion. I hope we can get off on the right foot. Because it’s at Sporting, it does feel a bit more special.

“It would be the cherry on the top of the cake to score my 1,000th goal with the national team. It would be the culmination of a beautiful story. I said I wanted to reach that target and I will reach that target. But I don’t have an obsession. If you are obsessed with something, you won’t get it … Just enjoy. Carpe diem, enjoy the day.”

Sports.title: Christian Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent after on-pitch collapse in June
Sports.content:
Christian Eriksen and the German side VfL Wolfsburg have agreed to terminate ⁠his contract by mutual consent, the club announced on Wednesday.

The 34-year-old collapsed during a Denmark friendly ⁠against Ukraine in June. Eriksen said in July he would ​return to his homeland to undergo a ‌rehabilitation programme. He previously suffered a cardiac arrest during Denmark’s opening Euro 2020 group match ⁠against Finland in Copenhagen in 2021.

The decision brings ⁠an early end ⁠to ​Eriksen’s contract, which was set to run until June 2027. The midfielder joined Wolfsburg as a free agent a year ago, making 34 appearances across all competitions. Eriksen scored three goals and provided 10 assists for the Wolves, but could not prevent their relegation from the Bundesliga.

“At the moment, it is important for me to ‌be close to my family in Denmark. I’m pleased that we were able to find a solution together,” Eriksen said in a statement. “My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows,” he added. “I know that the club is now ‌in good hands as it aims to make its way back to the Bundesliga, and I am convinced ​that a successful future lies ahead for VfL.”

The Wolfsburg ⁠managing director of sport, Dieter Hecking, said the second-tier club granted ​Eriksen’s request to ​cancel the agreement. His last appearance for the team came in May’s promotion/relegation playoff defeat by Paderborn.

“He has already ​experienced and achieved a great deal during his ​extraordinary career,” ‌Hecking said. “Despite his ​short time ​here, he has left a lasting impression on his teammates, our staff and the fans.”

Eriksen played for Ajax, Tottenham and Inter before his on-pitch collapse in 2021. He was fitted with an implantable cardioverter-­defibrillator (ICD) device, but had to leave Inter because Serie A rules prohibit playing with a pacemaker.

View image in fullscreen Denmark and Ukraine players gather around Christian Eriksen after his collapse in June. Photograph: Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix Foto/AP

After joining Brentford in 2022, Eriksen spent three years at Manchester United before joining Wolfsburg last summer. He said in June that his ICD device “did what it was designed to do” after he collapsed on the pitch for a second time.

“Receiving a shock from my ICD has had a major impact on both me and my family, but I want to reassure everyone that this was a different situation from what happened in 2021,” Eriksen posted on social media.

“I am feeling good, and my recovery has already started. I am incredibly grateful to the doctors who have cared for me and my heart over the years. Thanks to their expertise, my ICD did exactly what it was designed to do: protect me when I needed it.”

Sports.title: Manchester United report seventh straight annual loss and sell fans £125 grass clumps
Sports.content:
Manchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh ­successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019.

The financial results were released as it emerged United are raising revenue by selling small clumps of grass from the Old Trafford pitch to supporters. United relaid the playing surface for the first time in 14 years this summer, and an email to fans has offered them the chance to buy 7cm x 7cm clumps of turf for £125.

The £43m net loss for 2025-26 is a significant increase on the £33m for the previous 12 months, with compensation paid to the sacked manager Ruben Amorim a contributory factor along with the decision to increase the club’s borrowing facility by £93m to help fund the redevelopment of Old Trafford.

United’s continued losses come despite record revenue of £677.6m – up 1.7% on the previous 12 months – and the implementation of a major cost-cutting regime by Sir Jim Ratcliffe under which hundreds of staff have lost their jobs.

In discussing United’s results on an investor call, the chief executive, Omar Berrada, said the club’s summer transfer window, during which they spent £155m on three players, had been planned with “financial sustainability in mind” in an indication that the budget will continue to be tight for newthe manager, Michael Carrick.

That is underlined by the fact that United’s wage bill dropped to £301m, down 3.6% on the previous year, more than £100m lower than Manchester City’s.

While United reported operating profits of £22.6m for the 12 months to 30 June 2026 the increase in revenue was more than offset by the cost of financing the club. Net finance costs more than tripled to £69.2m from £21.2m in the previous year, partly owing to foreign-exchange ­movements, and the club refinanced several loans, increasing their net debt from £471.9m to £577.6m.

United sources have said the refinancing provided funding for the £63.5m purchase of a plot of land next to Old Trafford required to build their proposed new 100,000 capacity stadium, the first major investment in a complex project that could end up costing more than £2bn.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Berrada said the results demonstrated “the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football” and said: “This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength. While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.”

United are confident their financial outlook will improve over the next 12 months owing to the club’s return to the Champions League and the start of increased sponsorship deals with the training-kit partner Betway and shirt-sleeve partner SumUp, which will bring in £20m and £22m a year respectively. The club is forecasting revenue of between £740m and £760m for 2026-27.

Sports.title: Ireland manager gets prime minister Martin’s backing in row with Israel over ‘genocide’
Sports.content:
Ireland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, backed his country’s football manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, after Israel’s football federation accused Hallgrimsson of “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy” over comments about the war in Gaza.

“I think those are unacceptable remarks; they should be withdrawn,” Martin told reporters in New York, where he is attending the UN general assembly. “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.”

Hallgrímsson sparked the row after saying before two Nations League fixtures against Israel: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel.”

Quick Guide How do I 

Martin said Hallgrímsson’s comments reflected concerns about the scale of death and destruction in Gaza, also citing remarks by the UN secretary general, António Guterres.

On Wednesday Hallgrímsson, preparing for Thursday’s game in Kosovo, expressed gratitude for Martin’s backing. “What I said at the last press meeting has taken the attention away from maybe what’s most important; we are playing an important game against Kosovo,” Hallgrimsson said.

“Maybe, from a ‌leadership point of view, not clever for me to take the attention like this. But to answer the question, we are thankful for all the support we get. It’s a tricky time for ​us.“

The dispute comes amid mounting controversy in the Republic over the fixtures, scheduled for 27 September and 4 October. More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter calling on the national team to boycott the matches, and protesters gathered outside the team’s Dublin hotel on Monday. Further protests are planned around the country in the run-up to the games.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) passed a motion last November requesting that European football governing body, Uefa, suspend Israel from international competition. The FAI has said it has little choice but to fulfil the fixtures or risk sporting and financial sanctions.

Ireland’s designated home match on 4 October was moved from Dublin’s Aviva Stadium to Backa Topola, Serbia, after concerns over disruption and security. The 27 September match, officially Israel’s home fixture, will also be played at a neutral venue, in Debrecen, Hungary.

Israel strongly rejects allegations that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. Hamas led the deadliest attack against Israel on 7 October 2023 when militants killed 1,221 people and dragged into Gaza 251 hostages, 44 of them already dead, according to Israeli official figures.

Israel launched a massive retaliatory offensive that has displaced virtually the entire population at least once and has killed 73,919 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable.

Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy for Palestinians often linked to the country’s history of British rule. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway and has repeatedly criticised Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza.

Sports.title: Man United reveal how much money they've SAVED with sacked boss Ruben Amorim taking over at AC Milan - as they try to rake in more cash by selling bits of the pitch for £125!
Sports.content:
Manchester United saved £8.5million when Ruben Amorim took over as head coach of AC Milan, the club’s latest financial results have revealed.

United reported in May that the total compensation due to Amorim and his staff could rise to a maximum of £16.7m. But his appointment as Milan boss in June meant United have paid £8.2m, less than half that figure.

Wednesday’s results also revealed that the cost of financing United’s debt has now rocketed past the £1billion mark since the Glazer family’s leveraged takeover.

The club’s annual figures show that United paid £69.6m – an increase of £48.4m or 228.3 per cent from the previous year – in interest and other finance costs.

The overall debt itself still stands at more than £1bn despite the cost-cutting measures imposed by minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos which contributed to United turning a £18.4m operating loss into a £22.6m over the last year.

It consists of £577.6m of historic debt from the Glazer takeover in 2005, £111.4m owing on the club’s revolving credit facility and outstanding transfer fees.

Ineos co-owned Man United have announced record revenue of £677.6m for the 2025-26 season

The Americans’ £790m buyout has been the biggest factor in United bleeding over £1bn in the last two decades, and that infuriates fans who are fiercely opposed to the Glazers’ ownership and increasingly disillusioned with the Ratcliffe regime.

After spending just £163m in the transfer market this summer – substantially less than many of their rivals – United are 12th in the Premier League table after one win in five games.

The club are also at odds with large sections of the fanbase over their attempts to increase revenue and, more recently, crack down on ticket touts.

It has also emerged that emails have been sent out to members and season ticket holders offering them the chance to buy miniature squares of the Old Trafford turf – which was re-laid in the summer for the first time in 14 years – for £125.

United laid a new playing surface at the 'Theatre of Dreams' for the first time in 14 years over the summer, and the old pitch has been cut into 7cm x 7cm squares.

Those squares have been packaged in acrylic cubes and are being sent out to supporters who want them in a smart black casing.

The United website reads: 'Take home a piece of Old Trafford with this official turf cube, perfect for fans who want a keepsake from one of the most famous pitches in the world.

'Carefully preserved, this piece of turf makes a priceless memento of iconic games played at home and keeps the memories of match days alive.

The sacking of Ruben Amorim in January cost the club £8.5million in compensation

'Perfect for gifting to passionate Reds, this turf cube makes a great addition to desks or can be displayed in a cabinet with other Manchester United collectibles.'

The club have described the purchasable turf as a 'one-of-a-kind collector’s item' to club members and season-ticket holders in an email offering them 'exclusive' early access.

Despite the huge debt and costs of servicing it, United are still committed to building a new £2bn stadium. The latest financial results revealed that the club spent £63.5m in June on a 25-acre triangle of land located 350 metres away from Old Trafford.

While United were able to announce record revenues of £677.6m despite not playing in Europe last season, they reported an overall net loss of £43m – up from £33m last year – which sources say demonstrates the importance of maintaining financial discipline.

Chief executive Omar Berrada said: ‘We are pleased to have secured record revenues which demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football.

United are selling small cubes of last season's Old Trafford turf to fans for £125

‘This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength.

‘While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.’

Commercial revenue for the year was down £16m and sponsorship revenue by £27.9m, partly due to United having no training kit sponsor following the end of their partnership with Tezos.

The club have since signed a record £20m-a-year deal with Betway, as well as replacing sleeve sponsor DXC Technology with SumUp.

Retail & merchandising revenue for the year was up £11.9m, and broadcasting revenue by £33.9m due to United finishing third in the Premier League after Michael Carrick replaced Amorim in January.

Matchday revenue was down £6.8m due to the club’s shortest season since the First World War. Not playing in Europe and going out of both domestic cup competitions at the first hurdle meant that United played just 40 games.

Sports.title: 'We want to leave a legacy, to dominate English rugby': Inside Northampton's ambitious plan for back-to-back PREM titles - the curryhouse heart-to-heart, the former doorman solving their achilles heel and how they'll transform Franklin's Gardens
Sports.content:
'We want to leave a legacy, to dominate English rugby': Inside Northampton's ambitious plan for back-to-back PREM titles - the curryhouse heart-to-heart, the former doorman solving their achilles heel and how they'll transform Franklin's Gardens

In the heat of the summer holidays, Henry Pollock sprang a surprise on a couple of his team-mates in Mallorca.

Tommy Freeman and Fin Smith were visiting the Balearic Islands with their girlfriends and Pollock checked into a nearby hotel.

‘We decided to do a boat day on the Saturday,’ Freeman tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Most rental boats are small and slow but Pollock was like, “I’ve got a boat licence, which means we can get a quicker one”. We rocked up and got this huge RIB.

‘As soon as we got out the harbour, Pollock was like, “Bang! Gone”. We were going very fast and it was pretty scary. It was a good laugh. My hat fell off about three times and we had to loop back around for it.’

Pollock took the group around the south of the island, stopping off at a beachside restaurant for lunch.

It was around the time that Eddie Hearn, Pollock’s promotional agent, had made headlines by claiming the 21-year-old’s annual salary should multiply from £150,000 to £1million.

Northampton are ready for another strong season in the PREM, boosted by news that Henry Pollock has agreed a new contract

Pollock (left), Tommy Freeman and Fin Smith (right) soaked up the sun together in Mallorca - though had a distressing boat ride thanks to the England flanker

‘He got an earful about all the Hearn stuff,’ says Freeman. ‘Obviously there's a plan behind it all, but there's always a bit of stick, isn't there? It’s all good stuff. I might get my agent to come out and say I need a million, too!’

Pollock settled on a contract worth around £450,000. Despite the headlines, Hearn is yet to visit Franklin’s Gardens or the Northampton hierarchy.

Pollock discussed his ambitions with director of rugby Phil Dowson during the off-season – but the bulk of the negotiations were between recruitment boss Paul Shields and Stellar Rugby.

Locking down the youngster’s future was just one piece of Northampton’s business plan for the new season.

The club sold out 90 per cent of their PREM fixtures last season, thanks largely to the team’s effective and entertaining style of play.

Work is going on behind the scenes to achieve long-term sustainability. It is not feasible to expand the capacity of Franklin’s Gardens but the Supporter Village has been redeveloped over the summer, with enhanced facilities that can double up for corporate events.

There are also plans to move the team’s performance facilities out of the South Stand to create more space for commercial activity.

Coupled with a long-term vision to build a hotel on site, the club’s executives have been looking at matters far beyond Pollock’s contract extension.

The coaching team, Dowson and Sam Vesty, are tied into long-term deals and the RFU would have to pay a hefty fee to buy them out for potential roles with England.

‘Fundamentally, we are having a great time at Northampton,’ says director of rugby Phil Dowson

'We want to build a legacy,' says Alex Mitchell. 'We know we've got the squad and the coaches and the environment to do it. So why not go out and try to dominate?’

‘Fundamentally, we are having a great time at Northampton,’ says Dowson, when asked about the prospect of coaching England in the future.

‘We talk about the club flourishing, selling out, the village being renovated, the Saints Foundation having an impact in the community. From a personal point of view, at some point we would like to coach in international rugby because it is different.

‘Rugby’s different from the NFL. Bill Belichick stays at the New England Patriots because he's got nowhere else. There's no timeline on that.

'It's not just England. There's the opportunity to go and do something different, to test ourselves, either as a team or individually, to put ourselves under different pressure and to have new experiences.’

The immediate goal, however, is to secure back-to-back titles. In-house sports psychologist Oli Dixon has worked closely with the players to guard against complacency.

The club enjoyed a pre-season trip to Sri Lanka, where the new playing group bonded in unfamiliar surroundings. ‘All of the players went out for dinner together at a restaurant in Colombo,’ says scrum-half Alex Mitchell. ‘It was mainly curries. So spicy. Took my head off!

‘Fraser Dingwall started a conversation about how few teams have been able to go back-to-back. Saracens did it. We spoke about Wasps doing it with Lawrence Dallaglio and those guys. You look back on those teams and think, “What a team they were”. It’s a tough thing to do.

‘It would be quite cool if in 10 or 15 years, people look back at Northampton in the mid-2020s and say, "Oh, what a team they were”. That’s what we want to get after. We want to build a legacy. We know we've got the squad and the coaches and the environment to do it. So why not go out and try to go back-to-back and actually dominate?’

The club are already one of the finest attacking forces in Europe, often described as the All Blacks of English club rugby.

But they were presented with a humbling statistic over the summer: discipline. It is something they are looking to improve when they kick-off their campaign against Newcastle.

With the likes of Smith in their ranks, Northampton have become renowned as one of the finest attacking sides in Europe

Scrum-half Mitchell admits Saints' discipline is one of the few areas where they can improve

‘We were 10th for discipline,’ reveals Mitchell. ‘Penalties against us. We were 10th by quite some way, so that's one thing we want to try and rectify this year. We know we need to get better at not giving teams easy ins into our 22. Offsides, chat back, silly pens.’

The coaching team remains stable, although Jim Henry has moved into the role of defence coach, following Lee Radford’s departure to Scotland. Henry previously coached at Loughborough University, where he worked as a part-time doorman to supplement his sporting career.

‘Fundamentally, it's not a revolution,’ said Dowson. ‘It's an evolution of what Lee was doing. Lee came in and set a stall out in terms of our system and he set a stall out with an emotional point of view on what it means to defend. Jim's carried on both of those things. We just want to create a bit more pressure in defence. We want to create more turnovers.

‘We're probably defending for too long in phase counts. We want to get the ball back a little bit quicker. We want to have a bit more of an effort around post-tackle. You look at South Africa play, you look at Bordeaux, you look at Toulouse. Those two men on the tackle are making it tough to win fast ball and I think that's something that we can get better at.’

If Northampton can find another level after their title-winning campaign, they will prove difficult to stop.

Sports.title: Lewis Moody 'at peace' with MND diagnosis as former rugby star reveals hope his two sons will follow him into professional sport
Sports.content:
Lewis Moody said he would ‘absolutely love it’ if his two sons followed him into professional sport after eldest Dylan joined Arsenal ace Max Dowman in an England junior football squad.

Moody was a 2003 Rugby World Cup winner with England, earning 71 caps for his country. He also represented the British & Irish Lions and lifted 10 major trophies with Leicester Tigers.

Last year, the ex-flanker’s world was turned upside down when he became the latest former rugby star to receive a motor neurone disease (MND) diagnosis. MND affects the body’s nervous system. There is currently no cure.

Moody is not the only one with sporting talent in his family. Dylan, 18, is a goalkeeper for Championship side Southampton and alongside Dowman, is a current member of England’s Under-19 squad. Moody’s youngest son Ethan, 16, is a promising rugby player who is in Bath’s age grade set-up.

‘I'd absolutely love it,’ Moody said, when asked if he’d welcome Dylan representing England at senior level in football. ‘He’s got his professional contract and he’s doing really well with England.

‘He's got a lot of work to do until he gets to that stage, but he's got a great attitude and if he sticks at it and he really wants it, I'm sure he'll get where he wants.

Lewis Moody said he would ‘absolutely love it’ if his two sons followed him into professional sport

Dylan Moody, 18, is part of England's under-19 squad while his younger brother Ethan is a promising rugby player and is in Bath's age grade set-up

In a new documentary telling his MND journey, Moody has a series of tough, emotional conversations with his sons about his terminal diagnosis and the future

‘I’d like to think I’m supportive. I remember talking to Dylan and I asked him what he wanted to do. He said: “I want to play for England.” I had that classic adult response and went: “Is that a bit lofty?” But I apologised because it’s not my place to diminish his excitement. If that's his goal, I'm going to be there to support if he needs advice. I love the fact the kids are passionate about something they enjoy. Ethan is in the throes of the academy set-up with Bath. I’m excited.’

In a new documentary telling his MND journey, Moody has a series of tough, emotional conversations with both Dylan and Ethan about his terminal diagnosis and the future.

He also emphasises the need for further fundraising and awareness to support the bid to one day find a cure for MND.

Moody has taken part in a drug trial – funded by the My Name’5 Doddie Foundation, which was set-up by former Scotland and Lions star Doddie Weir who passed away due to MND in 2022. ‘I’m at peace with my diagnosis,’ Moody said. ‘I was at peace almost immediately.

‘There’s nothing I can do to change my circumstances, other than to use my energy to raise awareness so that the people who are fighting this disease have the resources they need so we can get to the outcome we all want. It isn’t far off.’

Lewis Moody vs MND was co-produced between 3 Rock Productions and TNT Sports. It premieres on TNT Sports 1 and HBO Max on Friday 25th September at 10pm

Sports.title: 'I'm not doing it for the money': Wayne Rooney reveals why he is pursuing punditry career after impressive World Cup BBC stint - and admits he may never return to the dugout again
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney has revealed he turned to punditry to give him a purpose following his playing career, as he admitted he may never manage again. The former Manchester United and England spoke of his move into punditry on the new Disney+ documentary The Real Rooneys. Rooney is now an established Match of the Day pundit and impressed with his forthright views during the summer's World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico. The 40-year-old joined the iconic football show at the start of the 2025-26 Premier League season, reportedly signing a £800,000-a-year deal. Rooney had turned to punditry after unsuccessful spells in management, with his final two roles being short-term spells in charge of Birmingham City and Plymouth Argyle. When showing off trophies won during his career – which had seen him score 253 goals for Man United and 53 for England – Rooney was asked why he had not retired outright. Wayne Rooney has admitted he turned to punditry to give him a purpose following his glittering playing career Rooney revealed the move into punditry as to give him a purpose after his playing career. 'I'm not doing it for money I'm doing it for a purpose rather than just being at the house all day,' Rooney said. 'There's a possibility I'll never manage again so moving forward. 'I need a role on The Masked Singer, but I'd get hammered'. Rooney's last job in management came at Plymouth, where he was sacked with the club at the foot of the Championship table in December. His dismissal followed a dismal run which had seen the Pilgrims win just four matches and suffer 13 defeats in 23 Championship games. When asked by his wife Coleen whether he was sad about about losing the Plymouth job, Rooney responded: 'No I'm a realist I think you know as a player when your career is going to end and you can prepare for that. 'So the next stage in management for instance you don't know whether you'll be there a year, two years, 10 years or 3 months. 'Your not prepared when you lose the job. Rooney acknowledged he may never manage again after several unsuccessful stints in the dugout 'I'm enjoying Match of the Day and it's time to learn and get better at what I'm doing.' Rooney has since been one of the BBC's leading pundits during the World Cup, where he has earned praise for his development in his new career. While typically giving his verdict on matches, Rooney entertained viewers by branding FIFA's World Cup final half-time show as 'c***', adding that he thought 'the best part was when it finished.’
