World.title: Is it unprofessional to bring iced coffee to a job interview? Gen Z is being dragged for it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The list of acceptable items to bring to a job interview might include, but isn't limited to: your CV, your portfolio, your winning personality, your best foot forward.

But what about your iced latte? That's the debate currently raging online after a job recruiter recently called out Gen Z for showing up to corporate interviews "with iced coffee, iced latte, in hand" in a now-viral TikTok video.

In the video, which has been viewed more than 420,000 times since it was posted last week, U.S. recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen says she believes showing up with an iced beverage comes across as too casual, "like it's just a stop in your list of errands for the day."

"It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks and now you’re stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing," Wehniainen said.

"Don't just waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand."

The video has divided generations and the internet, with some agreeing that bringing a beverage to a job interview is unprofessional and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.

"It's not about the f--king coffee,"someone posted on Threads. "It's about reading the room, being able to be part of a community and society, compromise, and tolerate discomfort," they added.

It's about basic etiquette, someone else commented on Reddit.

"Arriving at an interview with a beverage for only yourself would be just as impolite as if the interviewer were drinking coffee but didn’t offer you a beverage," they added.

Conversely, how a company reacts to a beverage is a litmus test, others argued.

"In 2026 being YOU is a competitive advantage, and any environment that tries to micromanage something as small as whether or not you brought coffee to an interview is NOT a place you will thrive," marketing professional Zoë Hartsfield wrote on LinkedIn Tuesday.

"N o wonder 58 per cent of Gen Z has a side hustle or runs their own company."

WATCH | How did the Gen Z job market get so bleak?: How did the Gen Z job market get so bleak? | Duration closed caption 5:25 Gen Z graduates between the ages of 15 and 24 are facing the highest unemployment rate the country has seen in decades, apart from the pandemic. CBC's Paula Duhatschek breaks down what’s behind the surge and what it could mean for a whole generation of Canadians.

Generational divide?

The iced coffee debacle isn't the first time Gen Z has been dragged over etiquette and other so-called soft skills. Last year, the term "Gen Z stare" entered the lexicon, which describes the "blank, expressionless" look that the younger generation gives to older generations, particularly in customer service settings, according to Know Your Meme.

And like the "Gen Z stare," some argue the iced coffee debate touches on deeper issues, like how young adults and teens are coping with the lingering effects of COVID-19 lockdowns while facing the worst youth unemployment rate in decades and having to navigate AI's impact on entry-level jobs and recruitment processes.

Gen Z largely came of age during the isolation of the pandemic, tend to prefer digital communication and report higher rates of anxiety than previous generations. Recent surveys have shown that some managers are hesitant to hire younger workers, citing a lack of soft skills like communication and collaboration.

But is the younger generation really bringing iced coffees into job interviews?

Allison Venditti, a Toronto-based human resources expert, says she can count on one hand the number of times it has happened to her, and that's no different to how often it happened 15 years ago.

"We just have TikTok to hear about it now," Venditti, founder of Moms at Work, an advocacy group for working mothers, told CBC News.

"Most folks, Gen Z or otherwise, take the recruitment process seriously and come well prepared and do a great job."

WATCH | Is the Gen Z stare for real?: Is the ‘Gen Z stare’ for real? | Duration 1:55 According to a recent debate on TikTok, Gen Z has been blankly gazing into the middle distance instead of speaking, especially when interacting with older generations. CBC’s Ashley Fraser breaks down how real this phenomenon is and what could be behind it.

Is there a middle ground?

That said, Venditti says she does have some iced coffee horror stories, like the time someone brought one in to an interview and accidentally dumped it all over themselves and their papers.

"We spent about 15 to 30 minutes cleaning it up. We also had to find a new room to do interviews as it was sticky. It was awful for all involved," she said.

But maybe there's a middle ground, others argued.

If you do bring an iced beverage into a job interview, don't swirl it around, slurp, put it on the interviewer's desk or hold it in your right hand, since that will make it wet when you shake hands, says Benjamin Chipman, a branding and marketing specialist based in New York City.

"You maybe have one sip that you get to take throughout the entire interview, because that is your opportunity to think a little bit when they are asking you a question," he said in a video posted to LinkedIn.

Which is better than responding with a Gen Z stare, some might argue.

Regardless, the short answer to whether bringing an iced coffee into an interview is unprofessional, is "yes," Venditti says.

"Would you bring a sandwich? No? Then don't bring that, either."

World.title: Trump greets Xi on tarmac as Chinese leader arrives for state visit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday, where he was met with a rare planeside greeting from U.S. President Donald Trump after their top officials agreed to extend a trade truce until January.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the extension of the truce — under which the countries agreed to scale back tariffs and refrain from imposing new trade restrictions — during a Fox News Channel interview as Trump welcomed Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington.

"I don't know whether a bigger deal can be done. I don't know whether we will just roll the current deal," Bessent said, noting the extension to Jan. 10 could give the leaders more time to talk about the issues at upcoming meetings in China in November and Florida in December.

Trade has been one of the biggest flashpoints between the two superpowers, along with artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. But much of Xi's three-day visit is expected to be far more about pomp than substance, starting with Trump's decision to greet Xi as he landed, rather than waiting for him to drive up to the White House.

Red carpet rolled out

A 30-metre-long red carpet was unfurled at the bottom of the staircase placed at the door of Xi's plane. A 21-person honour guard was arrayed on the sides of the carpet and Trump and his wife Melania Trump stood near a staircase on the side of the plane, where they greeted Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan with handshakes.

A red carpet is seen being rolled out at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Wednesday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

The welcome ceremony also included a flyover by two B-1 bombers, platoons from each military service, and a presentation of the flags and anthems of both countries.

Trump and his wife spoke to their counterparts, but their words could not be heard. Trump, who wore gloves and an overcoat though it was a relatively warm 17 C outside, removed one of his gloves to shake hands with Xi. At one point, he slapped Xi on the back and said something to him that was inaudible.

"I think they appreciate it, tremendous people," Trump said to reporters after he returned to the White House on Wednesday evening.

In a statement marking his arrival in the U.S., China's leader wrote that his country and the U.S. "should be partners, not rivals. Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand and the two countries can contribute to each other's success, thereby benefiting the wider world."

Senator criticizes 'lavish welcome'

Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend, all while giving him a pass on many issues.

WATCH | China, the U.S. and concerns about AI: Why U.S. and China may have to co-operate on AI guardrails | Duration closed caption 2:42 Chinese and U.S. economic officials have begun talks ahead of a meeting between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping, where AI safety is expected to be a top issue.

Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, chair of the Senate armed services committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." Wicker said during a speech Tuesday in the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader "based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party."

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. and China must interact at the highest levels because the countries are "the two largest economies in the world" and "probably the two most powerful militaries in the world."

Danny Russel, a former U.S. diplomat under President Barack Obama's administration, said the airport pomp delivered a propaganda win for Beijing.

"Such extreme deference is valuable evidence that China's leader is now held in extraordinarily high esteem by the President of the United States. Beijing uses this at home and internationally to show China's-and Xi's-growing stature," said Russel, now at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

WATCH | Xi arrives in U.S.: What to expect from Xi Jinping's meetings with Trump | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 4:17 Chinese President Xi Jinping was welcomed with a rare planeside greeting from U.S. President Donald Trump upon his arrival in Washington Wednesday. Jinping's state visit comes when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan.

China had wanted a longer extension of the trade truce, which had been set to expire on Nov. 10.

"It underscores that the United States is still concerned about China's full implementation of its commitments under the truce, particularly with respect to critical mineral exports and agricultural purchases," said Wendy Cutler, a former U.S. trade negotiator and now senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

The tight timeframe gives the U.S. a chance to test whether China will deliver on unmet promises to buy U.S. farm goods, said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

"This is less about buying two months of calm than making China earn the next extension," he said.

Trump has not yet commented on the extension. The two leaders are expected to talk about issues of substance more on Thursday, after an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Later, they will exchange toasts at a black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk.

Match of pageantry for Trump

Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new "work-of-art" helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not.

"I wish we had it for tomorrow night," Trump said again Wednesday. "We have a packed house tomorrow night for President Xi."

Trump on Wednesday was looking to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. While Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump, a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing.

A plane carrying Xi and wife Peng is seen taxiing at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Wednesday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

A military honour guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present.

Melania Trump said earlier Wednesday that her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrived in the Washington region because "they have a great relationship."

"He's coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect," she said of Xi and his wife during an interview on Fox News Channel's Fox & Friends.

The long red carpet recalled a similar extra-long one the U.S. laid out for Russian President Vladimir Putin when he touched down at a U.S. air force base in Alaska last summer for a summit aimed at trying to find an end to Russia's war in Ukraine.

On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries.

World.title: Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Southwestern Mexico braced for coastal flooding and mudslides Wednesday after Polo, a powerful Pacific cyclone, became a major hurricane. Forecasters also warned that Hawaii could face another onslaught of harsh weather later in the week.

Hurricane Polo, an "extremely dangerous" storm, is expected to skirt Mexico's Guerrero state, submerging coastal areas with 10 to 15 centimetres of rain through Thursday, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami. Guerrero has been repeatedly pummelled by hurricanes in recent years.

Polo, which was swirling a few hundred kilometres off the coast Wednesday afternoon, was not expected to make landfall, meteorologists and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said. Rain and strong winds had already started to pummel the coast, with waves crashing onto the normally pristine beaches.

Tropical storm conditions including torrential rain and extraordinary wind were also expected along the Pacific coast of Michoacan and Colima states through Thursday.

I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before | Duration 3:17 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a 'super' El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this 'super' El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

At its peak, Polo was a Category 5 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 290 km/h. It was a Category 4 by Wednesday afternoon, but still packing sustained winds of up to 230 km/h.

"Fluctuations in intensity are expected, but Polo is expected to remain a very powerful major hurricane during the next few days," the hurricane centre said.

LISTEN | Experts discuss what could transpire in months ahead: What on Earth? 25:02 Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?

Concepción López Villegas was busily bolstering her seaside restaurant in Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán, against the expected onslaught of rain.

Strong waves were already hitting some beaches and López Villegas said she feared the storm could destroy the small business she worked decades to build.

"We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed."

The hurricane centre warned that Polo's deluge could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, in particular in Guerrero.

The region most under threat from the hurricane is rural and mountainous, scattered with a few small tourist towns and ports. Much of the area is marked by poverty and residents routinely complain authorities abandon them to fend for themselves during natural disasters.

Mexico's government has called for evacuations in some areas and set up shelters for those affected. Thousands of military and Red Cross personnel have been deployed to the region as a preventative measure.

A partially submerged boat is seen in Acapulco Bay as strong waves and winds caused by Hurricane Polo were evident in Acapulco, Mexico, on Tuesday. (Francisco Robles/AFB/Getty Images)

Phil Klotzbach, research scientist in the department of atmospheric science at Colorado State University, attributed Polo's rapid intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, which has fuelled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods elsewhere.

In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said.

"There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said.

Mexican National Guard members on Tuesday warned beachgoers and tourists in Acapulco, Mexico, of the potential dangerous effects from Polo. (Javier Verdin/Reuters)

Separate hurricane could hit Hawaii

A tropical depression about 845 kilometres south-southeast of Hawaii's capital, Honolulu, could be a tropical storm by the end of the day and a hurricane by Thursday.

The hurricane centre advised the island chain to monitor the system, which was projected to drop 38 to 51 centimetres of rain on Big Island, raising the possibility of flooding and mudslides.

The centre of the cyclone was expected to close in on the islands by Friday or Saturday.

While wind and rain were mainly expected on Maui and Big Island, Kauai's electric co-operative urged residents to prepare for "the possibility of prolonged power outages," and to store non-perishable food and potable water.

Over 100 Kauai households remain without power from Hurricane Lowell, which passed west of the island on Sept. 7.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's primary utility, said crews would return to at-risk areas to help residents prepare for the coming storm.
