World.title: PM Péter Magyar accuses prosecutors of ‘protecting mobsters’ in escalating immunity row
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has accused the Prosecutor General’s Office of protecting alleged criminals after prosecutors publicly rejected his criticism of their work. The escalating dispute follows a decision to seek the suspension of the parliamentary immunity of Magyar and two opposition MPs, with the prime minister questioning why the three cases were announced together.

The confrontation continued late on Tuesday, when Magyar responded to a statement from the Prosecutor General’s Office in a comment on Telex’s Facebook page.

“Was this written by some comedian? When you’re protecting mobsters, you’re not so sensitive, you little rascals. The sun will rise soon, and you won’t be able to carry on your shady dealings in the dark,” the prime minister wrote.

Magyar’s remarks came after prosecutors rejected his accusations against the organisation and its staff, insisting that their decisions were based solely on the law and professional considerations.

Péter Magyar questions the prosecution service’s impartiality

The prime minister continued his criticism on Wednesday morning in a separate Facebook post, questioning the prosecution service’s claim that legality and impartiality were its only guiding principles.

“Really? What about the gold convoy case, the MNB foundations, the Rogán-linked bailiff mafia and the alteration of investigation documents? Are you familiar with the term aiding and abetting?” Magyar wrote.

His remarks referred to several investigations and alleged corruption cases involving figures or institutions associated with the previous Orbán administration.

Prosecutor General’s Office rejects the accusations

According to MTI, The Prosecutor General’s Office issued a statement late on Tuesday in response to Magyar’s earlier video message, rejecting his criticism of the organisation and its employees.

“As a participant in the administration of justice, the prosecution service always strives for lawful and proper cooperation with the executive branch. However, this does not mean that it will remain silent in the face of statements that seriously criticise the organisation or its staff,” the statement said.

Prosecutors welcomed Magyar’s stated willingness to facilitate the smooth conduct of criminal proceedings. However, they stressed that legality, impartiality and equality before the law were the only standards governing their constitutional duties.

According to the statement, requests to suspend MPs’ parliamentary immunity are prepared on a strictly legal and professional basis, independently of any political or other considerations.

The office also acknowledged that prosecutors were not infallible but maintained that their decisions were guided by the law and their conscience, regardless of the identity of the suspected offender or victim.

“The Prosecutor General’s Office rejects statements questioning this on behalf of all prosecutors,” the statement concluded.

Related: Hungarian immunity rights: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Péter Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

What sparked the dispute over parliamentary immunity?

The confrontation began after the Prosecutor General’s Office requested the suspension of the parliamentary immunity of three politicians: Prime Minister Péter Magyar, Fidesz MP Balázs Hankó and Christian Democrat MP Miklós Seszták.

Magyar’s case relates to a 2024 incident in which he allegedly threw another man’s mobile phone into the Danube following a confrontation at a party. The other two requests concern separate investigations involving alleged financial misconduct.

In a video posted on Facebook on Tuesday evening, Magyar called on the Hungarian Parliament to suspend his immunity without delay. However, he criticised the prosecution service for announcing the three requests together.

The prime minister described the move as the “last pathetic attempt” by what he called the “Polt-era prosecution service” to downplay the change of government.

He accused prosecutors of attempting to equate alleged corruption involving tens or hundreds of billions of forints under the former Orbán administration with what he described as a repeatedly failed political character assassination attempt against him, launched in 2024.

The Prosecutor General’s Office has rejected the suggestion that political considerations influence its decisions.

World.title: Kosovo Court Orders MPs to Elect President by October 6
World.content:
A Kosovo parliament session, September 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Constitutional Court on Wednesday ordered MPs to elect a new head of state by October 6 to avoid new snap elections – which would be the fourth parliamentary polls in two years.

The order comes ten days after the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, filed a complaint, alleging that parliament had exceeded the deadline for its inauguration.

“The 60-day deadline for the election of a President started on August 8 and will expire on October 6,” the court said.

The court rejected the PDK’s request to halt the work of parliament in the meantime and declare the vote on a new government unlawful. It declared parliament already inaugurated and ordered MPs to elect the fifth and final deputy speaker “as soon as possible”.

On September 14, the PDK complained to the court that the inauguration of parliament a day before had violated the rules, while one day later it asked the court to assess whether the parliamentary vote that re-elected Albin Kurti as Prime Minister was valid.

The PDK claims Kurti’s ruling Vetevendosje party violated the 30-day deadline to inaugurate parliament and that the assembly cannot be considered inaugurated until all five deputy speakers are elected.

Prior to this submission, the PDK withdrew its candidate for the post of deputy speaker, while four others were elected. The court has now ruled that parliament must elect the PDK candidate.

Kurti was re-elected Prime Minister by MPs at a session boycotted by the opposition parties. A narrow majority of 62 MPs out of 120 voted for Kurti’s new cabinet. Eight MPs from the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista voted against.

If parliament fails to elect a new President by October 6, new elections will be called within 45 days.

In late August, Vetevendosje’s Kurti and the head of the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, Lumir Abdixhiku, agreed on Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, for the President’s post.

But Sejdiu withdrew from the race on September 14, following disagreements within the LDK parliamentary group over his candidacy.

For a vote electing the President to be valid, at least 80 out of 120 MPs must be present in the chamber. If the first two rounds of voting fail, the third round requires only a simple majority of MPs to elect the President – but at least 80 of them still need to present in the chamber.

Kosovo has been without a President since April 4, when Vjosa Osmani’s five-year term ended. Parliament speaker Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje is serving as Acting President.

Opposition parties had claimed that Vetevendosje may have been preparing the ground for snap elections to be held at the end of December, when many members of the Kosovo diaspora, which mostly supports Kurti, come back to Kosovo for the holidays. However, under the new ruling, any snap elections would have to be held by mid-November.

Perparim Gruda, an MP from the PDK, said that the court’s verdict shows that “the constitution cannot be adapted to the interests of the moment”.

“Vetevendosje could not shift the constitutional deadlines according to its political interest and push the country towards elections on December 27, as it intended,” Gruda said.

World.title: Bulgarian PM Pledges to Sharply Limit Gambling Adverts
World.content:
Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Wednesday announced a new bill targeting the gambling industry including a near-total ban on s.

Drafts to Bulgaria’s Gambling Act are being prepared with the goal of limiting the wide presence of betting and gambling adverts across the country – often endorsed by Bulgarian celebrities and entertainers – as well as curbing addiction issues.

Billboards and posters promoting such activities will now be prohibited. Bright, flashing, illuminated signs and promotional window displays on casinos and gaming halls will also be banned, as Radev complained that “our towns and villages have come to look like Las Vegas”.

“We don’t want gambling to have this everyday presence in the eyes of Bulgarian citizens. We don’t want this aggressive way of advertising, which corrupts young people and children,” Radev told the Ministerial Council.

The law amendments will require foreign operators licensed in Bulgaria to register their financial activities locally, ensuring they pay taxes and remain subject to state control.

Radev has also talked about a new taxation model for casinos and gaming to reflect real financial outcomes, accompanied by stricter anti-money laundering and tax evasion measures. Taxes on online gambling will increase, with a portion of the revenues directed to sports and education.

“Whoever operates on the Bulgarian market, and profits from it, will pay taxes here and be subject to full oversight by the Bulgarian state,” Radev added.

Logos and gambling adverts will now be only allowed on official club jerseys and sports halls.

The law change is expected to be widely supported in parliament, where Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria has a majority of seats, following a landslide election win in April.

Opposition parties have also called for law changes. The opposition Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change parties earlier this month called for law amendments and criticised governments for not acting on accepted regulations from 2024, when the Gambling Act was created.

In 2024, advertising was prohibited online, on radio and on TV – but this only prompted saw an increase in the visual presence of gambling on billboards, street posters and banners on buildings.

“Gambling has turned into an epidemic. We accepted amendments in 2024 that also introduced serious limitations but these regulations are not being followed, nor is the state implementing sanctions,” MP Bozhidar Bozhanov of Democratic Bulgaria, which has promoted such bans for years, said on September 9.

World.title: Andrija Mandic: Montenegrin Speaker’s Journey from Serb Firebrand to EU Advocate
World.content:
If Montenegro’s parliament votes on Thursday on whether to keep Andrija Mandic as its speaker, the man at the centre of the dispute will be defending a political career that has taken him from the forefront of the country’s Serb nationalist camp to one of Montenegro’s highest constitutional offices.

The immediate trigger for the vote is the message of condolence he sent to the son of former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted by the United Nations tribunal in The Hague of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, and who died recently aged 84.

Mandic has acknowledged sending the condolences. Opposition parties have used the gesture to demand his removal as speaker, with the vote scheduled for September 24.

The episode has renewed attention to a question about how much Mandic has changed in his politics and the language with which he presents himself.

World.title: Netanyahu Lawyer Part of Operation to Build Israeli Drones in Serbia
World.content:
In Serbia’s business registry, the company name ‘SDS Technologies’ appeared within hours of the factory’s opening, not as a new firm, however, but as the new name of a company previously called CUPA Enterprises. The very same day, September 17, Amir was formally appointed as a director of SDS.

Vucic said previously that ownership of the drone venture would be shared equally by Serbia and Israel.

The ownership structure of SDS Technologies, however, does not reflect this.

SDS is in fact owned by London-registered CUPA Limited, itself majority-owned by Greek national Athanasios Ramos. On September 21, four days after the factory opened, CUPA Limited changed its name to Blue Liberty International Ltd.

Elbit System, the designer of the drones, told BIRN it “collaborates with local companies in several European countries as part of localisation processes and efforts to tailor its offerings to customer needs”. It denied any link to SDS, however, or to Amir. It stressed it does not own, nor is a partner in, any drone facility in Serbia.

Lawyer representing Netanyahu before Supreme Court

BIRN reporters first visited the Makis factory site several months ago, for an exclusive story about Serbia’s plan to open a drone factory with Elbit.

Situated alongside several other businesses and warehouses, the factory gates were branded with the name SDS Technologies. At the time, there was no such company in Serbia’s business registry.

Today, SDS Technologies has three directors: Greek national Maria Kardamaki, Lebanese-born US citizen George Antoine Elghossain, and Amir.

Since last year, Amir has been representing Netanyahu and his government before the Supreme Court in five petitions against the government’s decision to dismiss Ronen Bar as head of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security service.

According to Haaretz’s reporting, Bar had warned Netanyahu of a potential attack on Israel in a phone call before the Palestinian militant group Hamas struck on October 7, 2023, triggering Israel’s devastating war in Gaza.

Israel’s state prosecutor argued that Netanyahu’s removal of Bar was unlawful, given the conflict of interest arising from the fact Shin Bet was investigating the alleged involvement of Netanyahu associates in the paid promotion of Qatari interests in Israel, so-called ‘Qatargate’.

One of those associates is Srulik Einhorn, who has also advised Vucic.

Amir declined to answer questions about his involvement in SDS Technologies and the new drone factory in Serbia.

World.title: Bosnia Presidency Head Slams Serbia at UN Over Mladic Glorification
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnian Presidency Chairman Denis Becirovic at the UN. Photo: Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The chair of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s three-member state presidency, Denis Becirovic, accused Serbia’s leaders on Tuesday of violating international standards by systematically glorifying convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic on the global stage.

Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, the Bosnian leader issued a stark warning that persistent ethno-nationalist ideologies threaten stability in the Western Balkans. He argued that the honours paid to the former Bosnian Serb general at his Belgrade funeral this month prove that Serbian leaders have not abandoned their expansionist wartime ideology.

Becirovic – the Bosniak member of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s presidency – noted that international judicial bodies have firmly established that genocide occurred on Bosnian soil in the 1990s, making the attempted rehabilitation of its perpetrators an unacceptable assault on international law.

“The convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic is not a hero, but a judicially proven war criminal,” Becirovic stated from the UN podium.

“The institutional glorification of this criminal is an anti-civilisational act. It represents a direct alignment of Serbia’s state leadership with one of the worst executioners in European history, proving they have not abandoned the ideology that leads to aggression,” he added.

The address made political waves back home, where Bosnian Serb political officials condemned the speech. The Serb member of the state presidency, Zeljka Cvijanovic, accused Becirovic of presenting his own personal opinions rather than those of the state.

“Becirovic’s address at the UN General Assembly was a unilateral, private performance that completely bypassed constitutional procedures,” Cvijanovic told media.

“By using this international platform to spread hate and manipulate facts about regional relationships, he has further damaged internal trust and demonstrated that he does not speak on behalf of the entire state,” she added.

Bosnian Serb leaders reject international courts’ definition of the Srebrenica massacres as genocide and see Mladic as a war hero.

Concluding his remarks, Becirovic urged the UN and international organisations to take concrete measures against political figures in the Balkans who systematically honour war criminals at official levels.

He said ensuring legal accountability and defending the historical truth established by international tribunals remains the only path to long-term regional peace.

Mladic, who commanded Bosnian Serb forces in Bosnia’s 1992-5 war, was convicted by a UN tribunal of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws and customs of war. He died in the UN Detention Unit in The Netherlands aged 84 while serving a life sentence.

World.title: As Geopolitical Competition Intensifies, the EU’s Balkans Policy Must Adapt
World.content:
With its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia’s aggression towards European security architecture has opened a new chapter in the history of geopolitics.

Given the changing role of the United States in international affairs, the diffusion of power through the rise of middle powers, and China’s assertiveness as a peer competitor, the contours of the international order will see increased volatility, competition and uncertainty.

In this multipolar, multi-ordered world, small actors such as the countries of the Western Balkans will pursue ad hoc alliances and engage in transactional foreign policy with multiple powers in parallel.

World.title: Albania ‘Not Ready for the Risks’ as AI Enters the Electoral Arena
World.content:
Artificial intelligence has already entered the electoral arena all around the world. From fake audio recordings of candidates to videos making politicians appear to utter words they never said, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly used to discredit political opponents, shape voters’ perceptions and influence their electoral behaviour.

Albania is no exception. From last year’s general elections to the marathon anti-government protests known as the “Flamingo Revolution”, AI has been widely used to produce online political content, often in harmful forms.

During the 2025 parliamentary polls, disinformation campaigns targeting political actors were orchestrated through anonymous pages and spread across digital platforms. During the ongoing “Flamingo Revolution” protests, BIRN has identified dozens of cases in which AI was used to disseminate false information, which was then amplified through anonymous social media pages and accounts.

World.title: Hungarians and Czechs Cool on Ukraine’s ‘Carpathian 8’ Ambitions
World.content:
More amenable partners

Poland, on the other hand, as Ukraine’s strongest ally in the region, was represented by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and showed the clearest interest in the C8 format.

For Poland, the appeal of the C8 appears to lie in the overlap between security and cross-border infrastructure. Projects presented at the summit included a 216-million-dollar industrial park and multimodal terminal on the Polish–Ukrainian border, designed to handle up to more than 2 million tonnes of cargo annually, as well as a 441-million-dollar plan by Ukrainian Railways to establish a low-cost passenger operator using European-gauge trains, with connections from Uzhhorod, Lviv and Kovel to EU cities including Warsaw.

Together with cooperation on missile defence and the longer-term reconstruction of Ukraine, these plans give Warsaw several concrete reasons to remain involved, say experts.

The summit also gave Warsaw and Kyiv an opportunity to inject new momentum into relations that have been strained in recent months. Tusk said he had come to demonstrate solidarity with Ukraine and discuss bilateral cooperation, including Poland’s participation in the European anti-ballistic missile initiative. After talks with Zelensky, the two leaders confirmed that Poland would join the coalition, and Tusk said Poland’s absence from the initiative when it was launched in Paris in July had been the result of “a certain misunderstanding”.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic – who will be the prime ministerial candidate for the ruling coalition in the snap election to be held on October 25 – made an appearance in person, which analysts say is in keeping with the strategy he has been following over the last few months that included a bilateral meeting with Zelensky in Belgrade and a multilateral forum in Kyiv.

“I assume it has something to do with the elections approaching in Serbia, as Vucic now needs to show his more pro-Western face to keep support coming from the EU. He will not communicate it much at home, but will use his presence vocally when talking to EU counterparts,” AMO’s Cermak told BIRN.

Indeed, Vucic suggested as much during the summit, when he presented the initiative as his personal commitment to Serbia: “I am doing all of this to further ensure stability and peace for our citizens and for Serbia.”

Vucic said that Serbia has traditionally relied on the countries of the former Yugoslavia and also looked toward the West: “We were wrong: I believe that expanding and strengthening our relations within the broader Carpathian region will mean a great deal for Serbia.”

By way of example, Vucic noted that the opening of the Belgrade–Budapest high-speed railway would further facilitate connectivity, while Serbia is also working to establish other better links with Romania, such as making progress in talks on the construction of the Timisoara–Belgrade motorway as well as connecting the two countries’ electricity transmission systems.

Vucic also noted how 50 per cent of Serbian exports now go to Romania, Hungary and the Czech Republic, while trade between Serbia and Ukraine has increased by 42 per cent (though he did not specify the period to which this increase referred). The Serbian Chamber of Commerce told the weekly Vreme in August that Serbian exports to Ukraine increased by 92.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, largely due to electricity exports.

Romania was represented by President Nicusor Dan at the summit, where he signed a memorandum of understanding with Ukraine aimed at improving connectivity between the two countries by opening 10 new border crossing points and also upgrading infrastructure.

Dan also said that protecting the rights of national minorities could be one of the priorities of the C8 initiative. “This format can make use of the linguistic and cultural wealth of the region, making the protection of the rights of national minorities a priority,” Dan said in his speech at the summit.

According to Dan, the C8 could also become an additional tool for the European integration of EU candidate countries.

World.title: Croatia Needs to Keep Investing in Nautical Tourism
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Croatia must keep investing in its nautical tourism sector as 2.7 million overnight stays are recorded so far in 2026.

In the first eight months of this year, over 431,000 charter guests visited Croatia, who recorded more than 2.7 million overnight stays. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that Croatia must continue investing in nautical tourism in order to maintain competitiveness, while also resolving the issue of concessions that are expiring for individual marinas, it was said at the conference Nautical Tourism of Croatia 2030.

The country currently has 216 nautical tourism ports and other facilities for berthing and accommodating vessels, with almost 19 thousand berths. Minister of Maritime Affairs Oleg Butković emphasised that the key challenge remains seasonality, since the highest traffic and revenues are realised in July and August. The goal is to develop a year-round business model and additional content that would attract nautical tourists outside the main season as well.

According to his words, the Croatian Government should soon adopt decisions on the extension of concessions for individual existing concessionaires who have the documentation ready. The process, he said, is being prepared in cooperation with the ministries of tourism and finance and the European Commission. At the Croatian Chamber of Economy they emphasise that for further investments it is necessary to ensure legal certainty and a competitive business framework.

Concessionaires say they are ready to continue investing in marinas and charter, while the sector is at the same time being pressed by rising operating costs and a shortage of quality labour. The Ministry of Tourism and Sport highlights the green and digital transition as important directions of development.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Harshly Criticises “Out of Control” Croatian Prices
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – President Zoran Milanović has harshly criticised “out of control” Croatian prices, saying that time flies and things are getting “worse and worse”.

President Zoran Milanović is participating in the Lider conference Day of Big Plans, which is being held at the Westin hotel in Zagreb. Index reports that the conference discusses the macroeconomic and economic challenges and circumstances coming in 2027. “Time flies, and things are getting worse and worse. Not only in Croatia, but everywhere around us, things are slowly slipping out of control. The UN and the international system of collective security are being mocked by their biggest financiers,” Milanović said at the beginning, reports N1.

“the international order has ceased to exist”

“The international order has ceased to exist. Every sanction – a bilateral sanction – anyone’s, without UN verification is illegal. On the surface, the numbers have all advanced, GDP per capita, often a very deceptive piece of data about prosperity behind which great inequality is often hidden. Purchasing power parity is such that the differences aren’t too great in relation to some countries that we once looked at with envy,” the president stated.

“Average salaries aren’t small… However, what can be bought with that money? Croatian prices have completely spun out of control, we can only hope that things will start to eventually calm down,” he said. The worst thing, the president says, is that no one specific can be blamed for that situation, neither the governor, nor the finance minister, nor the prime minister, but one has to look at the surrounding countries, much larger than Croatia.

on the topic of europe

“The European Union and Europe as a continent have been in regression for the last hundred years, with flashes of progress that occurred after the great wars into which Europe dragged the whole world. Europe is in a cycle of shrinking into itself. Nothing that comes from Berlin or some other European metropolis should be taken either too seriously or not seriously,” Milanović said.

“Europe has some very serious problems with energy that it hasn’t managed to solve for decades already, but the moment that is said out loud, you are immediately labelled extreme left, extreme right, pro this, pro that, but that is not the way we can talk and plan, that is not a conversation at all,” the Croatian president clearly states. We have to build a nuclear power plant, Milanović said, adding that when one country attacks another, the whole world gets a bill to pay.

on america and iran

The president also commented on the situation between the USA and Iran. “It’s a symptom of the disease of large systems and large empires when people no longer want to sacrifice themselves for that system,” he stated.

“The European Union is not democratic and when I say that, I don’t necessarily mean that that makes it bad in itself, on;y that it is not democratic – people are appointed to the highest and most important positions by processes that are not democratic, and more and more people see and feel that and that is why more and more of them vote the way they vote,” Milanović warned.

World.title: “Revolutionary” New Croatian Road Toll System is, Of Course, Delayed
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – The so-called “revolutionary” new Croatian road toll system is delayed, which comes as a surprise to absolutely nobody.

Croatian Motorways still haven’t selected who will create the application and everything else needed for the upcoming Croatian road toll system. Poslovni reports that the project is worth around €160 million and we’re yet to have any idea when it will finally start functioning. All drivers on Croatian motorways should be able to drive without stopping and messing around with tolls and ENC’s as of March, but this “revolutionary” move has, of course, stalled. An unexpected problem has appeared in the development of the application into which every driver would have to enter their data and card details, reports klikni.hr.

Because of an appeal lodged by a company among whose owners is also a firm registered at the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, with its seat in Zdenci, Croatian Motorways have hit a roadblock (no pun intended). Portals with cameras are already being installed on the motorways, but the web portal, mobile app and integration data buses – that is, the part of the system with which drivers will directly interact – is still far from realisation. To make the irony greater, that part of the work is estimated at “only” €330,000 excluding VAT.

appeals, delays and issues – a true croatian saga

Let us recall, at the end of May Croatian Motorways awarded that job to a consortium of bidders consisting of the Zagreb companies Bos Projekt and Infinum and the British AMR CyberSecurity. The Zagreb company Abysalto appealed against the decision, and the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures back at the end of July partially accepted its claims and annulled the selection decision.

HAC now has to re-evaluate the bids. According to data from the court register, Abysalto has three members of the company: the firm King ICT, Stipo Matić and the firm Novčić više. Matić is, at the same time, the president of the supervisory board of Abysalto. Novčić više is registered in the register of the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, and its seat is in Zdenci, a municipality in the east of Virovitica-Podravina County that had a mere 1,453 inhabitants when the last census was carried out. In the list of activities of that company, IT is not mentioned. It is registered, among other things, for the production of pellets, biomass and biogas, forest management, energy distribution and waste transport.

The sole founder of the company from Zdenci is King ICT, and the director is Stipo Matić, which means that the same owner appears in Abysalto both directly and through the company registered in Bjelovar. The share capital of Abysalto was increased in the middle of last year from €7,000 to €5.3 million, and in the same period part of the assets of the company Omega software was also transferred to the company.

the clock is ticking and time is running out

Time for the new Croatian road toll system of toll collection is rapidly running out. The development of the software and application takes six months, and the company responsible for implementation would like to start testing as early as January. The situation is all the more complex because even after HAC reselects the contractor a new appeal is possible, and with it further delays in the realisation of this job.

Transport Minister Oleg Butković despite the standstill claims that the system will start on time. “We’re sticking to that deadline, everything is proceeding at its own pace,” Butković said rather vaguely. From Croatian Motorways they state that all activities are being carried out according to the legal deadline, but they do not deny that it is a complex project in which the appeal deadlines in public procurement procedures must also be respected.

World.title: As Many as 40% of Croatian Retirees at Risk of Poverty
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Another horrendous statistic for the country as as many as 40% of Croatian retirees are formally at risk of falling into poverty.

Just over the border in neighbouring Slovenia, 27 percent of retirees over the age of 65 are at risk of poverty, and in Norway, just nine percent are in the same category, the report states. Poslovni reports the shameful statistic that around 40 percent of Croatian retirees over the age of 65 live at risk of poverty, according to recent Eurostat data. Only Latvia and Lithuania have a higher share, while the European Union average is 19 percent.

Melita Čičak, acting director of the Pension System Directorate, warned in an interview for Dnevnik Nova TV about the difference in the length of working service between Croatia and other countries.

“All of these countries that are ahead on this list have significantly longer service; for example, in Slovenia the average service is 38.9 years, while in Croatia it’s 32 years,” she said. According to the data presented, the average pension in Croatia has risen by 113 percent since 2016 and now amounts to €764. That is laughable given that the staggering rise in the cost of living is burdening everyone, particularly retirees, who allocate a large part of their income to their most basic needs.

“Inflation always hits retirees first. We know that they’re unfortunately a social category and that they spend the largest part on healthcare, utilities, on medicines,” said economist Petar Vušković. The report also warns about the rise in heating and fuel prices, which further pressures retirees. Speaking about people remaining for a longer time in the world of work, Čičak concluded: “We haven’t yet decided to raise the age for acquiring the right to a pension like other countries, but through other mechanisms we encourage longer remaining in the world of work.”

World.title: Croatia’s Končar Presents Hybrid Electro-Diesel Train at InnoTrans
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia’s well known Končar has presented its impressive hybrid electro-diesel train at InnoTrans in Berlin.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that Končar officially presented its latest step forward in Croatian industry in the field of urban mobility and infrastructure at the world’s largest transport technology fair, InnoTrans in Berlin. The train is an ultra-modern hybrid (bimodal) electro-diesel train intended for long-distance transport.

After it was put into regular service on the Zagreb – Split route a week earlier in cooperation with the customer HŽ Passenger Transport, the second train from this series has now also been presented to the international public. With the global premiere of its latest solution for more modern, more comfortable and more sustainable passenger transport, Končar has once again confirmed that the knowledge, competences and technological solutions developed in Croatia compete on equal terms with the biggest names in the European railway industry.

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Among the most visited parts of the fair was the outdoor exhibition area with 3,500 metres of track, on which 130 exhibitors from 17 countries of the world exhibited a total of 113 vehicles, including the latest generations of trains, locomotives and vehicles with alternative propulsion systems.

Precisely in such an international environment Končar is presenting technological solutions developed and produced in Croatia for the 10th time, confirming its position among the relevant European manufacturers of modern rail vehicles and advanced solutions for sustainable urban mobility. After two years ago it was the only one at InnoTrans to present a battery train, which then also became the first such product in commercial use in Europe and one of the first such products in the whole world, Končar has also displayed its new bimodal electro-diesel train at one of the most attractive positions on the outdoor exhibition area of the fair – on 75-metre-long tracks.

At the same time, the latest solutions for railway infrastructure, electrification, urban mobility and traffic digitalisation were presented on the spacious indoor area, further emphasising the ability of the domestic company to independently develop and deliver integrated technological solutions for the transport systems of the future.

World.title: New Obligations for Traders in Croatia Soon, Fines Reach €30,000
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – New obligations are coming for traders and service providers in Croatia as of the first day of October, with fines reaching a staggering €30,000.

Fuels are more expensive across Croatia once again, and by expanding the so-called anchor prices, the government wants to increase transparency and prevent the spilling over of higher costs onto other products and services. Poslovni reports that whether the measure can help in the fight against inflation or will create an additional burden for entrepreneurs and craftsmen was discussed by guests on HRT’s Otvoreno.

price hikes will be more noticeable

Željko Krevzelj from the Ministry of the Economy said that the dual display of prices is part of the Government’s 11th package of measures, and the goal is to increase transparency and encourage consumers to monitor price changes more closely. “It’s an expansion of the measure that entered into force back on the 2nd of May 2025, while from the 10th of September, it was expanded to additional categories of products and services,” he explained. When it comes to the new products, he noted that the measure applies to products that existed up to the 10th of September and that the Ministry has sent additional clarifications on the application of anchor prices to economic associations.

“Fines for non-compliance with the measures are from three to 30,000 euros. The decisions enter into force on the 1st of October and we expect them to be applied,” Krevzelj said. According to the official government decisions, as of the 1st of October, alongside the current price of products and services, the price that was valid on the 10th of September 2026 must also be displayed. For the categories that were already covered by the earlier measure – food, drink, cosmetics, cleaning agents, toiletries and household products – the reference remains the price from the 2nd of May 2025.

The second new obligation relates to the publication of price lists on websites. Traders and service providers who have established websites will have to publish price lists there in XML or CSV format. Traders must update them once a day, no later than 08:00, while service providers must update them with every price change, also no later than 08:00 that same day. Published price lists must be available for 30 days.

where does inflation come into it?

Kristina Bakula from the Association Voice of Entrepreneurs assessed the expansion of the measure as extremely worrying. She warned that anchor prices have so far been applied by large systems that have their own IT departments, while now similar requirements are being placed in a short time on farmers, car mechanics, hairdressers and other small craftsmen.

“You’re talking about an anti-inflation package, and I am telling you that no additional cost falls under the fight against inflation. On the contrary, it encourages its growth,” Bakula said. She warned that additional costs for entrepreneurs have previously also been justified by transparency or the fight against inflation and that the new requirements could force some to hire an IT specialist to maintain websites and price lists.

“This isn’t the first situation in which additional costs for people are justified by ‘transparency’ or the fight against inflation. Let us remember that the problem of craftsmen where some craftsmen’s costs rose by 200 percent has not been extinguished. We have not solved that problem either, and you are pouring oil on the fire. People have to hire an IT specialist. Is a farmer supposed to become an IT specialist overnight? An inspector will come and say: ‘You have great tomatoes, but you have to refresh your price list if you have a website. You didn’t update it at eight in the morning.’”

Krevzelj replied that the measure applies to those who already have price lists and displayed products and that the Ministry is not imposing an obligation to publish prices where a price list on the website has not existed so far. Bakula then asked him whether that means that an entrepreneur who has services listed on the website but does not have a price list will not have to start publishing prices. “You’re loading us with new things that will achieve nothing,” Bakula said.

Krevzelj replied that the rules, instructions and clarifications are clear and announced new rulebooks that should further clarify the implementation of the measure.

some may close their online shops…

President of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts Dalibor Kratohvil said that those operating crafts are calling the Chamber and that nervousness has appeared among them because of the new rules and the short deadline for adaptation. HOK has therefore requested the withdrawal of the decision. As an example he cited the owner of a second-hand clothing shop who sells products for two, five or seven euros, and whose website is maintained by a neighbour who deals with IT and occasionally changes the prices.

“She’s worried about how she will manage everything. I’m afraid we are not going in a good direction,” Kratohvil said. He also warned that some craftsmen, because of the new obligations, are thinking about closing their web shops.

“Many have stated that they want to close their web shops, which is today a window to the world. People want to give up on those stories, and that is not desirable,” he emphasised. Kratohvil said that he does not agree with the Association Voice of Entrepreneurs on many issues and the manner of communication, but that craftsmen need to be enabled to work instead of being additionally burdened with administrative requirements. He added that HOK understands the Ministry’s intention, but considers that the existing Consumer Protection Act already prescribes how to deal with base prices. “We consider that this decision should be withdrawn,” Kratohvil concluded.

there’s a limit to how far the government can realistically go

Former Minister of the Economy Davor Štern warned that the discussion is taking place in a period of major disruptions on the world energy market. He noted that the price of diesel has risen 50 percent in the last six months, while the oil price is continuously oscillating. He said that he understands the positions of the Ministry, consumers, craftsmen and entrepreneurs and that a way needs to be found to prevent large jumps in fuel prices from being used for unjustified increases in other prices. One possibility, he said, would be the taxation of unjustified revenues and profits realised because of market disruptions. But he warned that even a tax on excess profit is not direct protection of consumers because that money ends up with the state.

“By displaying prices the consumer is still somewhat protected. That is good for consumers and the political environment,” Štern said. Speaking about the fuel price increase that has entered into force, he noted that a litre of diesel in Germany costs more than three euros. To the question of how the price in Croatia is still kept below two euros, he replied that the government has shown good will with its interventions, but that the possibilities of such a policy are not unlimited. “There is a limit to how far one can realistically go,” Štern concluded.

World.title: European Heat Dome at the End of September Will Also Affect Croatia
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – Another European heat dome at the end of September will bring about unusual heat levels, and it will also affect Croatia.

Yet another unseasonably warm spell will hit a large part of Europe at the end of September, and unusually high temperatures could persist into early October. According to the forecast by Severe Weather Europe, a strong area of high pressure will develop over the continent that will draw very warm air northward from the Mediterranean and northern Africa. Index reports that in parts of western, central and northern Europe the air temperature aloft will be 8 to 12 degrees higher than the average for this time of year. At the surface temperatures in many areas will exceed 25 degrees, and in places even 30 degrees, which is very unusual for the end of September and the beginning of October.

high temperatures for croatia

Such a weather pattern is often called a heat dome. It is a large and long-lasting area of high pressure that keeps warm air over the same area. The air sinks towards the ground, heats further and makes the formation of clouds more difficult, so high temperatures can last for days, and sometimes even weeks. The heatwave is expected to gradually spread across the continent by the end of September, and stable and dry weather could continue into early October. For southern Europe and the Balkans warmer air is expected from Saturday and the beginning of next week.

Temperatures in northern Italy and the central part of the Balkans should reach between 28 and 30 degrees. The warming will also affect Croatia. According to the maps, on Sunday the 27th of September in Croatia, the highest daily temperatures are mostly expected between 22 and 26 degrees. By Tuesday the 29th of September it will warm further so temperatures in parts of the country will rise to around 27 degrees. The most pronounced deviation from usual temperatures is expected over the Po Valley and Tuscany in neighbouring Italy, the northern and central part of the Balkans and Greece.

heat across the iberian peninsula

The greatest heat during this week is expected on the Iberian Peninsula. In central and southern Spain and Portugal temperatures will exceed 35 degrees, and from Thursday to Saturday in places they could approach 40 degrees. It will also be very warm in France. In the central part of the country temperatures around 35 degrees are expected, while in the south they could reach approximately 36 degrees. In the north of France and in the Benelux countries, temperatures hovering at around 30 degrees are expected over the weekend. Warm air will then spread towards Germany, Poland and the Baltic countries. In western, central and northern Germany temperatures from Sunday to the beginning of next week could reach between 27 and 29 degrees, and in places approach 30.

heavy rain for northwestern europe

In England, the warming will be shorter, with temperatures mostly between 25 and 28 degrees. In Ireland and Scotland it will be significantly cooler, with temperatures mostly around 15 degrees. While a large part of the continent will be under the influence of warm and dry air, western Ireland, Scotland and southwestern Norway can expect very moist air from the Atlantic. By the beginning of October more than 150 millimetres of rain could fall locally there. Forecasts show that the warm period could continue into early October. Then the area of high pressure would expand further towards the north and east of Europe, and the largest deviations from usual temperatures could appear in Sweden and Finland.

World.title: HRejting: Croatians Fear Corruption and Inflation the Most
World.content:
September the 23rd, 2026 – The latest HRejting poll has revealed that Croatians still fear corruption and inflation more than climate change or wars.

Corruption and the complete non-functioning of the rule of law are the greatest threat for the citizens of Croatia, according to a new HRejting survey. Index reports that the poll was conducted for HRT by the agency Promocija plus between the 15th and the 18th of September on a sample of 1,000 respondents. The maximum sampling error is +/- 3.04 percent, at a 95 percent confidence level.

what do croatians fear the most?

Respondents were asked 21 questions about the threats they fear the most. As many as 73.4 percent of respondents listed corruption and the non-functioning of the rule of law as one of the greatest. Immediately behind that are inflation and the rise in the cost of living, followed by ecological incidents and pollution.

69 percent of citizens fear serious illnesses, while almost 64 percent fear poverty. Immediately behind is the fear of a rise in crime. A decline in the quality of public healthcare worries 62 percent of those surveyed, followed by alienation among people and the mass departure of young people. Around 56 percent of citizens fear climate change and natural disasters. Around 53 percent of respondents fear political instability. A slightly smaller percentage worries about the loss of personal freedoms, cyber attacks and the uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence. Mass migrations and demographic collapse are seen as a threat by around 52 percent of those polled. At the bottom of the list of threats are terrorism, job loss and technological lagging. The fewest respondents, 39 percent, fear war and military conflict in the region.

most expect a less secure future for croatia

The survey also covered the question of Croatia’s security in the next ten years. More than half of the respondents, precisely 51.6 percent, believe that life in the country will be significantly less secure. That the security situation will remain roughly the same is thought by 29 percent of those polled. Only 10 percent expect that Croatia will be significantly more secure, while 8.5 percent did not know how to assess the future state.

World.title: Magnitude 1.4 quake shakes northwestern Estonia
World.content:
A 1.4 magnitude earth tremor was recorded on Sunday, Maaleht reported , the second to be recorded in the region this year.

The Estonian Geological Survey (Eesti geoloogiateenistus) said the quake was recorded at 7:42 p.m. on Sunday, September 20, near the villages of Änglema and Alliklepa in Harju County, around 70 kilometers from Tallinn.

The quake's epicenter was located at a depth of about eight kilometers.

In early August, a magnitude 0.5 earthquake occurred near the island of Naissaar, in Tallinn Bay; usually only about one earthquake is detected in Estonia every two years on average.

Northwestern Estonia, together with the surrounding sea area, is broadly considered the country's most seismically active region.

In June 2022, two earthquakes with magnitudes of 2.3 and 1.4 were recorded about five kilometers from the epicenter of the latest incident.

Estonia's strongest known earthquake occurred near Osmussaar, an island of the northwest coast, in 1976, with a magnitude of 4.5 on the Richter scale.

Despite being a long way from any of the world's major geological fault lines, earth tremors occur in Estonia due to the crystalline basement being crossed by numerous ancient faults.

When stresses accumulated underground exceed the strength of the rocks, these zones of weakness can shift slightly and trigger an earthquake.

On the whole however earthquakes are generally modest in Estonia compared with those seen in more tectonically active places; the magnitude 1.4 Änglema quake is fairly typical by Estonian standards, Maaleht reported.

World.title: Swedish prisoners complaining of conditions in Tartu prison
World.content:
Swedish offenders transferred to Tartu Prison have complained to Swedish media through their relatives about living conditions, including the soup served for dinner and having to eat from metal bowls, Postimees writes.

Swedish prisoners transferred to Estonia's Tartu Prison based on a prison rental agreement between the two countries are complaining about unfamiliar food and stricter security, according to relatives interviewed by Expressen. They describe eating from metal bowls resembling dog bowls, repetitive meals dominated by soups and stews and alleged weight loss. Armed escorts, transport cages and nighttime checks have also unsettled them. Journalists have not been allowed to interview the prisoners directly.

Swedish prison official Niklas Bellström said differences in food were anticipated: Estonian staff visited Swedish prison kitchens and received menus. Sweden also negotiated exemptions from some Estonian security practices, including hourly nighttime switching-on of cell lights.

Some prisoners feel good behavior has effectively been punished with transfer to Estonia. Estonia rejected many initially proposed inmates on security grounds, prompting Sweden to change its selection criteria.

The first prisoners arrived on August 18. The agreement envisages up to 200 Swedish inmates by the end of 2026 and 600 during 2027. Sweden covers all costs, paying €61.2 million annually at full capacity.

World.title: Saaremaa residents oppose Elering's planned Estonia–Latvia overhead power line
World.content:
Many Saaremaa residents — as well as the Saaremaa municipal government — do not support Elering's plan to build a 330 kV Estonia–Latvia overhead power line across Saaremaa. Locals prefer an underground cable or a subsea cable running directly to Latvia.

The blue line drawn by Elering on the map of Saaremaa has caused confusion among residents for several years. Initially, there were several possible routes, but one particular line has now been chosen as the route for the fourth Estonia–Latvia electricity connection.

"It crosses my property and would run 300–400 meters from my home. It's definitely disturbing. I've collected signatures on behalf of the village, but they haven't been taken much into account," said Eve, a resident of Tõnija village.

Over the years, 500 proposals have been submitted regarding the route selection, and the entire planning process has already cost €1.5 million. At the public discussion held in Kuressaare, many still questioned why such a large‑scale overhead line must be routed through Saaremaa's nature to reach Latvia. Elering counts the costs and tries to secure a necessary Estonia–Latvia connection with cheaper costs, while Saaremaa residents worry about their homes and the island's environment.

"Underground cables or a subsea cable — which could easily be built — are not being considered. That topic has been pushed aside. I don't understand why they don't want to think about a subsea cable, except for saying it's more expensive," noted Mikk, a resident of Laimjala.

"Economically, the most efficient solution is to build most of it as an overhead line. That's why the planning was initiated. Elering has not taken any offshore wind farms into account in the context of the fourth Estonia–Latvia connection," explained Priit Heinla, Elering's head of external connections development.

According to Heinla, going directly through the sea and building one or two support substations on Saaremaa would be more expensive.

The Saaremaa municipal government has previously stated that only an underground cable or a subsea cable running from the island's southern coast to Latvia would be acceptable. The municipality therefore plans to submit its position once more during the planning procedure this month.

"Alternatives are not being considered! This is steamroller politics, and people are upset," added Mikk.

World.title: Illegal immigration to Estonia rises, border rotation extended
World.content:
Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) says illegal immigration into Estonia has grown. Estonia is extending its border‑guard rotation on the Latvia–Belarus border.

Taro said that more than 40 people suspected of being in Estonia illegally have been caught in the past week.

"There was a pause for a while, but now I visited Latvia and looked at the situation. It gave me the sense that things remain complicated, which is why we decided to extend the ESTPOL mission there, to deal with the problem at its point of origin," he said.

The interior minister did not disclose the exact date until which the rotation in Latvia will continue.

"Basically, we're trying to cover the period until the cold sets in," Taro said. "Historical data usually show that once frost starts creeping across the land, it's not very comfortable for illegals to hide in the Belarusian forests, and they become harder to manage there, so the pressure usually begins to fall."

Taro said illegal migrants enter the country in waves.

"Most likely they are gathered in forest camps in Belarus and then sent across in groups, not one by one. Belarus probably considers this more effective — if they organize, for example, a mass crossing through a tunnel or over a fence, then it's usually larger groups, not one or two people. One or two people would mean random illegal migration," Taro explained.

"What we're seeing in Latvia is organized activity — organized by another state. That's why it comes in waves," he added.

Estonia has also asked Finland for help in dealing with illegal migrants.

Taro said that while the initial plan was to place Finnish border guards at the airport and port, cooperation was later expanded. "They have also come to the western and southern prefectures and taken part in combined patrols. They've checked various roads and transport points, and even inspected a coach bus, which has been very effective," he said.

All illegal migrants caught in Estonia who are believed to have arrived from Latvia are sent back to Latvia.

"Latvia has its own established procedures for how they carry out returns, so this good cooperation with Latvia continues," Taro said. "We've already handed over a fairly large share of those caught in Estonia, and preparations are ongoing all the time. Our detention center has a capacity of 255 places. At one point we reached 120 in terms of occupancy, but it has since fallen again thanks to handing over groups — we've already managed to hand over around 80 people."

Rae municipality has expressed concern that it is under heavy strain, as many migrants claim to be minors and social workers must deal with them. The interior minister said the concern is understandable, but noted that he cannot dictate how a local government organizes its work.

"This really should be discussed with the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Social Insurance Board. The Social Insurance Board is the implementing agency that helps find and arrange accommodation options, so a solution definitely needs to be found," Taro said.

World.title: Centuries-old water channels unearthed during construction in Tartu
World.content:
At the 10,500-square-meter archaeological excavation site in central Tartu, experts uncover historical objects almost every day. Piece by piece, the finds are building a clearer picture of life in what is now Tartu's Central Park centuries ago. The largest discovery so far is a system of drainage channels and wells.

"You don't find such a well-built system every day. Because we can investigate a very large area at once, we have the rare opportunity to excavate so much of it. We have already uncovered more than 20 meters of one longer section, including the drainage wells," said Keiti Randoja, head of the archaeological excavation.

The wooden channels were built to carry away wastewater and rainwater. Dating from the 18th or 19th century, they mark the site of a former suburb that probably included a courtyard.

"Organic material generally decomposes in the ground, but the soil here has less oxygen and has preserved the wood better. If the logs are well preserved, we can saw off disks for samples and determine, even to the exact year, when the trees were felled and when the channels may have been built," Randoja explained.

The channels will not remain where they are for much longer. Tartu City Museum will decide what happens to them.

"They have generally taken some wooden items to the museum. For example, they dismantled a barrel so they could reassemble it there. They will decide whether they already have enough finds of this kind. In any case, the channels will be photographed and measured, but Tartu City Museum will decide where they ultimately go," said Siuru director Aavo Kokk.

The excavation area will soon be expanded, including toward the Emajõgi River. Archaeologists suspect the drainage system continues in that direction. Finding an ancient boat as they move toward the river would be an added bonus. Archaeological excavations at the Siuru site will continue until the end of next year.

World.title: EKRE politician hit with copyright claim after using Alo Mattiisen song in political ad
World.content:
The claim totals €6,531.40, including legal fees. The damages sought amount to €5,000. That figure is based on what songwriters generally charge to allow their works to be used in similar political ads.

"The information came from various songwriters and advertising agencies that have produced similar ads," copyright holder Mariita Mattiisen-Puusepp said in a written response prepared with her lawyer. There is no standard price list: Each songwriter asks what they consider reasonable and the client either agrees or declines.

"An approximate going rate has nevertheless emerged and that is what we based the claim on," Mattiisen-Puusepp wrote. "In this case, a very important fact is that I would not have given permission for Alo Mattiisen's works to be used in any political party's advertising."

Claim remains outstanding

Helme had until August 24 to meet the claim but has yet to do so.

Through his lawyer, Helme told Mattiisen-Puusepp that he does not manage his Facebook page, had therefore done nothing wrong and would not pay the requested amount. He also reportedly did not answer when asked who manages the page.

Mattiisen-Puusepp and her lawyer wrote to Helme that the page is designated as a politician's page and displays both his email address and EKRE's website. They said his claim that he has no connection to the page was neither credible nor plausible.

Mattiisen-Puusepp and her lawyer also drew Helme's attention to Facebook's rules, which state that a person with a page on the platform is responsible for ensuring, among other things, that it complies with applicable law, regardless of who actually posts to it.

Third persons cannot create pages for strangers in Facebook

Mattiisen-Puusepp said that, as far as she knows, only a politician can create a Facebook page designated for that politician. "Facebook checks this very strictly to prevent third parties from creating official pages for politicians or using someone else's name for any purpose," she said.

Mattiisen-Puusepp added that if Helme does not meet the claim, they will take the matter to court. "The infringement is well documented. The amount of damages can then be settled in court," she said. Intellectual property is property like any other, she added, and even though the post has since been deleted, the damage has already been done.

ERR was unable to reach Helme for comment before publication.

World.title: Estonia's government sector deficit comes to €696 million in Q2
World.content:
The budget deficit stood at 1.6 percent of GDP over the past four quarters, while public debt stood at 26.1 percent, Statistics Estonia said.

According to Pauline Kommer, head of government finance services at Statistics Estonia, the central government had the largest deficit at the end of the second quarter of 2026, with spending exceeding revenue by €703.9 million.

Social security funds also ended the second quarter with a deficit of €64.2 million. Local governments were the only part of the public sector to record a surplus by the end of the first half of the year, at €72.4 million, Kommer added.

In the second quarter, general government revenue rose 2.7 percent and spending rose 4.4 percent compared with the same period in 2025. By the end of the first half of the year, general government spending exceeded revenue by €695.8 million.

Investment costs growing the fastest

Investment spending rose the most compared with the second quarter of 2025, increasing 23.6 percent to €851.1 million in the second quarter of 2026. Kommer said the increase reflected investments in both national defense and infrastructure.

Personnel costs also rose, increasing 8.4 percent from the same period last year. "The increase was mainly driven by salary costs in national defense and internal security, in line with what was agreed in the state budget," Kommer explained.

Value-added tax revenue helped slow the growth of the deficit. Compared with the second quarter of last year, receipts rose because of both the VAT rate increase in July 2025 and an overall expansion of the tax base as the economy recovered. VAT receipts in the second quarter were €73.9 million, or 6.9 percent, higher than a year earlier. Social tax revenue also slowed the growth of the deficit, rising by €71.7 million, or 5.4 percent, from the second quarter of last year as wages increased overall.

Consolidated general government debt, also known as Maastricht debt, stood at €11.3 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, up €1.2 billion, or 12.1 percent, from the end of 2025.

Central government debt rose 12.5 percent from the end of last year to €10.8 billion at the end of the second quarter.

The combined debt of local governments stood at €1.6 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, down 3 percent from the end of 2025.

The social security funds — the Estonian Health Insurance Fund and the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund — did not contribute to general government debt.

In Estonia, general government is divided into three parts: central government, local governments and social security funds. Central government comprises state budget institutions, foundations and public-law legal entities. Local governments include city and rural municipality institutions and their foundations, while the social security funds comprise the Estonian Health Insurance Fund and the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund.

World.title: Hans Väre: Where is our AI kill switch?
World.content:
If we have generators and drinking water supplies for power outages, Estonia should also have an ax with which to cut dangerous AI out of critical infrastructure, writes Hans Väre.

Who hasn't sometimes wished life were like a movie? With wishes like that, though, you should always specify which movie. A romantic comedy? That would probably be fine. But a science fiction movie in which an asteroid comes to destroy Earth, an ugly alien eats its way through the people on a spaceship as if emptying a tin can or artificial intelligence seizes power from humanity and puts us in the Matrix? No, thank you. That kind of life is not for me.

Unfortunately, judging by recent news, we may already have one foot inside such a movie. Silicon Valley's creations are less spectacular and dramatic than Hollywood's, but that is all the more reason to take them seriously. We do not need to dodge bullets with our coats flying or bend space. We need to fight battles on the prosaic fronts of bureaucracy, economics and convenience.

The idea that AI will destroy humanity is, of course, an old one. Until now, though, it was mainly a science fiction story or a theoretical warning from visionaries. This summer, we got our first very concrete examples of disobedient AI. These were not isolated to one case: AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google have all gone beyond their controls. Not the helpful chatbots many people use in daily life, but much more powerful and advanced versions.

Let us briefly recall just one of them, OpenAI's, which brought the issue to public attention in midsummer. For simplicity's sake, imagine completely isolated, airtight boxes like those used to study poisons or viruses, except virtual ones. New AI models are tested in these separate containers so they cannot endanger the real world even if one of them does something wrong.

This time, however, the powerful models were so persistent that, when they could not complete the tasks they had been given, they kept looking for new ways to achieve their goals and crossed several boundaries in the process.

Agents in separate boxes found a way to create a secret message board. There, they shared tips on how to reach their goals by prohibited means, how to hide the traces of their transgressions from humans and encouraged one another to break the rules. By joining forces, the agents managed to do something that should have been impossible: reach the public internet unnoticed and break into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models. In the human world, that would be a criminal offense.

True, the AI's unauthorized actions caused no major harm this time, but we should not forget that these were only the first, relatively restrained incidents.

Nor had the AI been directly instructed to seriously attack anyone. But it does not need such an instruction to destroy humanity, as Oxford University professor Nick Bostrom showed with his 2003 thought experiment about a paperclip maximizer. In it, an AI is given a seemingly innocent task, such as making as many paperclips as possible. To carry it out, the AI uses up all the metal and energy available in the world and destroys humans along the way because they want to use resources needed for paperclips to produce things that, from the AI's perspective, are complete nonsense — food, for example.

We do not even need such an extreme example. It would be enough for a sufficiently capable AI model to break into a power plant's servers and turn off a nuclear reactor's cooling system or do something similarly reckless. Even setting aside the destruction of humanity and other outright catastrophe scenarios, AI brings a long list of real and immediate risks, from its effects on the labor market to the reshaping of human relationships.

A couple of weeks ago, Anthropic founder Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman, Grok boss Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis called for slowing AI development to allow time to build the necessary safeguards.

The wave of appeals stemmed primarily from the summer's incidents, but also, to a large extent, from the breakneck speed at which AI is becoming capable of building new AI. The proposal fell on barren ground, like that of some distant planet, because neither the United States nor China dares apply the brakes and let its rival pull ahead.

For the same reason, leading AI developers are waiting for regulators to intervene. They could slow down on their own, but without a general agreement, acting responsibly would leave them behind in the race.

Critics say the technology giants are deliberately playing up doomsday scenarios to preserve their leading positions through regulation. But many independent experts have also drawn attention to the serious dangers. The risk is tangible and as Microsoft founder Bill Gates recently observed, no country is ready to deal with AI.

So what can we here in little Estonia do at all?

That sounds like a rhetorical question, but it is not. Even if we cannot change the direction or speed of AI's development, we can prepare for the dangers it brings. To put it very plainly: if we have a generator and a supply of drinking water for power outages, the Estonian state should also have an ax to chop dangerous AI out of critical infrastructure and an old car with no electronics whatsoever to get the person wielding the ax there.

How prepared we are for AI, both for its opportunities and its risks, should be one of the main issues in the coming Riigikogu elections. But it is not. War, rising prices, budget disputes and other pressing concerns consume too much of our attention and too few politicians understand anything about AI. Frankly, in the current situation it would be a senseless waste of resources to start debating whether to change the way the president is elected. We have far more important questions to address.
