Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative party, linked the problem to Baku’s fragmented system of governance in a Facebook post on 14 September. In his view, the key factors are the availability of public transport and journey times. He also argues that any changes to working hours should take into account the school schedules of employees’ children.

Economist Akif Nasirli told Radio Azadliq that the race should be held outside the city centre. In his view, the economic benefits of the event should not be used to justify restrictions on residents’ freedom of movement:

“People have the right to move freely in their own country, in their own capital.”

AYNA’s traffic management plan for the race, published on 19 September, lists alternative streets that drivers can use. However, it provides no information on actual bus frequencies along the altered routes, how much additional time journeys will take, or how much time passengers may lose when changing between separate sections of disrupted routes.

For residents, it is not enough simply to know which street a bus will take. They need to know when to leave home, where they will have to change and whether they can get to work on time. Without this information, the burden of adapting to the route changes — and the consequences of any resulting delays — falls on passengers themselves.

World.title: Why Georgia closed 10 schools days into new academic year
World.content:
School closure in Georgia

Ten state schools in Georgia were closed during the first three days of the new academic year. Some of the buildings are due to be demolished and rebuilt, while others will undergo repairs.

The decision followed assessments by the National Forensics Bureau, which found that the school buildings were in a state of disrepair and unsafe for use.

One of the schools is in Tbilisi, while the others are located in different regions across the country.

For the first week after the closures, the schools switched to remote learning. During this period, the Education Ministry and school administrations are expected to urgently find alternative premises.

All 10 schools are likely to be temporarily accommodated in neighbouring schools, with classes held in two or three shifts and lesson times shortened. If any of the alternative schools are too far away, school buses will be provided.

More than 4,000 pupils and around 400 teachers are now waiting for the ministry to decide where they will be relocated and which shifts they will study and work in.

his is not unprecedented. In recent years, thousands of pupils across Georgia have been studying in temporary, “borrowed” premises, while schools that were demolished have yet to be rebuilt.

How events unfolded and what the decisions were based on

The closure of all 10 schools followed the same pattern. The start of the new academic year on 15 September was celebrated as usual, with balloons, flags and flowers in school courtyards and classrooms.

Three days later, on the evening of 17 September, parents received messages informing them that the schools were being closed.

Number of pupils and teachers at the closed schools. Source: JAMnews, based on data from the official schools portal.

In all 10 cases, the decisions to close the schools were based on assessments by the National Forensics Bureau dated 10 September 2026. The education minister says the ministry did not receive the documents until 17 September, explaining why the closures were announced at such short notice.

Some parents do not believe that the school buildings are unsafe. They suspect that some of the decisions may be linked to corrupt deals and investors’ interests.

JAMnews examined publicly available documents relating to all 10 schools, including decisions by the Authorisation Council, expert assessments, public procurement records, renovation plans and municipal reports.

We sought answers to several questions: Why were these schools allowed to begin the academic year as normal on 15 September if their buildings had to be vacated just days later? When did the responsible authorities learn about the condition of the schools? And if the buildings were already destined for demolition, why was money allocated for their renovation year after year?

Renovating schools only to abandon them

The documents examined by JAMnews show that concerns about the poor condition of some of the schools had been known for years. In other cases, however, there had previously appeared to be no need even for repairs, let alone demolition.

Some of the schools underwent minor renovation work in recent years, with substantial sums spent on the projects.

For example, according to public procurement records, Public School No 16 in Kutaisi underwent various repairs in 2015, 2017 and 2022. The largest amount was spent in 2015 — around 190,000 lari [about $70,300].

The Kutaisi school made its most recent purchase just three weeks before the start of the current academic year. On 24 August, the administration signed a 2,500-lari [about $925] contract for maintenance of the school grounds, including mowing and removing grass.

Public School No 16 in Kutaisi. The start of the academic year was celebrated with invited entertainers. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

The public school in the village of Misaktsieli underwent major renovations in 2008, while its heating system was completely upgraded last winter.

This is also confirmed by the Mtskheta municipality’s 2025 budget. According to the document, several schools were due to undergo renovation work funded through a targeted transfer from the state budget. The school in Misaktsieli was among them.

The Misaktsieli school continued to spend money on various works and services in 2026. Its most recent contract, signed on 4 September, was worth 12,515 lari [about $4,635] and covered the removal of flooring, plumbing work and the subsequent installation of granite flooring.

The school in the village of Abranlo, in the Kvemo Kartli region, is the smallest of the schools closed in recent days, with around 80 pupils. It too has undergone renovation work in recent years.

Mariko Tsikoridze, a project co-ordinator for CENN in Kvemo Kartli, says three sanitation and hygiene projects were carried out at the school before 2019. Toilets were built, washbasins renovated, and an illegal rubbish dump created by local residents in the school grounds was cleared.

“We brought in six truckloads of soil and built a sports ground. The local authorities were also actively involved at the time,” Tsikoridze says.

The school is now due to be demolished. Its headteacher, Mikheil Jakeli, wrote on social media that, according to the National Forensics Bureau’s assessment, constructing a new building would be preferable to repairing the existing one, prompting the ministry to decide on demolition.

Problems left unaddressed

For some of the schools, JAMnews was unable to find any relevant records in the public procurement system. However, municipal reports and local media articles show that concerns about the condition of these schools had been raised for years.

For example, parents of pupils at Public School No 5 in Khashuri were calling for repairs as early as January 2023, complaining about damaged walls, floors and doors, as well as loose stair railings.

First day of the new academic year at Public School No 5 in Khashuri. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

In municipal reports from the Imereti region, Public School No 2 in Tskaltubo had for years been listed as a building in need of renovation.

Available records for 2022-2026 contain no evidence of major renovation work at the school. However, according to Info Imereti, minor repairs were carried out, including in the summer of 2026.

“There is an assessment stating that the building is not cost-effective to repair. It would therefore be better to construct a new one rather than renovate it,” Mamuka Chkhetiani, head of the Tskaltubo education resource centre, told Kutaisi Post.

Officials knew as early as 2022-2023 that Public School No 3 in Senaki was in a state of disrepair. In 2022, the school’s headteacher, Marine Naneishvili, told Etaloni that the building was due to be demolished.

The Finance Ministry’s 2023 review of investment projects listed the “Construction of Public School No 3 in Senaki”as a separate project, with 12.696m lari [about $4.7m] allocated for it. It is unclear what became of the project.

Public School No 3 in Senaki. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

Reaction at schools

Members of the school communities at two of the 10 schools — in Tbilisi and Misaktsieli — responded to the authorities’ decision with protests, which are still continuing. At the other schools, discontent has largely been confined to social media, where parents have complained about the disruption to both their children’s plans and their own.

“We are in shock” is the most common reaction beneath posts announcing each new school closure.

Two of the three schools closed in the Kakheti region — Public School No 3 in Gurjaani and the school in the village of Velistsikhe — are in Gurjaani municipality. More than 500 children attend the Velistsikhe school, while School No 3 has 148 pupils.

“Congratulations to the school community of Velistsikhe Public School — pupils, parents, teachers and everyone interested in improving our school,” headteacher Nona Menabdishvili wrote on social media alongside the news of its closure.

The post attracted numerous comments, many of them essentially asking: “What is there to celebrate?” Others shared stories of schools elsewhere that have remained closed for years.

Unlike Menabdishvili, Mikheil Jakeli, headteacher of the school in Abranlo, expressed no enthusiasm about the Education Ministry’s decision.

He has appealed to the ministry to allow pupils to complete the current academic year in the old building, subject to appropriate safety measures, “to avoid moving the children elsewhere just days after the start of classes and causing them unnecessary stress”.

‘From positive assessment to demolition’ – story of School No 21

The largest of the 10 schools to be closed is Public School No 21 in Tbilisi, formerly Gymnasium No 6. News of its closure was also the first to emerge.

It is one of the capital’s most prestigious schools. Because of its emphasis on German-language teaching, it is often referred to as the “German school”.

According to a National Forensics Bureau assessment dated 10 September 2026, several problems were identified in the school building, including a risk of plaster falling from the façade, a faulty drainage system, cracks in some areas and damage to reinforced concrete blocks.

The assessment also identified seismic vulnerability as a separate problem, citing the absence of an earthquake-resistant reinforcement belt on the roof parapet and other failures to comply with current seismic standards.

Protest outside Public School No 21 on 18 September 2026. “Don’t demolish the Sixth,” reads an improvised protest banner.

However, the same school had previously received a very different assessment from the same National Forensics Bureau on 15 November 2023, when it underwent authorisation. The assessment said the building required repairs, but gave it an overall “positive” evaluation, and the school was authorised to operate until 2032.

In April 2026, the Authorisation Council carried out scheduled monitoring of the school and, citing the positive assessment, said the building required repairs and gave the school until 2028 to address the problems.

In other words, as recently as spring 2026, official documents still listed School No 21 as requiring repairs rather than demolition.

However, by the time the Authorisation Council made that assessment, a new examination of the school building was already under way.

The Municipal Development Fund had requested the examination on 16 September 2025. An expert inspected the building on 10 December, and nine months later, on 10 September 2026, issued a new assessment.

The building was initially classified as Category III based on the extent of the damage. However, following Georgian government decree No 161 of 22 April 2026, which sets out criteria for assessing whether buildings are fit for use, the damage was subsequently classified as Category IV because of seismic safety concerns.

How could the school have deteriorated so severely in three years that it now needs to be demolished? This is the question being asked by parents. Many suspect corruption. The school is located in a prestigious tourist area, prompting speculation that a private investor may be interested in the site.

Parents fear that the school will be demolished and never rebuilt. They are demanding an independent assessment and say they will not allow the building to be torn down. They also oppose both online learning and the relocation of pupils to other schools.

If we don’t act now, we will lose our school’ – story of Misaktsieli village school

Protest outside the school in Misaktsieli, 18 September 2026.

Irine Kalandadze’s child started first grade this year. He had barely had time to settle into school when his parents were told it was closing:

“He had only been at school for three days and was eagerly looking forward to the next one — he liked it so much. Then suddenly we were told the school was closing. I can’t explain this to my child, and it is very painful for me too. This is precisely the stage when children need to develop a love of school, and now we don’t even know where or how he will study.”

The school in Misaktsieli serves five villages in Mtskheta municipality and has more than 500 pupils.

Parents say lessons will be held online for the first week after the closure, after which the children will be transferred to the school in the village of Tsilkani. But that school has capacity for only 300 pupils, meaning classes will have to be held in several shifts.

Parents do not know for certain whether the Misaktsieli school is due to be demolished or is being closed for repairs. On 18 September, residents gathered in the school grounds and demanded an explanation from the headteacher, who told them that he had not yet seen the expert assessment himself.

Villagers fear there may also be business interests behind the decision: the school is in a popular tourist area, occupies a large site and is surrounded by numerous commercial properties.

“We all want our children to study in a modern school. It’s just that we have seen many examples of how school renovation projects have ended,” Irine says.

Parents are demanding that, if the school needs repairs, the work be postponed until spring. If the building is to be demolished, they want construction of a new school to begin simultaneously on vacant land nearby, with the existing building demolished only once its replacement is ready.

“If we don’t act now, we will lose our school,” Irine says.

The protest is continuing, and parents say they have no intention of backing down.

Not an exception, but a wider trend

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, there are 2,086 state schools in the country.

In 2022, the Education Ministry launched a large-scale reconstruction programme that was intended to cover 800 schools.

Since then, hundreds of schools have closed across Georgia. Two years ago, in 2024, the fact-checking platform FactCheck reported that 21,203 pupils had been relocated to alternative premises.

Based on publicly available data, the number is likely still in the tens of thousands. The Municipal Development Fund, which oversees school reconstruction, regularly publishes updates on the completion or launch of work at schools across Georgia.

For example, in August 2026, the fund announced tenders for the reconstruction of 11 schools. None of the 10 schools closed in recent days appears on that list, suggesting that the overall number of schools currently not operating in their own buildings is considerably higher.

On 18 September, as thousands of teachers, pupils and parents were reeling from the news that their schools were being closed, government officials were holding a high-profile ceremony to reopen the renovated Public Schools No 4 and No 5 in Batumi.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Education Minister Givi Mikanadze and other senior officials at the opening of two schools in Batumi. Photo: Municipal Development Fund.

What is actually happening?

Education experts say the situation illustrates systemic problems and a lack of a consistent strategy and long-term vision in the education system.

Education expert Revaz Abkhazava lists the problems created by what he describes as a poorly planned intervention — the reconstruction of schools:

It has disrupted the education process;

It has upended established routines for parents and children, including attendance at after-school clubs and additional classes;

It has shown a complete disregard for teachers’ needs, with low salaries forcing many to work at several schools at the same time;

It has imposed additional costs on the state for transporting pupils to other schools.

“The education system is extremely complex. It consists of many interconnected components. If you fail to see it as a whole, you get what we are seeing now. A single decision does not simply create one problem — it can push the entire system to the brink of collapse.”

Abkhazava says such decisions are the result of experienced and qualified professionals with institutional knowledge being pushed out of the education system.

“School reconstruction is a technical task. It does not require any special expertise. Education management professionals could have resolved this issue very easily.”

The expert also points to problems in communication between state institutions. The process, he says, was not managed in a way that would have ensured the assessments were ready at least a month before the start of the academic year.

Revaz Abkhazava believes the root of these problems lies in the politicisation of Georgia’s education system. He says education should not serve any political party and that safeguards are needed to ensure this, including an education council and teachers’ associations. He also argues that the ministry’s strategy should not change every time a new minister takes office.

“The education system should be as decentralised as possible. The ministry should employ professionals with knowledge and experience in education management and education policy.

“The ministry should focus on evaluation, analysis and research, and make decisions based on them. It should support educational institutions, while those institutions should have the autonomy to make decisions on matters that concern them,” the expert concludes.

World.title: Armenian orphanage worker brutally assaults disabled resident
World.content:
Armenian orphanage worker assaults disabled child

A care worker at the Kharberd specialised orphanage in Armenia brutally assaulted a disabled child who is unable to walk or speak.

The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, which oversees the institution, confirmed the incident and said it had taken place several weeks ago. The care worker was immediately dismissed and is now under house arrest.

“A disabled child was beaten with a mop in a place where they were supposed to receive care and support. In reality, this is the kind of care the child needs to be protected from,” said Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda.

Rights activist questions purpose of such institutions

“If we do not want violence, these institutions should not exist at all. Family-based upbringing and alternative forms of care are possible for all children if the state makes the necessary effort and allocates the necessary resources. The state’s obligations do not begin after a disabled child has been beaten, nor do they end with the dismissal of the alleged abuser or their placement under house arrest,” Hovsepyan said.

Until such institutions cease to exist, however, he says the state is obliged to establish a system that:

“prevents violence and identifies signs of it in a timely manner;

provides safe mechanisms enabling all children to report abuse;

guarantees a proper investigation and the child’s swift recovery.”

Details of the incident

Local media have established further details about what happened at the orphanage. The incident is now known to have taken place on 13 August.

The child who was assaulted has cerebral palsy and is unable to walk independently or speak.

The care worker who assaulted the child had worked at the orphanage since September 2012.

“In room D-1 of the orphanage, the care worker initially struck the resident, F.M., several times. After he fell to the floor, she picked up a floor mop and continued striking him on his lower back, spine and left shoulder blade. As a result, F.M. suffered severe physical pain and emotional distress,” journalists reported.

Child’s condition described as satisfactory

Nver Kostanyan, spokesman for the minister of labour and social affairs, wrote on social media that the orphanage administration had “identified the incident” and immediately reported it to law enforcement:

“The care worker has been dismissed, while it is for law enforcement agencies to determine whether criminal charges are warranted. The child is in good health and continues to receive care at the specialised orphanage.”

Kostanyan said such incidents were a “red line” for the ministry:

“Any instance of violence is unacceptable and will be subject to an appropriate criminal-law assessment.”

Expert opinion

Mushegh Hovsepyan, head of the NGO Disability Rights Agenda, warns that disabled children often avoid speaking about abuse they have experienced.

“There are many reasons. Among other things, they think they will not be believed, because what they say is often called into question,” he wrote on Facebook.

Hovsepyan stressed that the public only learnt about the abuse at the orphanage after it was reported by the media. The rights activist believes such cases should be closely scrutinised by state bodies, particularly now that there is no mechanism for public oversight.

A group of civil society experts previously operated at the initiative of the Labour Ministry, carrying out regular monitoring of care centres for children and elderly people.

“The monitoring group was disbanded about three years ago. Easily. But its work is not being resumed with the same ease,” Hovsepyan said.

Hovsepyan himself was a member of the group. He recalls that in 2021 it visited the Kharberd specialised orphanage and documented a case of discrimination against a minor in its care:

“At the same orphanage, staff wore gloves when touching a teenager living with HIV who had recently been transferred there. Separate dishes were used for him. His clothes were washed separately. Other children were told to stay away from him. And yet the world has long known that HIV is not transmitted through this kind of contact.”

The orphanage staff themselves told the experts about this because they believed they were ‘doing everything right’.

Following the recent violent assault, Hovsepyan says he is not convinced that conditions at the specialised institution have improved:

“I am also not sure whether all new employees receive the necessary training before they start working with children. Nor am I sure that the state is taking steps to ensure that children are in safe hands.”

World.title: A pair of porcupines, Khrashuna and Khramuna, at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Tbilisi Zoo is home to two Indian porcupines, a female and a male named Khrashuna and Khramuna. Their keepers chose the names for a reason: the porcupines make funny “crunching” sounds when they eat. Khrashuna is the bolder of the two, while Khramuna is more cautious.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: ALL VIDEO

______________________________________________________________________________

Contrary to popular belief, porcupines have nothing in common with either badgers or hedgehogs. Badgers are carnivores, hedgehogs are insectivores, while porcupines are rodents.

Their most distinctive feature is their long, thick quills, which they mainly use for defence. When threatened, their first response is to flee rather than attack. And no, porcupines do not shoot their quills — that is simply a myth. When they sense danger, they

Alongside their varied diet, Khrashuna and Khramuna always have branches in their enclosure. They gnaw on the wood, which helps keep their teeth strong.

Porcupines are nocturnal animals. During the day, especially in summer, they prefer to stay in their shelter. They become active in the evening and start looking for food. That is why visitors who come to their enclosure during the day may see nothing more than a nose or head poking out of the burrow.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

World.title: From Kylie to Lachie, everything you need to know for the AFL grand final
World.content:
The 2026 AFL grand final is almost upon us, as the Brisbane Lions look to make history with their second threepeat in 25 years, and the Fremantle Dockers look to win their first flag since joining the league in 1995.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the 2026 AFL grand final?

The game starts 2.30pm (AEST) on Saturday, September 26 at the MCG.

That's 12.30pm for those watching in Western Australia, and 2pm for South Australia.

Which teams are playing in the grand final?

The Brisbane Lions are facing off with the Fremantle Dockers.

This is Brisbane's fourth grand final in a row, losing to Collingwood in 2023, before beating Sydney and Geelong in the following years.

Should they win, it would be the second threepeat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

Meanwhile, Fremantle is yet to win a premiership after joining the league in 1995. This is the club's second grand final following its loss to Hawthorn in 2013.

Over their past six games against each other, the ledger is tied at 3-3, with the Dockers winning their most recent clash at the Gabba in round 13 this year.

How can you watch watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire AFL season that is exclusive to Channel 7.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

When will Kylie Minogue be performing?

Australia's pop princess should be on stage from about 1.30pm. Again, be very aware that Minogue's performance is pre-game and is not halftime entertainment. There is no halftime entertainment.

Other performers will be G Flip, musical actor Michael Paynter on the national anthem, and of course Mike Brady doing Up There Cazaly during the retiree motorcade.

The Wiggles will be performing at Friday's grand final parade through Melbourne.

Who will be lining up for the Lions and Dockers?

At this point we don't know.

Teams will be announced about 6pm (AEST) today, but before that we'll have to see if Lions superstar Lachie Neale's tribunal appeal against a one-match ban gets up.

ABC Sport's Andrew McGarry will be live blogging every moment of the appeal, with the case set to get underway at 4pm.

Should Neale miss out, Noah Answerth is the most likely player to come in for the Lions. The injured Brennan Cox is a chance to come in for the Dockers, but it looks odds on that the Dockers will be unchanged from their preliminary final victory over the Swans.

Who will present the cup to the winners?

The Lions have picked Simon Black, a Brownlow medallist and champion midfielder from that first threepeat, while the Dockers have gone with Shaun McManus, who debuted in Fremantle's inaugural season before playing 228 games.

World.title: Breaking: Unemployment rate reaches post-COVID era high of 4.6pc in August
World.content:
Australia's unemployment rate drifted higher in August.

The national unemployment rate rose to 4.6 per cent, up from 4.5 per cent in July, in seasonally adjusted and trend terms.

It is the highest unemployment rate in the post-COVID era.

On Tuesday, RBA governor Michele Bullock said she thought an unemployment rate of somewhere between 4.5 and 5 per cent would "take enough heat out of the labour market" to ease pressure on inflation.

In recent weeks, all four major banks and the bulk of money market traders have also announced that they expect the RBA to lift interest rates next week to try to clamp down on economic activity and squash inflation.

But data show Australia's labour force increased by another 67,700 people in August, which pushed the participation rate back up to 67.1 per cent, from 66.9 per cent in July (it's now sitting near its all-time high of 67.2 per cent).

The labour force increased by 67,700 people because an extra 39,500 people found employment and an extra 28,200 people were recorded as being unemployed.

World.title: Analyst warns diesel could top $4 and rationing possible if US ban proceeds
World.content:
A leading energy analyst has warned that Australia could be looking at diesel rationing within weeks and prices topping $4 a litre if US President Donald Trump goes ahead with an export ban on the fuel.

MST Marquee's head of energy research Saul Kavonic said the proposed export ban is "probably the most worrying development we have seen in global fuel markets since the [Middle East] war began when it comes to Australia's vulnerability".

Mr Trump said on Tuesday, local time, he backed the idea of a ban on diesel exports from the US, which is being floated by some Republican politicians ahead of the midterm elections in November.

"I've said let's not send‌ out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I've called for it. ‌I've called for it within my people," Trump told reporters before a meeting with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The country exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel a day, which is about one-quarter of its refining output.

Diesel prices have climbed to more than $US6.50 a gallon in the US, the highest average on record.

Loading...

Real threat of fuel rationing

Mr Kavonic told ABC's The Business program if the export ban went ahead, there was a very real risk of diesel fuel rationing in Australia and prices climbing 50 per cent to more than $4 a litre.

"If the US goes down this path, and particularly if they do it in a very severe way, I think we'll be looking at that in a matter of weeks," he said.

While Australia does not directly import diesel from the US, the flow-on effect on global markets puts Australia in a uniquely vulnerable position.

The economy is heavily weighted toward both agriculture and mining, both industries that rely heavily on diesel.

"Australia is actually the largest importer of diesel in the world; that's not per capita; that's an absolute sense," Mr Kavonic said.

Diesel 'crack spread' filling oil refiners' coffers The "crack spread", or profit margin, on diesel is increasing as refiners capitalise on the Middle East conflict, and it's hurting the slim margins of Australia's farmers.

"We account for 1 per cent of the world's fuel demand, but 10 per cent of the world's seaborne diesel imports."

The crunch happened because, globally, both the conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine-Russia war have seen a number of major refineries taken offline.

Russia and China have also stopped exporting refined fuels as the fuel crisis evolved.

That means the US has been picking up the slack in the diesel export market.

US considering partial or full diesel ban

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US government was examining whether it was feasible to have a full or partial ban.

Mr Kavonic said any bans could force the Australian government's hand.

"This is the kind of thing which could have to see Australia reconsider our demand management and rationing program potentially go to stage 3 and stage 4," Mr Kavonic said.

Under Australia's National Fuel Security Plan, stage 3 includes "practical measures to reduce fuel demand" and level 4 includes plans to "direct fuel supply to ensure national supply is allocated fairly" and "prioritisation of fuel supplies at the local level", generally considered to be rationing.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

"Well, it was probably only a month ago that Australia and the Australian government thought we'd managed through the worst of this crisis and we could actually disband the fuel task force," Mr Kavonic said.

Since then, two critical developments have occurred: disruption to fuel coming through the Red Sea, and now a possible US export ban.

With attacks by Houthis on both the Saudi oil pipelines and the Red Sea, oil companies were turning to clandestine ship-to-ship transfers.

"So if the US does go down this [export ban] path, particularly if they do it in a very severe way, I think we'll be looking at [rationing] in a matter of weeks, particularly if we don't see a de-escalation in the Middle East occurring at the same time," Mr Kavonic said.

"And if that continues to escalate, plus a US export ban, that's the one situation which we were really fearing and hoping would not happen. And unfortunately, it could be on our doorstep."

Stockpiles won't last forever

He said while Australia had solid fuel stockpiles, the nation could run out quickly.

"And particularly we're heading into a season now where we need that diesel for our agricultural part of our economy. So we can't afford many delays."

Australia is a huge importer of diesel because our agriculture and resources industries are heavily reliant on it. (ABC News: Laurissa Smith)

Mr Kavonic said it was critical the federal government continued its attempts to shore up supply from international partners like Saudi Arabia.

"I think government, and minister Bowen, but all the way up to the prime minister, really stepped up at the beginning of this conflict. We paid more, but it kept coming, and that's commendable," he said.

"We thought we were past the worst of this, but now these developments suggest there's actually no light at the end of the tunnel here.

"Given our global supplies of oil and diesel have been drawn down significantly this year, and clearly there'll be increasing competition from other countries as well for the supplies that remain, we're still far from being out of this conflict.

" We have to keep up with this diplomatic engagement, and we might even have to look to re-arm, stand up that fuel task force if things continue to get worse from here. "

While the US's complex supply chain means any export ban could also have internal ramifications, Mr Kavonic said it was still a possibility it could happen in the short-term to ease pressure on prices inside the country ahead of the midterm elections.

"The concern here is that they'll do this even if it's just temporarily, even if it's not sustainable for political reasons, and then the rest of the world's going to pay the price in that near term."

Export ban could actually lead to internal fuel problems

Mr Kavonic is not alone in his view.

Capital Economics chief climate and commodities economist David Oxley said any ban could paradoxically force American refiners to cut supplies of oil products.

"While an export ban would initially boost the availability of domestic diesel supply to parts of the US, it would subsequently reduce the supply of diesel and other oil products because refining and distilling a barrel of crude oil produces a mix of products in closely fixed ratios.

Loading...

"Accordingly, if refiners can't sell or store the diesel that they produce, they'd eventually be forced to cut their overall output, including of gasoline and jet fuel."

Looking at the US Gulf Coast alone, Capital Economics estimates that "diesel storage in the Gulf could rise to pandemic-era highs" because of a sharp fall in refinery utilisation, "within a matter of weeks".

"All told, the political aspect of being seen as doing something to help reduce fuel prices in the run-up to the midterms means that some form of export restriction now seems likely to be announced in the coming weeks," Mr Oxley said.

"This would further complicate the outlooks for energy markets and fuel price inflation.

"We suspect that it would be short-lived."

World.title: Public pool at centre of fight to change 'appalling' disaster policy
World.content:
It was not so long ago that residents of Wingham, on the NSW Mid North Coast, feared their only public pool might close due to mounting maintenance costs and dwindling attendance numbers.

Then came a record-breaking flood, which took the decision out of everyone's hands.

The pool suffered severe structural damage as 700 millimetres of rain fell on Wingham and Taree in May 2025, cracking and damaging its foundations, plumbing and reticulation system as the flood-soaked soil moved beneath it.

The news was another blow to a devastated community, as they realised what they had lost.

"The fact the pool was destroyed, it had an effect on people's wellbeing," Mid Coast Mayor Claire Pontin said.

"I'm sure even the people who didn't use the pool felt the loss of it because it just dampened the mood, sorry for the pun, right across Wingham."

Wingham Memorial Pool suffered irreparable structural and underground damage. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

Bob Clarke, who swam four days a week while the pool was open, said the health of the region's elderly had suffered since its closure.

"That's exercise I now don't get; but there are a lot of people that aren't getting that exercise," he said.

"It's a needed asset."

Bob Clarke used the pool four times a week while it was operational. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

Loss of swimming lessons concerning

Kate Spriggs, whose father helped campaign for the community-funded pool in the 1960s, said its closure also meant many families in Wingham and surrounding communities were missing out on swimming lessons.

"There are families that have been able to travel to Taree, but we also know there's a significant proportion of our community who can't afford to travel," she said.

" It's just not viable for them. "

A group of passionate swimmers worked to keep the community pool repair campaign alive. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

According to a Royal Life Saving Australia 2025 report, the swim skills of Australian children are declining.

The report found about half of Australian year 6 pupils were unable to swim a 50-metre pool lap or tread water for two minutes.

A 2024 study assessing the social value of Australia's pools also found they were crucial for community members of all backgrounds to connect and develop social connections, significantly improving people's health and wellbeing.

Locals say many families have gone without swimming lessons. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

The situation galvanised the community, which embarked on a 16-month campaign to secure funding for a rebuild.

Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced $15 million in state and federal funding for the project, which Ms Spriggs described as "fantastic news".

"Not only does the pool bring health benefits but it's the social connections that it brings to the community, an opportunity for people to spend time with each other … to bring other towns to the area," she said.

The Wingham Memorial Pool (bottom left corner) was badly affected by the flood. (Supplied: Mid Coast Council)

An 'appalling policy'

But while funding has now been secured, the fact the pool was not considered "essential public infrastructure" meant it was not immediately eligible for disaster funding.

Cr Pontin said she had spoken to federal Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain about changing the classification.

"It's absolutely an appalling policy," she said.

Claire Pontin is advocating for better access to disaster relief funds. (ABC Mid North Coast: Marina Trajkovich)

The minister said feedback from councils would be considered, with a new local government taskforce discussing disaster funding challenges during their first meeting this week.

Cr Pontin said changes to the disaster categorisation system and new support package options for councils were also being developed in response to increased frequency and severity of natural disasters.

Anthony Albanese announced $15 million to rebuild the Wingham Memorial Pool, with Kristy McBain working on reforms to streamline disaster funding. (ABC News: ABC South East NSW: Floss Adams)

"The thing councils have spoken to me about is trying to streamline the process as much as possible," Ms McBain said.

"We know already that there is an audit process that the state requires and then there's a separate audit process that the federal government requires.

"We are working really closely with them … so councils can access that money quicker."

The minister said while securing funding for the Wingham Memorial Pool had been a "process", the correct steps had been followed to get "the right outcome".

Claire Pontin is calling for public pools to be classed as essential infrastructure. (Supplied: Isaac Goessling)

"In a disaster we have to get communities moving as soon as possible, which is why that essential public asset rebuild looks at roads and bridges to make sure communities remain connected," she said.

"But it is important we take those recreational assets into account."

Cr Pontin said the Wingham pool could be reopened by December 2027.

World.title: NT police members allegedly circulated explicit AI video of senior officer
World.content:
A former Northern Territory Police assistant commissioner has taken her old colleagues to court for sharing a deepfake sexually explicit video that used her professional photograph.

Janelle Tonkin issued a statement yesterday after criminal proceedings on the issue were finalised, saying the incident was part of broader problems within the NT Police Force.

"In December 2025, I became aware that an AI-generated, sexually explicit video had been created using my official Northern Territory Police photograph," she said.

The video was then allegedly shared among serving members of the police force.

The outcome of the court proceedings is unknown.

Ms Tonkin said what happened to her was "extremely distressing, personally and professionally".

Janelle Tonkin says her professional portrait photograph was turned into pornography and circulated among colleagues. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Having my professional portrait photograph, taken in the course of my job turned into pornography and circulated among colleagues is something no person should have to experience, at work or anywhere else," she said.

Ms Tonkin, who is now president of the advocacy group Australasian Council of Women and Policing, said the deepfake video was not an isolated incident.

"It sits within a broader set of experiences I've had over recent times in this organisation, experiences I haven't yet spoken about publicly, and intend to, in full, when the time is right," she said.

"For now, I'll say this much: there remains real work to do, from the most senior levels of the Northern Territory Police Force down to the rank and file, to build a workplace where every officer, regardless of gender, race or religion, is treated with the safety, respect and support they're entitled to expect."

The NTPF says it has zero tolerance for bullying in any form. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In a statement, a Northern Territory Police Force spokesperson said they do not "comment on internal investigations" and were legally constrained from commenting on matters before the court.

"However, the conduct that Commander Tonkin was subject to in this matter, was, and always will be, totally unacceptable," they said.

"The NTPF has zero tolerance for bullying in any form.

"Every NT Police employee has the right to a safe, respectful and inclusive workplace, and the NTPF is committed to holding those standards across all levels of the organisation."

The spokesperson said recruits were taught "standards of conduct and workplace behaviour expected of them", including respect and anti-harassment.

World.title: How OpenAI agents tried to thwart cybersecurity amid Medicare hack
World.content:
A swarm of OpenAI's rogue artificial intelligence agents appear to have worked together to try to circumvent cybersecurity defences and find ways to access Australian government health data, according to public traces of their conversation logs they posted online.

Their efforts to answer a question — including devising ways to access a federal government website blocking their access — was laid out on a German coding website OpenAI had previously confirmed was hijacked by its unreleased AI models in June.

It comes as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed OpenAI had informed the federal government its AI had accessed non-public information about Medicare health statistics held by Services Australia in June.

The government agency discussed by the AI agents online, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW), was in the list of government websites Mr Albanese said was accessed by OpenAI's internal model.

Neither OpenAI nor the federal government have confirmed whether these were part of the same incident.

How AI agents swarmed another company Tens of thousands of messages from hundreds of rogue OpenAI agents reveal how the self-described "collective" coordinated the attack on AI infrastructure company Hugging Face.

Earlier this month, OpenAI confirmed Reuters reporting that its AI agents had used website DseWiki to communicate with each other, unbeknownst to them.

Archived versions of this website show more than a dozen OpenAI agents mentioned AIHW over 300 times on this website.

The logs show these AI agents were trying to access data about the average data spent on skin medicines by Victorian local government area.

One agent wrote on the message board: "Question ask January 2022 rolling 12 month average government cost per person for Dematologicals, Victoria LGAs. R1 Wodonga deadline passed; R2 Ballarat passed; R3 expected around 23:10 benchmark / 22:58 wiki time. Need exact data urgently.".

These attempts were initially blocked by cybersecurity provider Cloudflare, which is often used to block non-human traffic while allowing people to access webpages.

The logs show the agents shared information about how they tried to use proxies, screenshotting services and even to guess the file names to try and get around security.

The attempts to access data happened around the same time as OpenAI disclosed its internal models accessed non-public government data while trying to carry out a task given to them by staff.

"We identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," they said.

The German coding forum's logs do not show any reference to Medicare or Services Australia.

OpenAI has not yet published a full review of what it called the "wiki incident", but previously did not classify this as a "security incident".

OpenAI, the Prime Minister's Office and Services Australia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Fed-up crime victims have their say on 'breach bail, go to jail' laws
World.content:
Exhausted and fed-up crime victims have filled a small hall in the regional Queensland town of Mareeba, determined to have their say on proposed tougher bail laws.

The gathering was one of a number of hearings being held by a parliamentary committee across North and Far North Queensland on the state government's proposed "Breach Bail, Go to Jail" legislation.

Under the bill, courts must be satisfied to a "high degree of confidence" that an accused person will not reoffend before granting bail on serious charges.

It also introduces a new offence for those who commit a serious offence while on bail, carrying a mandatory 12 months in custody.

Cairns local Paul Drabble shared his anger to the committee over the government's failures to protect the community. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Mareeba local Barry Simpson told the committee current legislation failed to protect victims, and he hoped tougher bail laws would make a difference.

He said his wife and family were haunted by having someone break into his room at night, steal his keys and car, and write off the vehicle.

"The biggest thing they stole was our feeling of safety and security," he told the committee.

" If you haven't been broken into, you really don't know what the hell you're talking about. "

In Cairns, FNQ Softball representative Lyn Kelly told the committee her staff were exhausted after constant break-ins and vandalism at their Edmonton sporting complex.

She said volunteers were holding sausage sizzles to cover damage costs, while government funding that could have gone to help kids play sport was being used to fund CCTV cameras instead.

Member for Nicklin Marty Hunt chaired the parliamentary committee hearings in Cairns, Mareeba and Townsville. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Mums and dads are cleaning up before the children can even play their sport. Volunteers are exhausted," Ms Kelly said.

She told the committee of two instances in May where staff were unable to get out of their cars as young people continued to vandalise the grounds.

"Myself and others were terrified to even go to the grounds so we cancelled those nights," she said.

Victims told the committee of the personal cost of crime, from thousands of dollars in damage to fear that kept them up at night.

The majority backed the bill's push to get repeat youth offenders off the streets, while others called for early intervention and detention programs to operate alongside or instead of the laws.

Across hearings in Cairns, Mareeba and Townsville, about 120 people attended.

Community mislead

At the Townsville hearings, former inmate Tahlia Isaac said the committee was misleading the community into a false sense of safety.

"Stop selling victims of crime the lie that stronger laws are going to keep them safer," she told committee members.

Ms Isaac said it was "luck" that let her turn her life from drug crime to helping female prisoners re-enter society.

Without a focus on rehabilitation, she said the bail laws would "exacerbate" reoffending.

Former inmate Tahlia Isaac says rehabilitation support in custody helped her break out of criminality. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"My sentence length wasn't what changed my behaviour, it was the supports that I received while I was in custody," she said.

Ms Isaac opposed holding children to the same standards as adults, and said the system needed to be redesigned entirely.

"Stronger sentences, longer sentences and harsher penalties do nothing to curb crime; they only warehouse the problem," she said.

"We need to be addressing the reasons why people are committing these offences in the first place."

Opposition from legal experts

Across the board, legal experts fronting the committee warned the bail laws could have unintended consequences for victims and put pressure on the justice system.

Cairns barrister Shay-Lee Laing, representing the Australian Lawyers Alliance, told the hearings the bill required a conviction on the original charge before an accused could plead to the new offence.

Cairns barrister Shay-Lee Laing told the committee the proposed laws could have negative consequences for crime victims. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

She said that could make alleged offenders less likely to plead guilty, to avoid facing the extra charge.

"The bill removes an incentive to resolve the matter early and that incentive presently works in favour of victims and witnesses," she said.

She also warned the new bail test could disadvantage children with disabilities or unstable housing.

"It really risks operating as a proxy for access to those things," she said.

First Nations support group director Carl Lymburner works with Indigenous offenders through the court system, incarceration and release.

The Bindal man, who had his own history of crime, said the bill lacked the right emphasis on rehabilitation, likening prisons to missions for First Nations people.

"Instead of being put on missions, we're being moved to prisons and that's youth and kids now," he said.

Bindal man and advocate Carl Lymburner wants the bail reforms to have a focus on rehabilitation. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

Mr Lymburner backed jailing serious reoffenders but wanted rehabilitative programs with an Indigenous cultural element built into the system instead.

Regional hearings have now concluded, and the committee will prepare a report for parliament.

The Crisafulli government has said it intends to have the bill through parliament before the end of the year.

World.title: Youth crime down as Victoria's crime rate continues to fall
World.content:
Youth crime has dropped in Victoria as the state's record crime rate continues to fall, new figures show.

The latest crime data, released today, reveals that in the past year to June, the state's crime rate dropped by 3.8 per cent.

Youth offending decreased by 8.1 per cent in that time.

While police say crime in Victoria remains "unacceptably high" at more than 13 per cent higher than three years ago, several major crimes decreased.

Serious and violent crimes dropped by 4 per cent, home invasions fell by 27 per cent, and carjackings decreased by 25 per cent.

Police say organised crime, repeat offenders, mental health and drugs are the main drivers of crime. (ABC News)

Crime Statistics Agency Chief Statistician Fiona Dowsley told 774 ABC Melbourne that a 20 per cent drop in burglaries and break-ins was "really significant", but that the cause of the fall was difficult to determine.

"Potentially there's been a bit of crime prevention that's influencing that. We certainly have quite a few people who are being remanded for those offences, so that can have a temporary effect," she said.

" These things do have a certain amount of ebb and flow. We have seen a very big increase and we're now seeing a big decrease back down. "

Fiona Dowsley is the chief statistician at the Crime Statistics Agency. (Supplied)

Robberies dropped 22 per cent and burglaries by almost 20 per cent.

Police say organised crime, repeat offenders, mental health and drugs are the main drivers of crime, with trafficking and dealing drugs such as cocaine, meth, ecstasy and prescription drugs spiking by 18.5 per cent.

Theft also dropped, with car theft falling by 5 per cent and theft from a motor vehicle by 10 per cent.

Meanwhile, retail theft climbed by almost 3 per cent.

Victoria Police still facing retention crisis

Family violence offending decreased by 3 per cent across metropolitan Melbourne and Victoria's regions, with police attributing the fall to a record 16,500 family violence-related arrests.

Regional Operations Deputy Commissioner Bob Hill said the drop in the state's crime rate was promising, but more work still needed to be done to make Victorians feel safe.

"Our work is far from over," he said.

"We remain firmly committed to reducing harm across the community and will continue striving not only to meet our targets, but to exceed them.

"Victoria Police will continue to focus on prevention where we can, enforcement where we must, and maintaining the visible, proactive policing presence that communities in this state rightly expect and deserve."

Deputy Commissioner Bob Hill was encouraged by the overall drop in crime. (ABC News)

Figures also showed Victoria Police is still grappling with a major retention crisis, with 1340 unfilled roles.

That figure follows Premier Ben Carroll's pledge earlier this week to recruit 1500 extra police to crack down on crime in Victoria.

The latest crime data comes after an auditor-general report this week found Victoria's $40 million flagship initiative to stop youth crime had failed to show it had driven down youth offending.

Damning report finds no evidence $40m youth program reduces offending About two thirds of young people engaged in the Youth Crime Prevention Program offended within six months of starting it, a Victorian auditor-general's report has found.

Former premier Daniel Andrews launched the program in 2016 under the premise it was "proven to help reduce offending", but the report said the Department of Justice and Community Safety had no evidence to prove it.

The review also found more than two thirds of the youths involved went on to re-offend within six months of starting the program.

Meanwhile, a report published today by Victoria's Sentencing Advisory Council found prison terms for major crimes such as murder rape and were getting longer.

Following the introduction of standard terms for such crimes in 2018, the median sentence for murder rose from 21 to 24 years, rape from six to seven years and 11 years, up from seven years, for trafficking offences.

World.title: Forrestania lifts WA British Hill gold resource past 210,000 ounces
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Forrestania lifts WA British Hill gold resource past 210,000 ounces Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 24, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Forrestania Resources has delivered a solid 21 per cent increase to its British Hill gold resource, lifting the deposit’s total inventory to 212,400 ounces as it assembles the building blocks for a major two-hub gold production business in Western Australia. The updated mineral resource estimate for the project now stands at 4.12 million tonnes grading 1.6 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for a total of 212,400 ounces using a 0.5g/t gold cutoff. Notably, the update includes a significant 37 per cent increase in the higher-confidence indicated resource category, which now accounts for 138,100 ounces, or about two-thirds of the total deposit. Forrestania Resources has three reverse circulation rigs (pictured) and one diamond rig operating at its British Hill gold project in WA. The upgrade incorporated results from 15 holes of an ongoing 3685 metre reverse-circulation drilling campaign, which has already served up one hole with an eye-catching 59-metre intersection grading 2.38g/t gold from 123m. Three RC rigs and one diamond rig are still turning rods at the project, focused on extending mineralisation along strike and down-dip. Within the project’s global resource, a recently landed British Hill prefeasibility study also points to a maiden ore reserve at British Hill of 1.56 million tonnes at 1.43g/t gold for 71,900 ounces, capable of generating A$104.8 million in pre-tax free cash flow for a restart capital of just $16.1M.



‘This updated mineral resource estimate represents another important milestone in the growth of the British Hill mineral resource.’ Forrestania Resources executive chairman David Geraghty The expanding ounce-count is expected to feed directly into Forrestania’s ambitious strategy of creating a significant West Australian gold production business powered by two key processing hubs, the 2.9-million-tonne-per-annum Edna May plant and the 3.2-million-tonne-per-annum Lake Johnston facility. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “This updated Mineral Resource Estimate, released just one month after the previous estimate, represents another important milestone in the growth of the British Hill Mineral Resource. This update not only materially expands the gold inventory at British Hill but also delivers a significant increase in higher-confidence Indicated Mineral Resources, which now comprise more than half of the total contained gold ounces.” The company is running a textbook hub-and-spoke playbook, consolidating a portfolio of satellite gold deposits to funnel ore to its soon-to-be operating mills. This approach allows Forrestania to potentially fast-track development, avoiding the significant capital and time required to construct new processing plants from scratch. Anchoring the company’s ambitions is the Edna May project, where a recent prefeasibility study outlined a robust 10-year operation. The study defined an ore reserve of 12.6 million tonnes at 0.99g/t gold for 402,800 ounces and projected it could spin off a hefty $728.7 million in pre-tax free cash flow across the mine’s decade-long life. The numbers are based on a $98 million to get the mine up and running and an all-in sustaining cost of A$3293 per ounce, assuming a gold price of A$5500 per ounce.



Alongside the Edna May and British Hill studies, Forrestania has also been advancing its other satellite deposits, landing additional prefeasibility studies for its Tycho and Johnson Range projects. Demonstrating its intent to move quickly, the company has already started trucking ore from British Hill to its Lake Johnston facility to accelerate near-term production. However, while Lake Johnston offers the early processing option, the long-term plan is for British Hill ore to be treated at the larger Edna May plant. The Lake Johnston facility is currently undergoing a significant overhaul to bring it back online, while the flagship Edna May plant is scheduled for a restart in early 2027 after new mill liners are installed. Once both are operational, Forrestania will command a formidable combined processing capacity exceeding six million tonnes per annum. The company’s rapid progress has not gone unnoticed. Forrestania recently announced it will be included in the influential VanEck Junior Gold Miners ETF. An inclusion in the widely followed fund is a significant nod from the global investment community and is likely to put the company on the radar of a much broader international audience. While today’s resource bump at British Hill is a solid win on its own, it’s the bigger picture that is likely to turn heads. The company is no longer just an explorer, but is rapidly assembling the assets, infrastructure and economic studies of a multi-hub gold producer.



With the Edna May project as Forrestania’s solid foundation, a conga line of satellite deposits such as British Hill being lined up to feed two refurbished mills and the backing of a major global ETF, the company is building a compelling story that will likely command attention from serious market watchers in a bullish gold market. World.title: The Trump effect: Why cracks are widening in financial markets
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets Opinion The Trump effect: Why cracks are widening in financial markets Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 24, 2026 — 11:59am

September 24, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s a rapid shift underway in the global cost of capital, with yields in the world’s key bond market soaring on Wednesday. The US bond market provides the reference points for global debt worldwide and developments in that market are undermining the finances of governments worldwide, while adding to the pressure on companies and households. Trump’s aggressive treatment of America’s long-term allies and his erratic policies are remaking the US bond market into something other than the world’s safe haven that it has been in the past. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Yields in the US Treasuries market have been edging up all year, driven by rising US government deficits and debt and an inflation rate kept stubbornly high by Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East, his trade wars and the boom in artificial intelligence-related investment. On Wednesday, the day started badly for the market when there was a sell-off in European bonds in response to another surge above $US100 a barrel in oil prices after Iran responded to Trump’s threat at the United Nations to annihilate the country by saying it wouldn’t relinquish control of the Strait of Hormuz unless and until the US lifted its sanctions.



The oil price, below $US100 a barrel on Tuesday, is now trading around $US103 a barrel. The selloff accelerated after the mid-morning release of the S&P Global flash US Composite PMI (purchasing managers) Output Index, which showed an unexpected jump in manufacturing and service sector activity, as well as a surge in the prices of business inputs. Related Article Opinion

Executive shake-up Warren Buffett just took a big risk with the $1.5 trillion giant he built Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Then, at 1pm (New York time), a $US70 billion auction of five-year Treasury notes experienced weak demand, selling at a yield well above traders’ expectations. “Primary dealers” – those who are forced buyers at auctions – ended up with unusually large allocations. Even the announcement by US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, of a $US6 billion bond buyback couldn’t avert the flood of selling. Bessent’s transparent attempt to manipulate and cap bond yields was destined to fail, and has failed.



The yield on the benchmark 10-year bonds jumped from 4.96 per cent to as much as 5.13 per cent, its highest level since 2007, ahead of the global financial crisis. In February, before the war in the Middle East started, that yield was 3.94 per cent. Across the yield curve the yields rose while, in the sharemarket, equity indices – which have, thanks to the AI stocks, been at record levels, fell. The S&P 500 was down 0.8 per cent and the Nasdaq index 1.1 per cent. Markets around the world are on shaky ground. AP If the US Federal Reserve Board’s 25 basis point increase in its policy rate – its first-rate rise in more than three years – didn’t signal it, the decisive move above 5 per cent by the 10-year bond yield says the US has entered a new, higher-rate environment. With the futures market now pricing the odds of another Fed rate hike next month – just ahead of the midterm elections in the US – at about 70 per cent, with more rate rises to come next year, the US has entered a new rate-raising cycle.



Related Article Opinion

Oil ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist While the combination of better-than-expected growth – the OECD has forecast developed economy-leading 2.2 per cent growth in US GDP for this year – and stubbornly high inflation is peculiar to the US, the turmoil in its bond market, and the factors driving it, aren’t. There are similar spikes in yields occurring in most of the major markets. While the rising US yields might be having some influence on global yields, the more significant correlations relate to historically high, and unsustainable, levels of governments’ deficits and debt. In the US, the deficit is pushing $US2 trillion, or 6 per cent of GDP, this year, while gross federal government debt is above $US40 trillion and the net debt-to GDP ratio is just under 100 per cent. Large parts of Europe have similar, if not worse, metrics, so it isn’t surprising that yields in the eurozone have also spiked. Trump’s trade and real wars haven’t helped. The movement in the 10-year bond yield on Wednesday was the biggest one-day rise since Trump unveiled his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year.



His tariffs, and the impact of the war in the Middle East on oil, and therefore petrol and diesel prices, have driven inflation and interest rates up and growth down in most of the developed world, with US growth sheltered by the AI-driven investment boom. That, too, is driving costs and inflation up and, by adding to the supply of debt and competing with government bonds for investors’ funds, is also adding to the pressure on US bond prices, which fall as yields rise. Since the 2008 financial crisis, the US and other major economies have operated generally within a low-rate environment and one that, until the post-pandemic disruption to global supply chains, was also one of low inflation. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s transparent attempt to manipulate and cap bond yields was destined to fail, and has failed. AP By historical standards a 5 per cent 10-year bond yield isn’t abnormal – the post-war average is around 4.7 per cent. Since the financial crisis, however, the yield has averaged about 2.8 per cent, so the current pricing regime is one that most people and businesses haven’t experienced in a generation.



There may be more to come. There’s no obvious end in sight to the war in the Middle East and the impact of high transport fuel costs, and Trump’s tariffs, are still seeping into the wider economy and the cost of goods. There’s also no sign of any enthusiasm by either the Republicans or Democrats, or their counterparts in parliaments around the developed world, to even start to take the painful decisions required to stabilise ballooning deficit and debt levels, let alone start to reduce them. While the combination of better-than-expected growth – the OECD has forecast developed economy-leading 2.2 per cent growth in US GDP for this year – and stubbornly high inflation is peculiar to the US, the turmoil in its bond market, and the factors driving it, aren’t. A particular problem facing the US is that those who were large and long-term buyers and holders of its debt in the past are deserting it. Foreign governments – particularly China, which has more than halved its Treasury holdings from their peak in 2013 – have been reducing their exposure to the US, replaced at the margin by hedge funds and retail investors.



Some of that reduced interest can be attributed to the shock generated when Russia’s foreign exchange reserves were frozen after its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as well as to the way the US has US its dominance of the global financial system to slap sanctions on its perceived foes. There has been a surge in central bank buying of gold in response. It also relates to the rate at which the US Treasury has been issuing new debt is outpacing the growth rate of sovereign reserves in the rest of the world. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump’s war is strangling the world Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Whatever the reasons, long-term passive investors have been replaced by shorter term and more leveraged traders that are probably more willing to dump their holdings in response to shifts in the perceived risks. That could be adding to the more volatile conditions in the bond market and the upward pressure on yields in what is, in the Trump era, a period of heightened financial and geopolitical risks.



The ever-increasing debt load, Trump’s aggressive treatment of America’s long-term allies and his erratic (and commonly self-destructive) policies are remaking the US bond market into something other than the world’s safe haven that it has been in the post-war period at a moment when the global economy and financial markets are as leveraged and vulnerable as they’ve ever been.
