World.title: Missing tourist last seen at scenic mountain lookout near Queenstown
World.content:
Police are appealing for help to find a missing tourist last seen at a scenic mountain lookout near Queenstown nearly a week ago.

Erika was last seen on Skippers Saddle near Coronet Peak last Friday, wearing a black hat, tan brown puffer jacket, black tights and hiking boots.

Missing person 'Erika'. Police / supplied

Her rental car has been found, but she remains missing.

Police search and rescue and local Coastguard are searching the land and water in the immediate area.

Erika has dark, curly hair, is of Brazilian descent and usually wears glasses.

World.title: 'Bright as': Fireball lights up skies above Taranaki Maunga
World.content:
An expert says it's possible a fireball seen over the North Island on Wednesday night left behind space rocks for scientists to examine, and enthusiasts to look at - but not touch.

The meteor lit up the skies over Taranaki - including the maunga - just before 11pm, and was caught on camera.

Andy Banks didn't see the event live, but early on Thursday morning heard about it and realised he might have caught it on one of his cameras in Kaponga.

"Turns out the roof camera had the best view, and what a view," he said in an email to RNZ. "Having the mountain as a backdrop just added to the phenomenon."

He wasn't the only one to capture it - Fireballs Aotearoa said it "fell over the ocean west of Marakopa".

"I was having a joint on the doorstep and looked up," one follower commented on Facebook, calling it "bright as".

Te Whatu Stardome Observatory and Planetarium education lead Dr Kaitlyn Martin said it was difficult to tell from the videos how large the rock was when it lit up, but it "would have been considerably larger before entering the atmosphere than any fragment surviving near the end".

"Something between a softball and a rugby ball would be a reasonable rough illustration - certainly we're not talking about a car-sized asteroid… The glowing that we're seeing in the videos isn't the size of the rock itself, but the light produced as it travels through and interacts with the atmosphere."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405510051112

While it was heading offshore, Martin said there was a chance parts of it were on land.

"When the fireball 'goes out', that doesn't necessarily mean the rock has disappeared. If fragments survive, they slow dramatically and enter what's called dark flight: they're no longer travelling fast enough to produce the bright meteor, but they're still falling.

"Where they eventually land is harder to predict because of factors like wind and size/shape of the remaining fragment impacting the trajectory. But that kind of modelling can be done - Fireballs Aotearoa have successfully used it to recover meteorites or fragments from events like Takapō in 2024 and the Ruamāhanga fireball in July this year."

Fireballs Aotearoa told 1News they were not planning a hunt for this one, as it likely fell into the ocean, though parts of it may have ended their interplanetary journey on land.

Martin said without more analysis it wouldn't be clear if this rock was part of a known shower or a "sporadic meteoroid" - a lone traveller.

"The increasing availability of footage from security cameras and citizen science projects like Fireballs Aotearoa [and] their network of cameras is so useful - the data from multiple observations of the same fireball is really what makes us able to do any type of analysis on path, orbit, size, and speed beyond, 'Wow! Bright flash!'"

If you did find a space rock, she suggested not disturbing it "because you could contaminate or damage a scientifically valuable sample".

"The best thing you can do is take photos of the meteorite and its landing site, mark exactly where and when you found it, don't disturb, and send that information to Fireballs Aotearoa and the Royal Astronomical Society of New Zealand."

World.title: New Zealand First campaigns on slashing tax rate for small businesses to 20%
World.content:
New Zealand First will campaign on slashing the tax rate for small businesses to 20 percent.

The party says the drop from 28 percent is a "much-needed bold step" to encourage more investment, expansion, productivity and employment.

The rate would apply to businesses with turnover under $30 million, and cost the government $1 billion.

The party said that would be "more than covered" in the medium term by more companies collectively paying a lower tax rate, higher employment, a growing economy, and more spending.

"Corporate taxes can reduce productivity, particularly in entrepreneurial and innovative sectors," it said in a statement.

"Lower company tax rates can improve long-run productivity growth, and stimulate the creation of new companies."

It said the policy was a move away from "short-term sugar hits to consumers" and towards long term investment in businesses.

Australia made a similar move in recent years which provided a credible international model, it said.

World.title: Government hits pause on council amalgamation plan until after election
World.content:
Audio player for " Andrew Little reacts to decision to pause council amalgamations " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1552378%2Fgovernment-hits-pause-on-council-amalgamation-plan-until-after-election

Andrew Little reacts to decision to pause council amalgamations Midday Report Download MP3 6m

The Government has told mayors around the country it's deferring decisions on amalgamating councils until after the election.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop and Local Government Minister Simon Watts said they would be taking additional time before deciding which proposals, part of the Head Start local government reform process, should progress to the detailed design stage.

"It is clear from the response we received that there is genuine appetite for change," Watts said in a statement.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405514951112

Eighteen proposals were submitted in August against the Government's objectives for a simpler, more effective and accountable local government system.

"While the overall quality of proposals was high, none came with the unanimous view of the region, and some needed further analysis before they can progress. These are important gaps we must fill in prior to making final decisions."

Particular areas that required further development included ensuring fair and effective representation with streamlined governance, and the transfer and delivery of regional functions, the ministers said.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts and RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop when the amalgamation was announced. SAMUEL RILLSTONE / RNZ

"Rather than asking councils to commit further time and resources to finalise proposals now, the Government will now work to fill in these gaps over the next few months. Cabinet will consider these proposals in early-2027."

Bishop said the Government remained committed to local government reform.

"The Government continues to expect proposals endorsed by Cabinet to be developed in detail and considered for final approval in 2027, with Head Start changes intended to be in place ahead of the 2028 local government elections."

"Work is also continuing on the backstop process for areas that do not progress through Head Start. Decisions on that process will be informed by lessons from the Head Start pathway, consultation feedback and further advice from officials. We continue to expect decisions on this in early 2027."

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Ministers made promises they couldn't keep - Wellington mayor

But Wellington City mayor Andrew Little said the announcement showed the Government was not serious about the process.

Little, who is also co-chair of the Wellington and Wairarapa Mayoral Forum, said councils across the region put forward strong proposals that met the Government's requirements and would have worked, while spending nearly $250,000 collectively to put forward a proposal before the recent deadline - which was "significant time and ratepayer money".

Little told reporters councils had done everything the Government had asked of them, and they had "been let down".

It was "poor organisation" - the government had made a promise it couldn't keep, Little said, as it clearly didnt have the numbers to enact reform.

He said there had been mixed views among residents and ratepayers on whether to amalgamate or not, "but on balance people supported it".

The government's attribution of the delay to the fact that the proposals were not unanimous - an aspect that wasn't requested of them in the first place, Little said - was "effectively shifting the goalposts".

Andrew Little. RNZ / Baz MacDonald

Millions had been spent nationwide by councils in preparing headstart proposals, he said.

If the government wanted change in time for 2028, councils were "rapidly running out of time", Little said.

"Ministers asked us to move quickly. We did exactly that. It is now clear the Government was not ready to follow through, and didn't have enough support around the Cabinet table."

Little said ministers made promises they couldn't keep and have now abandoned the process.

"Wellington ratepayers are entitled to ask why they were asked to pay for an exercise the Government was not prepared to complete.

"At a time when councils are doing everything possible to keep costs under control, facing an arbitrary rates cap that will affect services and facilities that communities rely on, spending nearly a quarter of a million dollars on a process that goes nowhere is unacceptable."

He said the three-month deadline was "totally unreasonable" and criteria continually shifted.

"We met all of the government's requirements to get a proposal in before the deadline.

"The only party that has not thought through their policy is central government themselves. It claims it is wanting to simplify local government, but today it has confirmed it has no plan for how to achieve this."

RNZ / Angus Dreaver

'Communities will not tolerate ratepayer money being spent on unclear processes'

Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) said councils moved heaven and earth to meet an unrealistic deadline for proposals, and now need certainty.

LGNZ president Rehette Stoltz said the Government's inability to decide which proposals will progress has left councils feeling frustrated.

"Councils were put through a rushed process, only for the Government to now acknowledge that the work could not be completed properly in the time available," she said.

"Communities will not tolerate ratepayer money being spent on unclear processes that are repeatedly reshaped after the work has been done. Before councils do more work, they need certainty the goal posts won't be moved again."

She maintained reform should be locally led, not driven from the Beehive.

"Local government reform is too important to be subject to a constantly changing process."

Selwyn district mayor Lydia Gliddon. RNZ / ANNA SAREGNT

More mayors react

Selwyn district mayor Lydia Gliddon said it was disappointing that councils had been asked to quickly develop and submit proposals only for the decisions to now be deferred.

"Selwyn invested significant effort into this process, including consulting with our communities. We owe it to those who took the time to share their views to ensure their voices continue to be heard," she said.

The council remained committed to working with the government to achieve the best outcome for its communities.

"The position of Selwyn residents has been very clear. Through our consultation, people told us overwhelmingly that they wanted Selwyn to become a standalone unitary authority, and we will continue to support and advocate for that view going forward," she said.

"As New Zealand's fastest-growing district, Selwyn faces unique growth, infrastructure and service delivery challenges.

"Our district is experiencing growth at a scale few other parts of New Zealand are facing, and it's important any future local government arrangements recognise those realities and give our communities a strong voice."

The Waitaki District Council straddles two regional council boundaries, working across the different planning systems, regulatory approaches and policy frameworks.

Waitaki district mayor Mel Tavendale. Jackie Tav

Waitaki district mayor Mel Tavendale said it created duplication, burdening ratepayers and the council with added cost, time and pressure, which was unsustainable.

She did not want to lose the momentum for change after councils invested a lot of time, money and effort to develop a solution on a tight deadline.

"The need for reform has not gone away, and we are disappointed because we did the work asked of us," she said.

"Waitaki put forward a credible, practical and well-considered proposal in good faith that reflects communities of interest and responds directly to the need for greater scale, capability and affordability."

Tavendale said Waitaki wanted a seat at the design table so that local communities could decide their own future.

The council has faced flak after originally proposing a 45 percent rates rise to plug a $14 million operating deficit, prompting backtracking, death threats and protest before settling on an average district-wide rates increase of about 17 percent.

Hundreds of Waitaki ratepayers rallied on 25 June 2026 against a 17 percent rates hike they say is unaffordable and will force people to choose between paying their bill or necessities like power and food. RNZ / Tess Brunton

"Ministers have been critical of Waitaki's rates rises, but those increases are being driven in part by a system that clearly needs reform," Tavendale said.

The mayors of Timaru, Mackenzie, Waimate and Waitaki districts lodged a single unitary authority proposal that would see a new region stretch from Aoraki Mount Cook to the coast, and from Ashburton to Waitaki.

Tavendale said it would create a stronger regional voice and ensure rural communities remained heard.

"The government also needs to consider how it will support local communities through the change process, so the weight of reform does not fall entirely on ratepayers."

Labour said the government's plans for council reform were an embarassing and expensive distraction.

Government has delivered a 'false start', Labour says

Local government spokesperson Tangi Utikere said ministers Chris Bishop and Simon Watts had promised a "head start", but delivered a "false start".

"They gave councils three months to spend time and money planning major structural change, only to pull the plug on getting anything done before the election.

"That's a huge embarrassment for a government that has spent months telling councils this was a priority."

He said Labour was not opposed to local government reform.

"There are sensible conversations to be had about councils working together, sharing services and delivering better value.

"But timing matters - local economies are struggling, businesses are under pressure and construction workers and tradies are crying out for work."

World.title: Labour pledges $4 billion for state houses, school repairs and hospitals
World.content:
Audio player for " Ginny Anderson discusses new building plan policy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1552827%2Flabour-pledges-4-billion-for-state-houses-school-repairs-and-hospitals

Ginny Anderson discusses new building plan policy Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Labour is promising to create more jobs by building homes, improving classrooms and repairing hospitals at a total cost of more than $4 billion.

The party says it will deliver at least 6000 additional social housing places over four years, school improvements at more than 2000 schools and hospital improvements, too.

Its allocated nearly $3b for building new state houses, $450 million for school repairs, and $200m toward health.

It also allocated $760m to cover the additional Income-Related Rent Subsidy and operating costs for Kāinga Ora and Community Housing Providers.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins and Labour jobs spokesperson Ginny Andersen made the policy announcement in Hamilton on Thursday.

Chris Hipkins in Hamilton on Thursday. RACHEL MOORE / RNZ

They pointed to an 11-year high in unemployment and struggling construction businesses, saying the party would get building projects underway and "more Kiwis back on the tools".

Hipkins said: "Labour will build the infrastructure New Zealand needs, create jobs and ensure the benefits return to local businesses and communities."

"Right now, homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing. We can do all three while creating good jobs for Kiwis."

He said government funding for a building project saw benefits beyond the worksite, with builders hiring tradies, tradies buying materials, suppliers getting more orders, apprentices getting hours, and local businesses benefiting from workers spending in their communities.

Andersen said unemployment at an 11-year high under National meant Labour wanted to get Kiwis back to work.

Chris Hipkins speaking with people in Hamilton. RACHEL MOORE / RNZ

"That means building homes, fixing schools and repairing hospitals, not sitting on our hands," she said.

"This is about putting government investment to work - improving public infrastructure, supporting local businesses and giving the construction sector greater certainty."

World.title: Warriors veteran centre Adam Pompey granted early release to join Australian NRL club
World.content:
Veteran centre Adam Pompey has been granted an early release from his contract with the NZ Warriors.

The Auckland-based NRL club announced the 28-year-old will depart for Australia after eight seasons with them.

While the Warriors did not confirm which club Pompey was moving to, Fox Sports reported he was expected to sign with the Melbourne Storm.

Pompey made 136 NRL appearances for the Warriors since his debut in 2019, scoring 288 points - including 39 tries and 66 goals.

"Adam has performed consistently for us since his arrival in 2019," Warriors general manager Andrew McFadden said.

"We appreciate the contribution he has made in his time here and wish him and his family the very best for what lies ahead for them in Australia."

Pompey sent to the sin bin against Dolphins. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Pompey is the latest to depart the club along with Roger Tuivasa-Sheck, who heads to Super League club Wakefield, Luke Metcalf who joins the Dragons, and Mitch Barnett who is headed to the Broncos.

Barnett will leave in exchange for outside back Grant Anderson.

Earlier this year, the Warriors announced the signing of Storm winger Will Warbrick on a three-year contract.

World.title: Fonterra reports $3.4 billion operating profit following sale of Mainland brands
World.content:
Fonterra has delivered a full-year profit of $2.6 billion in its financial results announced this morning.

The full-year operating profit of $3.4b was thanks in part to $1.2b from the sale of its Mainland brands to French dairy giant Lactalis.

Total revenue for Fonterra for the year was $27b, with nearly $20b in cash returns to New Zealand farmers.

The co-operative's return on capital was 14.2 percent, well above its previously stated target range of 10-12 percent.

The final Farmgate Milk Price for the 2025/26 season was $9.69 per kgMS.

The co-op also declared a final fully imputed dividend of 33 cents per share, bringing fully imputed total dividends for the year to 73 cents per share. This includes the 24 cent interim dividend and 16 cent special Mainland dividend paid in April.

Fonterra forecasts payout will drop by up to 50 cents a kg RNZ / YouTube

Fonterra paid outgoing chief executive Miles Hurrell a total of $8,158,782 in the last financial year, made up of a combination of salary and short and long-term incentive payouts.

Hurrell received a salary of $1,915,858 in FY26 alongside a short-term payout of $2,503,396 and a longer-term payout of $3,484,914.

Benefits, including Kiwisaver, added another $250,000.

Fonterra chief executive Richard Allen said the co-operative's disciplined approach to strategic execution has once again generated strong results.

"FY26 was a year of delivery. Our teams collected, processed and shipped near record volumes of milk, allocated products for the highest possible returns, and reliably delivered them to our customers right around the world."

"Despite some challenging conditions, including weather events and geopolitical volatility, we leveraged our full supply chain network and logistics partnerships to keep milk moving, achieving record shipping volumes and materially improving our delivery performance."

Fonterra chairman Peter McBride said the co-operative has continued building momentum and delivered at the top end of its performance expectations.

"Consistency is important to farmers and our shareholders. We're proud of the collective effort that's delivered another strong result, at the top end of our earnings guidance. The team hasn't missed a beat despite the Mainland divestment process and the significant change that followed.

World.title: Man charged with murder of Star Sami in Auckland's Blockhouse Bay
World.content:
A 23-year-old has been charged with murder following the death of Star Sami in Auckland's Blockhouse Bay.

Police say Star Fetu Peretiso Sami, 21, was on Holbrook Street in Blockhouse Bay on 22 August when there was what police described as a "violent altercation" and he was stabbed.

He got into a car and was driven a short distance to a bus stop where an ambulance was called but died the following day in hospital.

Acting Detective Inspector Craig Bolton said search warrants were carried out in Avondale and Massey on Thursday morning.

The arrest comes more than four weeks after Sami was left at a bus stop with stab wounds.

Bolton said the investigation was continuing and the man is due to appear in the Auckland District Court on Thursday afternoon.

"The Operation Falconer team has been working hard on progressing the homicide investigation over the past month, and it's a great outcome to have got to the point in laying a murder charge," Bolton said.

Earlier, police went to the coroner and asked for name suppression for Sami's name and gang affiliation.

That application was supported and continued by Sami's family who sought privacy after receiving abuse on social media.

Coroner Rachael Schmidt-McCleave, acting as the national duty coroner, granted an interim non-publication order prohibiting publication of the man's identity as well as the gang they were associated with.

Media were not informed of the application, which was granted on 25 August in chambers on the papers, or given an opportunity to oppose the non-publication order.

However, after allowing various media organisations including RNZ to respond, Coroner Janet Anderson found the case did not meet the threshold to continue suppression.

The coroner heard an impassioned plea from Sami's family for the suppression orders to continue. They pointed to receiving abuse on social media platforms and stressed that Sami was much more than a gang member.

"No one should receive unpleasant or offensive messages through social media," Coroner Anderson said in her decision released on 9 September.

"However, generally speaking it has been recognised that, 'the court is not the arbiter of social media standards'."

Dr Saleimoa Bill Sami, an uncle of Star Sami, issued a response to the coroner following her decision to lift the suppression order.

"As the restrictions now come to an end, our hope is simply that those who choose to report on Star do so with accuracy, fairness, balance and appropriate consideration for those experiencing trauma and grief.

"We also hope that reporting does not create an implication that Star's death was gang-motivated when police have expressly advised that there is presently no evidence of that."

The family said Star Sami was much more than the circumstances of his death.

"He was our son, brother, grandson, nephew, cousin, father and friend. We will continue to uphold his mana and awhi the whānau he has left behind as best we can."

Sami was also a former student of Kelston Boys' High School and part of its First XV.

World.title: Matildas name three uncapped players in squad for October friendlies
World.content:
After suffering a gut-wrenching ACL injury on the eve of her potential Matildas debut, midfielder Hana Lowry has been handed a national team recall.

Coach Joe Montemurro has named three uncapped players for his 26-player squad, which will face world number three Germany and world number 47 Haiti in Europe in October.

One of them is Lowry, who was previously selected in 2024 but was ruled out with a knee injury, and has been building ever since.

The 23-year-old signed a deal to move from A-League Women's club Sydney FC to Norway earlier this year and has impressed, scoring a goal and assisting another in her first seven games with the new club.

Former Sydney defender Tori Tumeth has also received a maiden call-up after shining for the Vancouver Rise in Canada's Northern Super League. At the same time, Melbourne Victory's Courtney Newbon is the third potential debutant.

But the Australians will be without stars Alanna Kennedy and Charlize Rule due to injury, while Arsenal midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross also won't join the team as she continues her return to football.

Midfielder Isabel Gomez and goalkeeper Ilona Melegh have been dropped after they were part of the side for their two-game series against Mexico in June.

Superstar Sam Kerr has been named to feature in the friendlies. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Defenders Charli Grant and Alexia Apostolakis, along with midfielder Daniela Galic, will return to the national team set-up.

European stars Mary Fowler, Caitlin Foord, Ellie Carpenter and Steph Catley have also been named, as well as Gotham City's Sam Kerr.

The October international window marks a crucial stage in the Matildas' preparation for the FIFA Women's World Cup, which gets underway in Brazil next June.

There are only a handful of international breaks before the showpiece tournament, meaning every game is crucial for Australia as they look to build on their fourth-place finish in 2023.

"We have a good mix of experience, players returning to the squad and players earning their first senior call-ups, which is important as we build towards the Women's World Cup," Montemurro said.

"We want to use these games to strengthen our connections, build confidence and continue developing as a team.

"Germany will test us against one of Europe's leading teams, while Haiti will provide a different style and perspective. Both will be valuable as we continue to prepare for the FIFA Women's World Cup."

Matildas squad

Alexia Apostolakis, Mackenzie Arnold (GK), Ellie Carpenter, Steph Catley, Alex Chidiac, Caitlin Foord, Mary Fowler, Daniela Galic, Charli Grant, Winonah Heatley, Sam Kerr, Chloe Lincoln (GK), Hana Lowry, Leticia McKenna, Holly McNamara, Alana Murphy, Courtney Nevin, Courtney Newbon (GK), Jamilla Rankin, Hayley Raso, Amy Sayer, Remy Siemsen, Kaitlyn Torpey, Tori Tumeth, Emily van Egmond, Clare Wheeler

World.title: 'That's why Taliban is scared': Cyclist's incredible journey to silver
World.content:
The easy part for Fariba Hashimi was winning a silver medal in the women's cycling road race at the Asian Games.

The nearly impossible part for the cyclist from Afghanistan was trying to train in her country. To do that, she dressed as a man in a place where women have few rights.

"All the time when I was going to training I was dressing as a guy," she said.

She said she also hid her face to avoid being recognised.

"Because sometimes when they recognised me, they were trying to throw … stone[s] or hitting me," she said.

Hashimi, who is 23, won silver overnight AEST in a time of 2 hours, 50 minutes, 5 seconds, which marked another leg in a journey that began in 2021 when she left Afghanistan, escaping to Italy with the help of former road racing world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.

Hashimi (left) with gold medallist Guo Li of China and bronze medallist Leung Wing Yee of Hong Kong. (Getty Images: Cen Yunpeng/Xinhu)

"In 2021, when the Taliban moved into my country, I escaped my country because I wanted to follow my dream," she said.

"I want to show the Afghanistan women in the world that … we can have an opportunity."

Hashimi talked about having many dreams for women in Afghanistan, dreams for herself and dreams that might take time to be realised.

"I'm really, really happy and I'm full of emotion. I don't know how I can explain it for you," she said.

"I hope one day I come back in my country and ride the streets of Kabul — and riding with the women side-by-side to share the same passion.

"And I hope in the future changing some things.

"I think we are really tired of the situation of our country and I hope the Taliban is watching. I know how much one woman can be powerful, and that's why Taliban is scared [of] women."

World.title: Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers
World.content:
Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers.

If Lachie Weller hadn't requested a trade to Gold Coast, would Andrew Brayshaw be at the club?

What if Adelaide had taken Hayden Young instead of Fischer McAsey in the 2019 draft?

AFL recruitment, especially at the draft, is an element of good preparation and good luck.

The current Dockers list has been described as "pure" from a recruitment point of view, with no father-son selections, no free agents and no players taken with AFL concessions or free agent compensation picks.

The Fremantle squad that trained this week for a grand final has been carefully put together. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it all began in 2016.

"It was pretty clear the list was old, but finishing so high on the ladder in 2015, it's sort of hard to basically finish on top and then enter a rebuild phase," Fremantle's former national recruiting manager Brad Lloyd said.

"We entered [2016] with an old group, which is fine to have an older group, but you need to be getting the results.

"And that wasn't evident through the start of '16."

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

The Dockers were winless until round nine that season, after winning 18 games the year before.

"Some decisions were made to reset again, which ended up in some pretty experienced players finishing up and the club going back to the draft," Lloyd said.

Starting over

Lloyd, who joined the Dockers in 2008, was no stranger to building a list — he was part of the recruitment team which put together Fremantle's 2013 grand final side.

In 2008 and 2009, Fremantle used 23 draft picks to bring together the core of the squad that would be competitive across the mid-2010s.

Ross Lyon coached Fremantle to the 2013 grand final and 2015 minor premiership, but the side fell off a cliff in 2016. (AAP Image: Gary Day)

"We'd had a really good crack at it through '13, '14 and '15, and played in a grand final and in preliminary finals, but couldn't quite secure a premiership," Lloyd recalled.

"We had the oldest list and were now struggling on field [in 2016] and decided to sort of enter another build to get going again."

From career crossroad to grand final When Neil Erasmus runs out onto the MCG on Saturday, it will vindicate his decision to stay at Fremantle after almost leaving a year ago.

Lloyd believed a complete rebuild would take between six and eight years, and Fremantle embarked on drafting and trading in players it thought would deliver success.

It's been 10 years since that decision was made and the Dockers have resolutely stuck to the plan, though it hasn't been without some misses along the way.

The recruitment of Jesse Hogan, Shane Kersten and Cameron McCarthy, among others, didn't pan out, while some talented draftees such as Adam Cerra and Lloyd Meek now ply their trade at other clubs.

Jesse Hogan was traded to the Dockers from Melbourne, but struggled in his time in purple. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

But under Lloyd and long-time recruiter David Walls, the club did bring in Luke Ryan, Andrew Brayshaw and Sam Switkowski, as well as Sean Darcy, who became the foundation of the club's list.

The stand-out draft

The Dockers' rebuild was slowly unfolding as the 2010s ended, but the 2019 draft accelerated it considerably.

Fremantle selected Hayden Young, Caleb Serong and Liam Henry with picks seven, eight and nine, before securing Michael Frederick at pick 61.

Hayden Young overcame injury woes to help launch the Dockers into the grand final. (Getty Images: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Mark Micallef was part of the Dockers' recruitment team that year.

"The 2019 draft was something that we pegged in that we thought could really change the platform of the footy club," he said.

Securing Young and Serong attracted much of the media attention at the time, though Micallef believed the selection of Frederick so late in the draft was equally important.

"You're trying to find the diamonds in the rough and you're looking for guys that could have a trait or an ability that not many others can see," he said.

Michael Frederick was a late pick in the 2019 draft, but has become an integral part of the Freo side. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"We thought Frederick was the right talent. He had a speed skill set that we really, really liked. He had a really good demeanour and a character.

"He had a good talent threshold, but he also had the work ethic and the character to back it up as well. So that's what really makes a back-end pick."

There were several other excellent drafts for Fremantle, including in 2021, which saw Jye Amiss, Matthew Johnson and Neil Erasmus selected, along with defender Karl Worner in that year's Rookie Draft.

Playing the long game

While the players selected by the Dockers in 2019 have become stars of the side, there was another future stud Fremantle wanted but knew they couldn't get in the draft.

Luke Jackson is emblematic of Fremantle's forward planning as they rebuilt an old squad into a flag contender. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Luke Jackson was described as a "unicorn" — a ruck who played like a midfielder — but he was slated to go very early in the draft.

Fremantle thought they could lure him back within a few seasons, and laid the groundwork in the build-up to the draft.

"We knew he was going to the top three, but we actually put a lot of groundwork into him that year saying, 'if you ever decide to come back, we want to be the club of your choice,'" Micallef said.

"I think you always look at trades and stuff like that and people think it just happens within that trade period, but there's a lot of time and a lot of work and a lot of resources that goes into that [future planning]."

Shai Bolton's arrival at Fremantle was seen as the cream on the cake after a long rebuild. ( Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Jackson and Shai Bolton both eventually returned to Western Australia as premiership players and are now vital cogs in Justin Longmuir's machine.

A special place

While both Micallef and Lloyd have long since moved on to different things, their time at Fremantle remains dear.

"Fremantle was a very special place. They were very good to me personally. Right from Steve Rosich and Chris Bond, the CEO and footy manager, and Steve Harris, who was the president at the time, to [his successor] Dale Alcock," Lloyd said.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It is remote compared to the rest of the AFL, so they don't get a huge amount of turnover of staff.

"When you're watching them celebrate the other day [after the win over Sydney], you just see staff that have been there for decades. It's a very stable club that's operated in their own area.

"You see so many past players in the rooms and they're a very good club at looking after their people.

"I wish them nothing but the best and particularly for the recruiting team that I've worked closely with — David Walls and Dave McMullin and Ed McMullin and that team, wish them well and even their football manager, Joe Brierty."

Lloyd and David Walls (pictured) worked closely together for a decade at the Dockers. (AAP Image: Con Chronis)

Micallef was only at the club for one year, but he's enjoyed watching their success unfold.

"Kudos to the club. They've done an unbelievable job," he said.

"We set a plan and I think they sort of stuck to it, trying to get WA players back, and it worked really well.

"I loved my time at Freo, and Freo has some really special players and people involved in that footy club and even the fans, they just deserve it more than anyone.

"I really hope they get the job done on Saturday."

World.title: V'landys steps down as Racing NSW boss to secure firmer grip on NRL
World.content:
Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman is set to be made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.

V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.

His resignation looms as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.

Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.

But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.

When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.

At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.

In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.

Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.

Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.

V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.

He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.

"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."

In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.

Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.

"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.

"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.

"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."

Waterhouse says right time to move on

Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.

Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.

The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.

Australian horse trainer and businesswoman Gai Waterhouse. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.

"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."

Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.

"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.

Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.

"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Excitement, nerves as Dockers hold final home drill before grand final
World.content:
Thousands of Fremantle Dockers fans have packed out the club's headquarters to watch the team train for the last time in Western Australia before they head to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

It has been 13 years since the Dockers last made a grand final, and the open training session in Cockburn saw so much demand that the team ticketed the event.

All 3,000 tickets were sold.

Long-term supporter Katie said the Dockers' success this year had special significance for her and her son Finlay.

Katie wants the Dockers to win for her son Finlay. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Finlay was just six weeks old when the 2013 grand final was held. Two years later, he developed cancer, and relapsed a year later.

"It's 10 years now since his relapse," Katie said.

"So it's his year and it's the Dockers' year, and all he wants is the Dockers to win on grand final day … that's his celebration."

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox and his teammates at the open training session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Imogen Somerville, who has also supported the Dockers "her entire life", described the event as overwhelming.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It was really cool to be able to get down here," she said.

"It was like five bucks to get in, which was awesome, so couldn't miss out on that."

Doing the right thing

Fans cheered the team on the field, then posed for photographs with their football heroes, who signed jerseys, posters and autographs.

Thousands of fans thronged to the event. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it was not just the public who were in the stands — past players, the club's chief executive Simon Garlick and Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti also attended the session.

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

Lee Spurr, who played in the 2013 grand final, said he felt "nothing but proud" to see his club back in the running for the flag.

"I was pretty nervous watching the prelim, but now that they're there, I feel like I'm almost playing. My phone's been blowing up," he said.

After experiencing the lead-up to the AFL's biggest week, Spurr said it was important for the players to turn off their phones and stick to preparation.

Former Dockers grand finalist Lee Spurr advises the team to lock in ahead of the game. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"My advice would be don't get caught up in doing too much, " he said.

" This week's about doing the process, doing what's right and preparing. "

Pure excitement

Superstar ruckman Luke Jackson said he loved having the fans participate in the club's biggest week.

Several Dockers said they loved having their fans take part in the session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"Just pure excitement. Can't wait to get over there and can't wait to play on Saturday in front of all these fans. It will be good fun," he said.

Jackson was in his second AFL season when he won his first premiership with the Melbourne Demons in 2021 in Perth.

He said he was looking forward to playing at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where the Dockers will face the Brisbane Lions.

Dockers defender Jordan Clark (left) talks to coach Justin Longmuir at Fremantle's open training session in Cockburn. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Defender Jordan Clark was also excited, and grateful, to see the fans.

"They support us through thick and thin, as they have done for the last 30 years," he said.

All the tickets for the training event were sold. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"So they're pretty happy with this moment and they rightly deserve to be, so it's pretty special when we get this support."

With no chance of making the training session, dozens of Dockers fans 1,600 kilometres away flocked to Broome airport today to catch the only direct flight to Melbourne before Saturday.

David Leslie, who goes by Docker Dave, has followed the team since its inception said his faith had been “restored” after their stellar final performances against Swans and Geelong.

The last direct flight to Melbourne from Broome this week was packed with Dockers fans. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

"We are going to flog the lions," he said.

World.title: Heeney 'extremely thankful' after addressing entire Swans club on return
World.content:
Sydney Swans forward Isaac Heeney says he is "thankful" for the opportunity to address his teammates and the club for the first time since he and four other players were suspended.

Heeney and his fellow banned teammates arrived at Swans HQ in Moore Park for their exit meetings on Wednesday evening after Sydney's 2026 season came to an end last week.

"It was really nice to address the whole club," Heeney said in a short statement.

"Extremely thankful they could give us their time and understanding … so yeah, it was really good."

Heeney (right) and Warner (centre) were the only banned players to speak to reporters at Swans HQ on Wednesday. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

It is Heeney's first public comment since he and four teammates — Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice — were suspended by the club for a breach of standards last month.

Warner and Bice arrived at Swans HQ first before Heeney, Jordon and Blakey arrived as a group shortly afterwards.

Warner was questioned by reporters on whether he would apologise to his teammates and said: "I don't know, we'll wait and see."

The banned players were met at the door by Swans executive general manager of football, Leon Cameron. Blakey, Jordon and Bice did not speak.

Sydney's season came to an end last week after it was defeated by Fremantle in the preliminary final. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Heeney polled a team-high 26 votes at the Brownlow Medal on Monday evening, well short of medal-winner Nick Daicos's record total of 47.

No decision has been made by Sydney on the playing futures of the five suspended players beyond this season.

Warner and Jordon are contracted through 2027 while Heeney and Bice are contracted through 2028. Blakey's contract with Sydney runs through the 2031 season.

An undermanned Swans side shocked grand finalists Brisbane in a qualifying final earlier this month before being beaten by Fremantle in last week's preliminary final.

World.title: Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object
World.content:
If we're ever going to solve that old question about unstoppable forces and immovable objects, the best way might be letting Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew run straight into each other.

The Penrith and Newcastle wingers will go head-to-head in Sunday's preliminary final with collisions that promise to rock the foundations of Stadium Australia.

Between them they boast a little over 200kg of prime Samoan beef, forged by pumping ludicrous amounts of steel in one case and fuelled by a truly startling quantity of Coke Zero in the other.

With a grand final berth on the line they will do what they do best: taking the ball and smashing into each other and anything else that gets in their way.

To'o has long been counted as one of the NRL's top wingers. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

They'll do it returning kicks, they'll do it early in sets, they'll do it close to the line to try and barge in and score and they'll do it over and over again until one of them is grand final bound.

Nobody can do all those things, grand finals included, like To'o, which is why he's the best winger of his time, but having played against Marzhew since the two's junior days he'll readily admit to taking some inspiration from the Knights wrecking machine.

"He's someone I like to base my game on, he's really strong and a big part of their team. I'm honoured to battle it out with my uso Greg," said To'o.

"It's our job to put our body on the front line and get the set started. It doesn't matter if it's one person in front of you, or two or three or four or five, just go as hard as you can."

Marzhew has enjoyed one of the best years of his career in 2026. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Likewise, Marzhew has looked to To'o plenty of times before and this season has the Panthers legend covered for tries (24 to 16), line breaks (27 to 21) and tackle busts (124 to 112), although To'o has him beat for average run metres (194 per game to 188)

Marzhew's form has earned him Newcastle's player's player award and he believes the challenge of taking on players like To'o has brought out the best in him.

"Penrith are one of my favourite teams to play against, they have so many representative players and I'm getting to go up against one of the best wingers to ever do it," said Marzhew

"I pride myself on that kind of stuff [big carries]. I try to excel with it because it's what the boys expect of me, if the crowd gets on top that's the cherry on top."

Fighting against greater numbers and winning is To'o's specialty. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's been doing it for so long now it's hard to imagine a time when To'o didn't relish the contact but he did have to learn to love it.

"When I was a bit younger, I was a bit shorter than I am now, I wouldn't say I was scared but there was that feeling that I might get knocked around," said To'o.

"I don't know if that counts as scared, I guess it pretty much does.

"It wasn't until my old man said, 'You're running it straight and getting knocked down or you're coming off and going home.'

"So I decided I'd run it straight. That was probably under-13s, I just dialled in and decided."

For Marzhew, who's got about 10kg on To'o, the issue was much simpler — there's never been any fear because he has always felt made for this

"Nah, that's the job description [running into people]," said Marzhew.

"That's what I signed up for."

The duo have plenty in common aside from their belief that the best way to solve a rugby league problem is to run right through it.

Both can really put on the dancing shoes — To'o's been hitting a little samba-type number after scoring recently, most notable after wrapping up Penrith's qualifying final over the Roosters with a late intercept try following one of his best games of the season.

"It's a Brazilian dance on TikTok, all the kids in my family, my nieces and nephews are always doing it," said To'o.

"My son does the dance and a Spider-man celebration as well, so I just wanted to honour all the kids.

"Now it's become a thing, I'll see kids down at the shops and they'll ask me to do it.

"But Greg's got me. He's built different. I've seen his moves, he's got the hips for it."

To'o's not kidding — Marzhew was a champion breakdancer in his youth, twice travelling to the United States to represent Australia in the world championships.

He says he's too big to move like he used to but the popping and locking and clean backflip he landed at the NRL's fan fest before the season opener in Las Vegas says otherwise.

But Marzhew needs just one try to equal Dom Young's record for most four-pointers in a season for the Knights and he'll likely have to go over To'o to do it, so the dancing will have to wait.

Marzhew and the Knights will be out to defy the odds yet again. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

"I'll let him take it, my mind is on something else — maybe after the game," said Marzhew.

"No dance, but I'd love to equal the record and share it with my brother, Dom Young, on the other wing."

If Penrith win, it will mark To'o's sixth grand final appearance while Marzhew is after his first.

A crowd of over 50,000 is expected, with a horde of Knights fans expected on hand for the club's first preliminary final since 2013.

The support comes as no shock to Marzhew, who has loved the city ever since arriving from Gold Coast in 2023, and he's ready to run into, over or through anything that gets in the way of Newcastle premiership dream.

"It's not a surprise, I wouldn't expect it but I love it and to play for them in this situation is an honour," said Marzhew.

"It's always a privilege to play in any game for Newcastle. I love playing for this town. It was home right from that first year."

World.title: Umpire felt 'threatened' by player, fan abuse after unruly AFL finale
World.content:
A 34-year-old Seaford man is expected to be charged for allegedly throwing a plate of food at a woman and child during last week's AFL preliminary final between Hawthorn and Brisbane.

He is expected to be charged on summons with aggravated unlawful assault and discharge a missile.

AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

Police have interviewed the man and another 56-year-old Tullamarine man, who was identified after allegedly throwing a bottle onto the MCG's field of play at the conclusion of the match.

The Tullamarine man has been fined $418 under the Major Events Act.

He is the second man to be fined after security detained a 40-year-old Croydon man for throwing a bottle onto the field of play, before he was spoken to by police.

Bottles and cans were thrown onto the field after the game, including some aimed at the umpires as they walked off the MCG after a holding-the-ball decision by field umpire Hayden Meyer against Jarman Impey that gave Brisbane a go-ahead goal with 18 seconds remaining.

Umpire says he felt 'threatened' by Hawks duo

Sicily and Barrass (number 37) were seen having words with Meyer (left) immediately following the final siren. (AFL)

Meyer, who will officiate in this weekend's AFL grand final, was confronted by Hawthorn captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass in the aftermath of his decision.

He said he had received an apology from Barrass but was still waiting to hear from Sicily.

"The abuse that came my way, I felt threatened," Meyer told reporters on Wednesday.

"I expressed exactly that [to the AFL] — the language, and the way that those two players, James [Sicily] and Tom [Barrass], came at me, I felt threatened and intimidated in that situation.

"So I spoke to [umpires boss] Steve McBurney the day after and gave my view of the situation, and how I felt and what occurred, and he then transferred that to Swanny [AFL football boss Greg Swann] and the MRO to eventually come up with a decision around the fines.

"[Barrass] was very apologetic and very sincere in his apology. I accepted his apology and thanked him for taking the time out of his day to give me a call."

Meyer says Sicily (pictured) is yet to apologise for abusing him on the final siren. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Meyer refused to make a call on whether the Hawks pair, who were fined over their actions, should be suspended instead.

"That's out of my control, that's not my decision … I suppose what I take from it is that it's not a great look for junior umpires and kids that are sitting on the couch that we want to recruit into umpiring," he said.

"They see that after the game on the weekend and, if I'm sitting on the couch, I'd be like, 'Do I really want to go to my local umpiring community group and sign up to be an umpire?'

" That was the big disappointing thing for me, that we struggle with umpiring recruitment in local communities, and that doesn't help. "

Despite the protestations from Hawthorn fans, Impey admitted the umpires made the right call.

"It was the right decision," he told the Kick It Forward podcast at the Brownlow Medal on Monday night.

"Naturally, when you think there are 30-40 seconds to go, you try and hold it in go from there, but credit to Hayden.

"I hope there was no hate message towards him, so sending love to him."

Jarman Impey (left) admitted the umpires had made the right call in penalising him for holding the ball in the final seconds. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

Ahead of this weekend's grand final, Meyer pleaded for fans to not "cross the line" again.

"I've never experienced bottles being thrown at me post-game. It was pretty scary, to be honest, and I hope it never happens again in any game, any sport," he said.

"[To fans attending the grand final], I would say be passionate, cheer for your team, but respect others, respect the people you're sitting next to, respect the umpires — have fun, but don't cross the line."

Police are continuing to make enquiries regarding the fan behaviour during and after the match.

Tech.title: Meta is making a standalone Muse AI gadget
Tech.content:
Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent. The product, called Muse Charm, was briefly shown off by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the end of tonight’s Meta Connect presentation. It looks almost like a chunky smartwatch without the strap — just a big screen, plus a little lanyard for carrying the device around.

The Muse Charm has a fingerprint sensor on the top right corner that you can press to activate and begin speaking to the agent. There appears to be a small camera on the device as well, plus what looks like at least three holes for microphones on the front. Zuckerberg said you don’t have to unlock a phone or open an app to use the Charm, but he didn’t share how it’s actually connecting to Meta’s servers.

Meta plans to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but as of now Zuckerberg says the company has “only built a few of these so far.” The company still needs to finalize “the finishing material,” he said. Throughout the keynote, he teased the device and made references to a translucent exterior that would let you see the gadget’s internals. He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.”

Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.”

Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta. The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address.

There are a lot of companies racing to win the still-undefined and largely experimental realm of AI hardware. The closest analog to the Muse Charm might be the Rabbit R1, a similarly sized cutesy device that housed an AI agent, which was not nearly capable enough to make the product worth carrying around. Connect is nothing if not a reminder of how badly Meta wants to win the race to whatever that next big hardware platform is — it’s moving quickly to see if Muse as a device is something that can stick.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.

You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.

Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.

The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.

The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.

Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses

Image: Meta

The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.

Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.

Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades

Image: Meta

Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”

The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.

Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles

Image: Meta

Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.

Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.

Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”

Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features

Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.

Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”

Screenshot: The Verge

After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”

Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.

Meta is making an AI ‘charm’

Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

Tech.title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
Tech.content:
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket.

The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. It felt like a lightweight Vision Pro, and is perhaps a better execution of some of what Apple wanted to do with that device.

The back of the Meta VR Glasses. Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

To keep things light, the VR Glasses’ display and the sensors are all you actually wear on your face. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.

The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same.

Here’s the compute puck. It has a solid clip. Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

You primarily use your eyes and hand gestures to control the glasses. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands.

Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. In the entire VR environment around the screen showing the film, there were graphics that thematically lined up with what was actually happening onscreen that also changed as the clip went on; when a huge energy beam appeared at a major moment in the film featuring Thor, I saw one shoot out at the top of the VR environment, too. Meta says that VR enhanced versions of Avengers: Infinity War and Star Wars: A New Hope will be available when the VR Glasses launch.

Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Gaming remains a major use case, too. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. It makes sense when you play it, and the one song I played was really enjoyable. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers).

Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. My favorite demo from my whole session was actually one about typing. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. To my surprise, the virtual keyboard and trackpad were actually good. Of course, the experience wasn’t as speedy as using a physical keyboard and mouse, but in a pinch for a short message or email, I think it could be quite useful. (I should note it’s not technically new; Meta introduced this for Quest headsets earlier this year, and I haven’t tried it on those devices.)

Image: Meta

The glasses cost $1,299.99 and will go on sale in spring 2027. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

Tech.title: Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
Tech.content:
Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at.

Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.

Meta’s introducing some new audio and photo features as well, including Dolby Atmos Capture, which will allow users to record videos with 360-degree spatial audio. A new Dynamic Photo feature automatically captures multiple frames when you take a photo with Meta’s glasses, then uses Meta AI to suggest the best frame from each batch.

The Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are getting the new “Hologram” feature Meta announced for its new VR Glasses, which it says is “a photorealistic digital version of your face for calls from Meta Ray-Ban Display” that “infers” your expression using your voice. The feature’s “rolling out in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”

A couple new heads-up navigation features are coming to the Meta Ray-Ban Display as well. Starting later this month, users in the US and Canada will have an option to use their voice to ask for real-time cycling or public transit directions. The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect. A few other new features are on the way for the Display glasses, including an option for editing photos directly on the glasses’ display, a new “Explore” app for finding new apps, an improved calendar, and mirroring for phone notifications.

Tech.title: Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.

Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.

To hear Meta tell it, that’s a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making.

“Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.”

There are multiple combinations of colors and lenses across two styles for the audio-only glasses. Clubmaster is in the middle here, sandwiched between two Burbanks. Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Himel has a point. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Plus, the camera-less glasses are lighter. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.”

The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. The arms are thinner. They come in two styles: the Mad Men-esque Clubmaster and the more Wayfarer-reminiscent Burbank. The hinges extend for wider faces; the temple arms and nose pads are adjustable. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too.

Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.

I think Clubmaster looks fetching on me. But these look like ordinary glasses. Photo by Victoria Song / The Verge

“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”

Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
