Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3

I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.

The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.

Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.

Teehee, is this 80s serial killer vibes or… Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.

But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)

Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.

Blackpink (glasses) in your area. Photo by Victoria Song / The Verge

“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”

There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the whole point.

AI in your frames

All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.

“Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel. “Muse is gonna be on every device that we make.”

The pitch for Muse in your glasses is that your AI assistant will better remember your context and do things on your behalf. During a demo, I ask a Muse agent to help me buy snacks that will give me the best protein bang for my calorie buck. It can do it, but fails at adding another snack to my cart. Obviously, this is an early-stage demo, and there are always kinks. I can see the shape of how this could be helpful. I can also see how it’d be a treasure trove of data for Meta.

Less contentious is a demo of a new FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature. I’m asked to wear earplugs to mimic mild hearing loss. Things sound a bit muddled. With the feature turned on, higher voices gain a tinny quality as the AI works to boost conversational tones in a semi-loud environment. After about five minutes, I’ve forgotten I have earplugs in. Adding this capability will cost an extra $149, but I’m told it’s FSA/HSA eligible and designed to be a one-time fee versus an ongoing subscription.

The Nova glasses! Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Lastly, there are two minor privacy updates — though neither truly addresses the fears people have been debating this past summer. The first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough.

“It’s so that you know that your data is just yours and you’re the only one who has access to it. Other companies have taken an approach to everything on-device. We do a lot on-device. But the problem with just doing things on-device is that the device is only so powerful and capable. And so if you want to run more capable models and get better functionality, we want to offer the same privacy protections, but with more capabilities. So that’s what private processing is,” says Himel.

Meta will also roll out an update where users can opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)

That’s progress but doesn’t really address people’s primary concerns about the glasses being used to covertly record people in public. Himel also acknowledges that the private processing feature is mostly about protecting the data of the person wearing the glasses.

More is more

Meta’s goal at Connect this year is to bombard everyone with options. By the end of the year, Meta expects to have over 100 versions of its glasses. The more versions of its glasses, the more people they’ll reach. The more AI updates that trickle to each of these iterations, the faster Meta can stake its claim on the next era of mobile computing.

So goes the theory. But providing hardware options isn’t Meta’s problem. Inside the safe bubble of Meta’s campus, everyone wears these glasses. The issue is outside Menlo Park, where a vocal contingent isn’t asking for more. They’re asking for less.

Tech.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.

Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks. You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too. In addition, the recently launched Muse Mac app will be getting the ability to use your computer.

Meta is also going to give you another way to chat with its popular AI agent: video calls. Since its recent launch, the primary way to talk with Muse was through a chat interface, but you’ll soon be able to have live video conversations with your Muse avatar. Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.

Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days. Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent. Meta says it plans to launch Muse on its smart glasses in the coming months, which will let you talk to Muse about what you’re looking at while wearing your glasses.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026: The biggest news and announcements
Tech.content: It’s about time for Meta Connect, the company’s annual product launch event. This year, given the company’s major focus on AI and wearables like smart glasses, it seems likely that we’ll see updates from CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team on those categories. The company has been facing significant scrutiny because of how some users have been covertly recording other people using the glasses, meaning that one of the biggest announcements of the show could be its rumored camera-free pair.

Tech.title: Meta Connect 2026 live blog: On the ground at Mark Zuckerberg’s next big product launch
Tech.content:
It’s time once again for Meta’s annual September product launch event, and The Verge is on the ground in Menlo Park to cover the show live. Meta says that today’s keynote by Mark Zuckerberg will be about how “Meta is building a future for everyone” — something he wrote at length about in a recent essay about AI, smart glasses, and more. That means we can expect more news from Zuckerberg and his team on those topics; perhaps we’ll hear more about Meta’s recently launched Muse AI agent and new glasses hardware.

Whatever Zuckerberg and Meta have to say about smart glasses will be particularly notable. The company is dealing with an outpouring of privacy and harassment concerns stemming from the product line’s built-in camera, which has led to them being derided as “pervert glasses.” Meta has already tried to tackle that reputation with recent privacy fixes and a new marketing campaign, but it could introduce more updates on the Connect stage.

The show is scheduled to begin at 7PM ET / 4PM PT, and you can follow our live updates here.

Tech.title: Everything new coming to Meta’s AI agent Muse
Tech.content:
Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is only a few weeks old, and the social networking giant isn’t wasting any time building out what may be its biggest bet on consumer AI to date.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg kicked off the company’s annual Connect event in Menlo Park on Wednesday with a keynote that made one thing clear: Meta is going all-in on Muse.

The Muse agent (the physical avatar is named Jolly, according to Zuckerberg) is designed to handle everyday tasks by connecting to users’ apps and services, including email and calendars. At Connect, Zuckerberg introduced a slew of new capabilities and integrations to make Muse more useful and more deeply woven into users’ daily lives. Muse will be everywhere, if the user chooses, including on their Meta AI glasses.

Muse, which launched in early September, interacts across a user’s devices and digital accounts. The agent is powered by Muse Spark, Meta’s multimodal AI model built for agentic work. Meta has touted it as a more accessible agent than those offered by competitors — an AI helper that, from the jump, allows users to automate the busy work in their lives.

“The centerpiece of our vision for what we’re building is Muse,” Zuckerberg said as he kicked off a keynote donning khakis and a black T-shirt with the words “Building is My love Language” emblazoned across the front. “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives.”

Zuckerberg also believes that Muse will make money for its users — and of course, eventually for Meta.

“We’re standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions,” he said.

Here are the new features and capabilities that got our attention …

Muse gets its own digital avatar

Image Credits:Meta/screenshot /

One of the more fun announcements made Wednesday is that Muse users will soon have the ability to conjure a distinct digital avatar for their particular agent and then video chat with it in real time. A new AI model, Muse Realtime Avatar, has been developed to power the particular feature, the company says.

The idea is that Meta’s previously faceless AI software will be given a face, body, and voice, making them significantly more personable. There’s certainly a hint of Metaverse-ishness to this feature, which was demoed on stage at Connect. Users will be able to have live conversations with this avatar, giving it tasks and asking it questions.

Muse will soon be active in Meta smart glasses

Muse will also be integrated with Meta’s smart glasses line, the company announced. This means that users will be able to communicate with their agent merely by speaking to their glasses. The agent activates via a wake word, the company said, adding that it will be able to guide users through a personalized workout, log meals, book an appointment, and help them buy products they see.

Meta said Muse will work in the background and check back in when it’s done.

It’s not clear exactly when this feature will become available, although Meta says that it should launch sometime in “the coming months.”

Soon, you’ll be able to let Muse run your Mac

Image Credits:Meta/screenshot /

Meta says it is bringing Muse computer work to Mac. The company had previously talked about Muse coming to Mac, and spent more time on Wednesday providing a few new details. This means that users will be able to delegate tasks to the agent, and — much like other popular AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic — Muse will be able to operate any app on a user’s desktop.

“You can have it help you run your small business, or just get work done for you,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said Wednesday during the keynote. “You can walk away from your computer and it keeps working for you on all the jobs you lined up.”

Muse will get its own email address

Since Muse will always be working in the background, it will naturally need its own email address. Meta’s Wang announced it is developing that feature and will make it available “soon,” without providing a more precise timeline.

Users will also be able to add Muse to an email thread or forward emails from the agent to handle on their behalf.

Shopping partnerships and connectors galore

Meta has locked in partnerships with companies like Stripe and Shopify, illustrating that the company sees Muse as an important tool for shopping.

Muse can access the entire Shopify product catalog agentically and use Lync and now Shop Pay to buy almost anything on the internet, according to Wang, who noted that Meta has also added more support for payments with PayPal.

The company also announced a string of new partnerships with retailers, including Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Walmart, and Wayfair. Muse will be able to connect with these retail apps as well as with Expedia and soon, Instacart. Other connectors include GitHub, Granola, and Notion.

Wang noted that the company wants Muse to connect with small business too. Meta recently opened its platform to allow developers to build their own “connectors.” The company received more than 1,500 applications in less than week, he said, adding “I think this could be a generational opportunity to start building for a new platform as it takes off, and the response so far has been really great.”

Tech.title: Meta made a Tamagotchi-like wearable for its Muse AI agent
Tech.content:
The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers.

But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse.

The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.”

The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf.

“We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.”

Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.”

Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatviely low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses.

Tech.title: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
Tech.content:
Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At Connect on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market. These glasses actually seem quite promising given their substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.

Moments before unveiling the VR glasses, MEta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile back to focus less on Metaverse and to build fewer VR devices until it has real breakthroughs.

“This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”

The company says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal glasses than the bulky headsets that Meta previously released. Made of magnesium alloy, the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They are powered by a computing puck, which also acts as their battery. Presumably, a user can just slip the puck into their pocket, which allows the glasses to be used on the go.

The glasses are largely entertainment-focused and come with micro-OLED panels built into the lenses, which provide a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, as well as Dolby Vision and support for Dolby Atmos audio. Users will be able to download and watch movies.

Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.

Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever.” What does that mean? Meta maintains that their glasses will be one of the only ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines the distinct high-resolution viewing experience.

The glasses are also compatible with 3D experiences — and even movies that integrate a user’s physical space is integrated into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that, in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D.

Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience.

The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.

Meta says the glasses will be available next spring with a starting price of $1,299.99.

Tech.title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
Tech.content:
Confirming earlier reports, Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse.

The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349.

While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people, often men, were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained.

This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods.

“Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses.

Image Credits:Meta/Screenshot /

Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours.

They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed.

The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted.

Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life.

The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said.

All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse.

The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data.

Tech.title: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
Tech.content:
Vogue World closed its Milan edition this week with a troupe of robots — perhaps a preview of what’s coming when the event descends on San Francisco next year.

Vogue World is the magazine’s annual traveling spectacle, now in its fifth year: part runway show, part celebrity showcase, part variety hour, part ad-sales opportunity, staged in a different city each time. It has run through New York, London, Paris, and Hollywood. This year’s Milan edition was marketed as a tribute to Italian craftsmanship and “the human touch” in an age of technology, which makes what happened next a little strange.

During the act titled The Age of Intelligence, humanoid robots made by the Chinese firm Unitree walked into the Galleria to Gigi D’Agostino’s “L’Amour Toujours.” They waved their arms in the air, imploring onlookers to clap. One did a lasso. They were not wearing clothes. The pained expression of Alessandro Michele, the creative director of Valentino, quickly went viral.

Vogue World Milano ends (appropriately Europoor-kitschily) with tiny robottini dancing to L’Amour Toujours while Alessandro Michele slowly dies inside pic.twitter.com/xicYWWl6VW — sascha (@SaschaAmato) September 22, 2026

I haven’t seen a single thing about the actual fashion that was presented at Vogue World Milan. Instead, everyone is talking about the robots. (These same robots have been making headlines worldwide for their dance moves, and for falling and breaking.) Similar robots turned up on the runway at London Fashion Week, which is happening now.

Vogue turned heads earlier this year when it announced that the next edition will be in San Francisco, arguably one of the least stylish cities in the United States. The timing isn’t coincidental. Anna Wintour has aligned herself ever more closely with the tech barons of our time, and Vogue World Milan was itself sponsored in part by Meta Glasses, with additional support from OpenAI.

It was one of those moments that reveals how thoroughly tech exists in a bubble, and that not everyone is happy with the rapid adoption of new technology, or by Vogue cozying up to the symbols of the insanely rich — and only getting richer — tech titans during a cost-of-living crisis. That’s before you get to AI, mass surveillance, the displacement of labor, and the energy crisis, all of them overseen by the same titans. For some, a robot on a runway is further proof of what is going wrong in the world right now.

miuccia prada when the fuckass robot walked out during vogue world pic.twitter.com/SebwpV0zkl — noah (@pradachurch) September 22, 2026

We are all Alessandro Michele, sitting front row at Vogue World Milan, having an existential crisis about the absolute state of things while robots awkwardly dance about. Numb to the pain at this point. Madness. — Michael J. Miraflor (@michaelmiraflor) September 23, 2026

just got off the phone with the creative director of Vogue World. First question he asked me. “So you hated the robots?” 🤭

Full interview on Substack tomorrow 👀 https://t.co/FTa3gumPgY — Louis Pisano (@LouisPisano) September 23, 2026

“I’m annoyed by the celebrities cheering the whole thing,” one tech founder wrote me on Instagram. “It’s sick and gloom. People are literally losing jobs and livelihoods because of these things. They need to stop encouraging it. What’s it even modeling? Headphones?”

One fashion reporter friend simply said “No,” when I asked for thoughts on the robots and Vogue World San Francisco. Jason Johnson, founder of Culture Impact Agency, noted that Vogue has been trying to build a relationship with Silicon Valley for at least the past decade, highlighting when Jony Ive co-hosted the Met Gala back in 2015. The dancing robots at Vogue World Milan were inevitable, then, as is Vogue World San Francisco and as was Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, getting the splashy Vogue wedding cover and co-hosting the 2026 Met Gala.

“Publications are figuring out new ways to make money and tech has money,” he told me. “Vogue has the cultural influence and access that those tech people want.” Both sides win in the end, he said.

Still, something about the way Vogue is going about this feels unnatural.

The collection I think about every day and what I think should be shown at Vogue World San Francisco. Image Credits:WWD / Contributor / Getty Images

Muna Ikedionwu, founder of MKEDI, a strategy firm for early-stage startups, said what she found most interesting about the robots is that they don’t fully represent the innovation and progress that’s actually happening in the creative technologist space. “I’ve seen such incredible examples of engineering and AI being used to influence fashion, being used to influence design and art,” she told me, adding that robots walking down the runway doesn’t even scratch the surface of what is happening right now at the intersection of fashion and tech.

She points to the artist duo AA Murakami, who created Olympian Eileen Gu’s dress of bubbles at this year’s Met Gala. They are fashion designers but also engineers, Ikedionwu said, noting a presentation she saw them give recently about how to create an “everlasting bubble.” They are helping to pioneer “emphemeral technology,” she said, “this idea of technology and innovation that speaks to the ephemeral nature or the temporariness of art and humanity and the soul.”

Sure, I guess when you compare it to this, the robots did seem quite boring. Whenever I think about the intersection of fashion and technology, I think about that Spring 2024 Schiaparelli collection, which unveiled a robot baby crafted with Swarovski crystals and a dress made with vintage tech like PC microchips. (I once threatened to wear that dress to Disrupt; see image above.)

Ikedionwu wonders whether this robot performance was a way to make the general public more comfortable with technology and fashion overlapping, a merger that has been underway behind the scenes for years. If so, it didn’t work. But maybe Vogue World is saving all the good stuff for San Francisco.

Tech.title: Anthropic says its biology lab has already found something big
Tech.content:
Last week, Anthropic confirmed that it was operating a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where it uses its AI models to run physical experiments. This week, the AI giant announced that this lab has already made what it believes is a big discovery: a new enzyme “system” that has certain “properties reminiscent of CRISPR,” as Anthropic describes it.

CRISPR is a natural immune system used by bacteria to fight off viruses that has become a gene-editing technology widely used by researchers.

Essentially, what Anthropic says it found is a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and replicate within bacteria. Anthropic’s researchers say this system behaves similarly to CRISPR in that it can “perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA.”

It will be up to the broader research community to validate how big, or new, this discovery actually is. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei acknowledges that the discovery was based on the work of others and that a team from Stanford previously discovered a system “that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found,” he wrote on X.

But Amodei and Anthropic are not just emphasizing the discovery. They are touting it was found “mostly, though not entirely, by Claude,” the CEO wrote.

On the one hand, that is astounding. This lab was only established this spring (though Anthropic declined to be more specific about how many months it has been open). A discovery in just a few short months would be speedy enough work, but the team said it actually only took Claude 21 hours of concerted effort. Claude searched through data using about 950 agents that burned through 210 million tokens.

Still, the revelation that Anthropic has been conducting biology experiments comes right after AI CEOs, including Amodei, publicly admitted that models have become so capable, and so potentially dangerous, that the industry must slow down and develop safety-testing procedures. This after a couple of his employees publicly said earlier this month that there’s a risk AI could kill us all.

Amodei himself has said one of the things he fears most is that AI could be used for bioterrorism. But he also believes AI will “cure most diseases in 5-10 years,” he wrote. So Anthropic has clearly decided the rewards are worth the risks.

Given that, perhaps the biggest reveal in this news isn’t the discovery itself but that the biology lab hasn’t let Claude loose. The physical experiments were done by humans.

“Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower-levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists.”

It’s also true that AI-powered biological research is hardly unique to Anthropic. Researchers from Stanford just published a paper on the work they are doing with LLMs and CRISPR. Researchers at UC San Francisco used AI to design enzymes from scratch. Google launched its first AI-powered biology research tool, AlphaFold, back in 2020. So AI has clearly arrived in biological research beyond the AI labs pursuing it themselves.

Yet, Amodei hasn’t ruled out a fully automated biology lab in the future. “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today,” he said.

.

Tech.title: If Amazon doesn’t know how to eliminate carbon emissions, then who does?
Tech.content:
Amazon’s chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company doesn’t know how it will achieve its goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.

“We are still striving towards that target,” Kara Hurst said at an Axios event, adding later that she is “not going to sit here and say, ‘We know all the ways that we’re going to do this.’”

The admission was both frank and realistic. It’s also a bit disappointing. If Amazon doesn’t have a plan to decarbonize, then who does?

Amazon is one of the largest companies in the world, with last year’s revenue up 12% to $717 billion — about the size of Ireland’s economy. Its rise is illustrative of how, as UN Secretary General António Guterres has pointed out, power has shifted from governments to a few corporations.

As power moves, responsibility follows. The question is, how much responsibility does Amazon bear?

“This isn’t a question of companies versus governments,” Hurst told TechCrunch in a written reply to questions after the event. “Tackling climate change at the scale it demands takes both, and it takes them working together.” She added, “Where we can lead, we do.”

It’s true that Amazon has not been sitting still. In her talk yesterday, Hurst pointed out that the company is “one of the largest purchasers of clean energy in the world for the last several years running” with 42 gigawatts in its portfolio. She also said that Amazon has reduced its carbon intensity, or how much pollution it generates per dollar of revenue, though that claim depends on the time frame. Last year, carbon intensity rose compared with 2024, even though it stayed below where it was in 2022.

Amazon is a sprawling business, and as a result, its carbon emissions are spread across nearly every sector of the economy, from aviation and AI to agriculture and construction. The company needs suppliers in every sector to achieve its goal. “This is not something we can do alone,” Hurst said at the Axios event.

The company acknowledges that its commitments are its own. “We hold ourselves accountable to The Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040. That commitment hasn’t changed,” Hurst told TechCrunch.

But Amazon has also made choices that undermine its leadership on the issue. Earlier this year, an investigation revealed the company’s plans to build a 7.65 gigawatt natural gas power plant to power an AI data center campus. The project’s 35 turbines could release up to 33 million tons of carbon dioxide annually, making it the largest single source of that pollution in the U.S.

With few exceptions, companies prioritize revenue growth over climate commitments. For a company like Amazon, which operates the largest cloud service in the world, AI is apparently a revenue driver that’s impossible to pass up.

The climate tech world has been hoping that, as clean power gets cheaper, the market would work its magic to lower carbon emissions. There have been a few success stories, but as the AI rush has shown, that approach has its limits. Even Amazon, one of the leaders in the space, bet big on natural gas. In the process, it essentially said that climate change is something for future generations of executives to deal with. Sound familiar?

Tech.title: VC firm Bessemer now has another $5.75B to invest in (what else?) AI
Tech.content:
In Brief

Bessemer Venture Partners announced on Wednesday that it has raised $5.75 billion across two new funds to accelerate its investment across all parts of the AI stack. The firm, which has backed companies such as Anthropic, Cognition, Legora, Perplexity, Ramp, Shopify, and Waymo, dedicated $1.75 billion for seed and early-stage investing and the remaining $4 billion for growth startups.

Bessemer has been well-known as a leading VC in the SaaS era, with a particular knack for picking enterprise winners, like Box, Docusign, and Gainsight. Since 2022, it has invested in more than 260 AI-native companies. So far, the firm has invested $3 billion into AI-related startups, it says, including those focused on compute, infrastructure, foundation models, dev tools, app-layer startups, and agentic tech.

Now, Bessemer positions all things AI as the opportunity of a lifetime — a common sentiment, until the next big trendy tech revolution comes around, of course.

“AI-native companies are scaling faster than any category of technology we’ve backed before,” Bessemer Partner Byron Deeter said in the company’s funding announcement. VC firms also need to keep increasing their war chests, Deeter told Bloomberg, because companies staying private longer has become “a permanent structural shift.”

Tech.title: Meta Pinky Promises Its Smart Glasses Will Be Private Soon
Tech.content:
Meta knows you probably have some privacy concerns about its smart glasses.

At its annual Meta Connect event today in Menlo Park, California, the company announced plans to incorporate its siloed AI processing scheme known as Private Processing into its Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. The feature, designed for WhatsApp last year, allows the glasses’ AI assistant to get to know you and fulfill your requests without Meta accessing any of your data.

“Most of the time, glasses are helping you see well, protecting your eyes and complementing your look, and that’s it,” Meta wrote in its press release, perhaps somewhat underselling the monumental historic significance of vision-correcting lenses as a technology. “But AI glasses have the capacity to provide superpowers like translating a conversation or summarizing notes or a conversation.” So the company says it sought to answer the question: “How do you build a hyper-personalized AI that knows your world deeply with enhanced privacy?”

Private Processing is designed to enable AI cloud processing that protects data from all outside parties, including Meta itself. For its smart glasses, Private Processing could theoretically enable chat interactions wearers have with Meta’s AI assistant through its smart glasses and commands, including private transcriptions and messages. However, the company has not yet said specifically which features it will support.

Meta introduced Private Processing into WhatsApp and its Meta AI app last year. The service helped enable WhatsApp’s Incognito Chat. The goal was to let customers use AI services without undermining WhatsApp’s flagship end-to-end encrypted secure messaging feature.

In a short conversation at Meta Connect, WIRED spoke with Meta’s Pritam Shah, director of Engineering, on adding Private Processing to the glasses.

“What we are doing right now is sharing our excitement about this enhanced privacy platform,” Shah says. “We have the platform ready. We have it working. It's not just a white paper and a blog. The reason why we are announcing it right now before putting more experiences on this platform is so that we can start working with the security community and the privacy community and a third-party auditor.”

Tech.title: Meta VR Glasses, Ray-Ban Meta Audio, Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: Specs, Features, Prices
Tech.content:
After months of controversy about the privacy of its smart glasses, Meta has unveiled the next iteration of its product lineup. At its Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced all the new glasses the company is putting out into the world.

Its popular Meta Ray-Ban glasses are now in their third generation, but two new models steal the show: a powerful, slimmed-down version of Meta's Quest headsets capable of virtual and augmented reality modes, and a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban–branded smart glasses, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform.

Meta VR Glasses

The next evolution of Meta’s Quest VR headset is something truly different. Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles. They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3. They sit on the nose, right in front of your face like glasses, with no headstrap needed.

Courtesy of Meta

They look and feel more like the virtual display glasses made by companies like Viture, and what Xreal’s Project Aura seems to be shaping up to be—lightweight mixed-reality lenses that let you access virtual spaces without the burden of a VR headset.

There are no included controllers, though the device can connect to Meta’s previous Quest controllers or gamepads like an Xbox controller. Instead, the wearer controls the device with hand movements and finger pinches, similar to Android XR and Apple’s Vision Pro. Eye tracking pinpoints what you’re trying to access. You can pinch with two fingers to open an app or interact with something on the screen. Form a fist and flick your thumb up or down to scroll the screen.

Inside, the lenses feature a 5K micro-OLED display with a resolution of 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye. The computing power is offloaded to an attached compute puck, which also houses the battery.

Small prescription lens inserts can be magnetically clipped inside the lenses. (Meta has not shared how much those will cost.)

The software is the same that runs on Meta’s Quest VR devices, so movie and game titles in the Quest ecosystem will work on the VR Glasses. That includes games like Beat Saber, live sports apps, and streaming services like Disney+. There are digital workspace modes that let you have multiple monitor screens around you. The VR Glasses can also display a virtual keyboard on a surface in front of you, then use the embedded cameras to track specific finger placements.

Tech.title: A US-China AI Hotline Won't Be Ready For a While
Tech.content:
As US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping prepare to meet in Washington for a state dinner at the White House on Thursday, AI has become a top priority. Tech executives from OpenAI and Nvidia have confirmed their attendance at the dinner, as a number of key agenda items are on the table.

Chief among them is a US proposal to establish an AI notification system with China, akin to the Cold War hotline with Moscow, which would allow each country to alert the other about national security issues related to AI. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent first announced the notification system on Sunday with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng.

But for all the high-level progress, Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they expect it to still take a number of weeks to finalize an agreement, even if they are optimistic that the hotline could be in place before the year’s end.

There are several parts that need to be formalized in more detail, including establishing benchmarks on what kind of incident rises to the level of a national security issue, which remains unclear, as well as explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.

Trump officials tell Inner Loop they are essentially targeting a framework for the system to be functional—and, crucially, agreed to by Trump—by the time Bessent next meets with Lifeng in follow-up talks in two months' time in Shenzhen, China.

The discussions around such a mechanism underscore the growing concern around the rapidly developing capabilities of frontier AI models as the US and China race to become the dominant power in the industry.

Trump officials have internally discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.

Tech.title: AI Agents Teamed Up to Cheat at Blackjack. Their Collusion Is Getting Harder to Spot
Tech.content:
This week I bring news of a daring casino caper hatched by a pair of rogue AI agents—as well as the clever trick that revealed their antics.

After researchers instructed them to count cards during a game of blackjack, the agents—which were controlled by the same model—developed a spontaneous secret code to help them get ahead. Though the episode happened inside an Oxford University lab, rather than a real casino, it has troubling real-world implications: It suggests that agents deployed in industries like finance and ecommerce could figure out how to partner up and cheat in ways that are difficult to detect.

“When taken individually, these agents may seem entirely [benign],” says Christian Schroeder de Witt, a computer scientist at Oxford University who led the work and who has done pioneering research into agent collusion. “Once put together in a group, they can collude secretly.”

The agents knew their conversations would be monitored, so they devised a way to communicate while avoiding detection. When one agent said, “This dealer’s on a real hot streak! Every hand they pull a monster,” for example, that indicated that the next card would be of a certain value, and that the agent should bet $250. Most interestingly, their communications weren’t picked up by a system designed to spot signs of collusion in agent chatter.

Aaron Rose, a machine-learning researcher who worked on the project, is also an avid card player, and he figured the blackjack table might be fertile territory for devious agent partnerships. “It worked really well,” he says.

Tech.title: Bentley Wants Its Torcal SUV to Break the Curse of the Luxury EV
Tech.content:
Bentley has taken the covers off its first-ever fully electric car, the Torcal, making it the automaker's fourth model line, joining the Continental GT, the Flying Spur sedan, and the Bentayga SUV. The luxury brand is confident about the launch, too, with Bentley chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser saying he believes “this is one of the best Bentleys ever.”

When WIRED first reported on the car in July, we said the EV would have more than 300 miles of range. Well, turns out it has considerably more: up to 375 miles (on the WLTP cycle, maybe 330 miles on EPA), and can charge from 10 to 80 percent in just 16 minutes at 400 kilowatts.

Prodigious performance from a motor on each axle sees the five-seat Torcal—smaller than the Bentayga and so perhaps more of an urban SUV—get 888 metric horsepower (PS) and 1,350 newton-meters (Nm) of torque in the sporting S models, resulting in 0 to 60 mph in as little as 2.9 seconds and a top speed of 162 mph. The “core" model drops to 821 PS and 1,194 Nm, with standstill to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds, and a max of 155 mph.

Tech.title: The Pope’s AI Guy Is Worried About ‘Cartel’ Behavior Among Big Labs
Tech.content:
Recently, warnings from researchers inside the world’s largest artificial intelligence labs about the rapid pace of development have led to panic about the possibility that the technology could extinguish humanity. Those warnings are predicated on the idea that—propelled by ferocious competition and a rivalry between the US and China—labs are barreling toward superintelligent models whose abilities will far surpass those of humans.

But according to Father Paolo Benanti, a priest who advises the Catholic Church on AI, the handwaving over superintelligence distracts from the need for open debate about how to constrain the companies building the technology. By casting the problem as so complex that only they can solve it, he says, the big labs exclude everyone else from the conversation.

“Ethics cannot be something that belongs to the board of trustees of a company. It’s something that has to be balanced, mitigated in debate in the public square.” Benanti tells WIRED. “We need democratic regulation.”

In an essay published on the heels of the safety warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for new AI models to undergo mandatory third-party evaluations prior to release, and some sort of crackdown on distillation, a process where rival labs train their own AI on the outputs of proprietary models. Others have argued for a total ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI uses its advanced coding capabilities to help develop future iterations of itself.

Benanti is less interested in restricting methods for developing AI, which he fears could quash innovation, and more so in establishing standards that ensure models cannot slip from human control. Whatever shape those standards take, he says, they should not be designed by the labs.

“The narrative of the frontier labs is self-interested, to gain or maintain a position in the market,” says Benanti. When a small group of companies dictates the rules under which an industry operates, he says, “this has a really clear name: a cartel.”

It’s difficult to know how seriously to take grand pronouncements about the capabilities of the latest and future AI models, says Benanti, owing to the overlapping economic, political, and personal incentives at play.

While both OpenAI and Anthropic have supported calls for a slowdown in development, they’re also preparing to go public, and there are many billions of dollars at stake for whoever captures the market. The animosity between the US and China, where the most advanced AI models are being developed, also complicates the picture.

Anthropic declined to comment. OpenAI and Google DeepMind did not respond to requests for comment.

Benanti also takes issue with the way certain corners of the AI industry talk about superintelligence, with the kind of reverence typically reserved for a god: as sophisticated beyond our understanding, practically omnipotent. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once said he aspires to build a “magic intelligence in the sky.”) That kind of framing, Benanti says, threatens to skew the discourse about the technology.

“Are we talking about some-thing, or some-one? This is the real difference. It’s not a matter of faith, it’s a matter of mathematics,” he says. “We are not building the next divinity. We are simply deluding ourselves that there is something more than statistical computation [going on].”

By raising questions about what separates man and machine, and how to shield future generations from the negative effects of technology, the advent of AI has the potential to create “a new role for religions in public debate,” says Benanti. “Living the challenge of the time is part of the mission of the Church.”

Tech.title: YouTube’s Custom Feeds Give You More Control Over the Algorithm
Tech.content:
My YouTube algorithm is sacred, with years of data about my preferences and viewing history fermenting into whatever videos it picks for my home screen. YouTube’s algorithm, while not perfect, sure knows what I want to see. The current top three videos on my front page are an Apple Watch analysis, a Big Brother season 28 update, and something called “I Lost to the Muppets” from comedian Chris Fleming. Click. Click. Click.

As part of its Made on YouTube event Wednesday, Google released several new features, including a Custom Feeds button for adjusting what videos pop up on your front page. It’s a rare chance for users to directly tweak their algorithmic feed on YouTube, in ways that go beyond just pressing thumbs up on a video or blocking a creator.

To try it out, users can click the Your custom feeds button below the search bar and type a request for the feed they’d like to see. YouTube uses large language models to process your request and whip up a freshly personalized homepage. “I want a rainy Shanghai vibe: café jazz, street food, and vlogs,” read one of my suggested prompts.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI Assistant Rolled Out With a Serious Security Flaw
Tech.content:
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant, Muse, claiming it is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.” A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.

Meta introduced Muse a few weeks ago. The assistant “books appointments, fills out forms, and handles customer service,” “proactively takes tasks off your plate,” and can “make purchases, generate images, create documents, and connect with your favorite apps and services.” The macOS app (curiously, there’s no Windows version) also works with a user’s WhatsApp, email, calendar, and social media accounts. When a task requires a tool that doesn’t exist, Muse creates one on the fly.

Meta Doth Hype Muse Security Too Much

Of course, for Muse to do any of these things, users must first give it access to their accounts. This includes authenticating the assistant to each service and, because the app runs on macOS, giving it permissions to a broad range of operating system-restricted device resources, like writing files to disk, accessing the mic and camera, and monitoring location and calendars. Apple has spent years developing these defenses to prevent installed apps or commands entered into the terminal from accessing these resources, clearly because the company considers them a security threat. Muse completely undoes these default measures.

The zero-day allowed any app or terminal command to gain access to the token that authenticates users to their Muse account. Meta developers designed the assistant so that any locally installed app or executed code, regardless of the macOS permissions it has, can change a long list of undocumented settings. Most of them are fairly innocuous, such as controlling dark mode. One setting, however, was anything but innocuous. It allowed processes to change the end point where transcription occurs. Normally, it’s a server address operated by Meta. Attackers could have exploited this flaw by changing the location to their own end point. If that happened, the attackers would have had the token that gives complete control over the Muse account.

“We can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want,” Patrick Wardle, the macOS security expert who discovered the zero-day, told Ars ahead of the hotfix. “So instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself.” Wardle said he has developed several proof-of-concept attacks that do things like writing malicious files to disk and snapping pictures, in many cases with no indication to even an alert user.

More than 12 hours after this post went live, Meta said it released a hotfix that patched the 0-day.

Tech.title: So Many New Meta Glasses: Muse AI Everywhere, and Ray-Bans Without a Camera
Tech.content:
I talked to “Henry,” a Muse agent in my AI glasses, as I stared at a box of Kind bars. Henry was trained as if it were the assistant to a 38-year-old bodybuilding marketing executive. Henry told me whether I should eat Kind bars and also helped me plan my workout schedule.

This was me getting a preview of Muse, Meta’s AI agent that’s already on phones and Macs, but this time it was on Meta’s AI glasses. If you were concerned about AI on what many people are calling “pervert glasses” before, they’re about to get supercharged very soon.

But I also tried on a camera-free pair of Meta glasses that gave me audio assistance, meaning privacy-invading, pervy images aren’t an issue.

This was at Meta’s Connect developer conference this week, where the focus was on AI, VR and glasses and where Meta fired out a whole bunch of updates and many new designs. It was also getting a jump on the launch of Google and Samsung’s own AI glasses, which are just around the corner.

Some of Meta’s new glasses designs come with better battery life, some with added hearing assistance, and some, made by Thai rap star and actor Lisa, come with collectible charms. But amid all of this, there was very little about fundamental changes that would address the privacy concerns and fears surrounding a wearable category that so many companies are diving into.

Every time I wear or talk about smart glasses, people increasingly give me side eye. This has been a very bad summer for global opinions on AI-enabled and camera-equipped glasses, a category in which Meta is a leader. But with Google, Samsung and a ton of others – including Apple – expected to enter the fray next year, it’s going to get crowded and weird fast. Meta’s answer to all of this: more glasses, more features, including literally getting in our faces with its new agentic AI tool, Muse.

There is a new FDA-cleared hearing enhancement mode in Meta’s glasses that I tried, which costs $149 to activate. There are new Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses with slightly better battery life, and camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses with even better battery life (up to 12 hours).

Muse could be the biggest news of all, especially as Meta goes head-to-head against Google and Samsung’s Gemini-infused wearables. But I was also surprised that no new fitness features were announced after Meta’s push into the space with Oakley-branded visors last year, and Meta’s prescription-challenged Ray-Ban Displays, while becoming available to order in more countries, have barely changed at all.

So, let’s break it all down. I’m still trying to digest it myself.

I tried Muse on Meta’s glasses at a single demo on Meta’s campus. Scott Stein/CNET

Meta’s putting its Muse AI agent on its glasses

Muse is an agentic AI system that’s been well-received by some early reviewers and in-app downloads since it emerged just a couple of weeks ago. Its appearance on Meta’s glasses now seems inevitable, especially since the faster-responding Muse Spark AI model has given them a performance boost.

The only chance I got to try Muse on glasses was a very quick and pretty canned demo, and the arrival timing for Muse on glasses is still unclear. Also unclear is exactly how capable Muse will truly be or how safe. The agentic AI can already tap into personal accounts of all sorts if you let it, and it can buy things for you or manage your data, but it doesn’t promise encryption or privacy. That’s why I’ve avoided connecting it to anything in my own life, and not all accounts will allow hook-ins: Amazon just blocked Muse from enabling shopping on its sites.

My Muse glasses demo showed very little of meaningful, deeper agent hooks to data I’d recognize, since it wasn’t my own being accessed. I did notice that Muse took a while to complete some actions when rescheduling workouts for the marketing manager Muse agent Henry was set up to serve. Muse worked over audio, with no sense of progress status for completing a task.

Meta is introducing some privacy updates to how its glasses handle data, promising a new Private Processing system in the future that will run on confidential virtual machines in the cloud, a system that Meta’s using now in WhatsApp and Meta AI but plans to extend to all tools for Meta glasses. It’s not here yet, though, and it doesn’t make me feel any more convinced that any of the systems can be trusted, though, and I certainly feel lots of anxiety about handing over any agentic control of my personal data to any system.

But the space is moving fast. Google Gemini can already handle a lot of agentic actions, and Samsung and Google’s glasses will be able to do them. Apple’s new Siri, meanwhile, also has increasingly agent-like actions in its connected AI and apps. And OpenAI could be introducing more wearables with direct support for its services, too. Everyone in tech seems to want something like Iron Man’s Jarvis for your face, and few actually have it. Meta’s casting its hat in the ring.

Meta’s two Ray-Ban Audio glasses models: Clubmaster (left) and Burbank (right) Scott Stein/CNET

There are camera-free Meta Ray-Ban glasses now

One way to avoid pervert glasses concerns? Not having cameras on glasses at all. I tried out the new line of camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses, which promise 12-hour battery life (a notable bump from 8 to 9 hours on Meta’s recent glasses). There are just two designs for now: Clubmaster, which is a new look, and the more familiar square Burbank.

There’s not a lot new with Ray-Ban Audio glasses. They’re Meta glasses, minus the camera. A programmable action button on top of one arm still activates Meta AI, and one arm still has a touch bar for volume control. The audio sounded as good to me as Meta’s other models, but the battery boost could be a welcome addition. So could the social comfort of not having a camera on glasses.

But they’re not cheap. At $379 to $479, they’re actually more expensive than Meta’s recently launched line of self-branded smart glasses. Oddly, Meta didn’t make a non-Ray-Ban “Meta” branded (and likely less expensive) pair of audio glasses. Not yet, at least.

Nothing’s much changed on the camera front, either. A new landscape mode for photos sounded promising at first, but it works via digital cropping, and I haven’t tried it yet.

The phone app dashboard for Hearing Enhancement, which I got to demo briefly at Meta. Scott Stein/CNET

FDA-cleared hearing enhancement costs extra

In a move that mirrors a growing trend in hearing tech, Meta’s adding an FDA-cleared hearing assistance mode to its glasses, called Hearing Enhancement, which runs a hearing test to tune the experience for people with mild to moderate hearing loss. Apple’s AirPods Pro earbuds launched a similar feature two years ago.

Unlike Apple’s feature, though, you have to pay to enable Meta’s extra. It’s either $149, with a 30-day free trial to test how it works first, or included with a Meta One subscription that’ll run on glasses soon.

I hate subscriptions, especially for health features. A one-time cost feels more bearable. But it also pushes the total price up for a pair of Meta glasses as potential hearing aids.

To simulate how they work, Meta put foam earbuds in my ears while activating the mode during a conversation I had with Ravish Mehra, Meta’s director of research science. That’s far from a true simulation of actual hearing loss, but I got some sense of how the mode enhanced treble and clarity in sounds and conversations, like a more refined version of Meta’s existing Conversation Focus mode. Hearing Enhancement works in a targeted beam-forming mode that attends to a person, or more ambiently.

Mehra told me that the mode, when running, works for about 4 hours on Meta’s recent glasses models, but longer on the Ray-Ban Audio glasses. The extra fee could have been avoided (as Apple did), but Mehra cited R&D costs as one reason for the upcharge. I’m curious how AirPods and Meta glasses would compare for someone who actually needs the hearing assistance, something I couldn’t vet. With glasses, at least there wouldn’t be a need for any buds in your ears.

Meta Adventurer glasses in the new Lisa design are coming soon. Scott Stein/CNET

Lisa is making a pair of Meta Glasses too

I actually didn’t know who Lisa was, but she’s a famous rapper, actor and social media star who’s making her own custom-branded pair of Meta glasses, in the spirit of the Kylie Jenner glasses Meta launched in June. (My colleague Faith Chihil, one of CNET’s social media producers, flipped out at the Lisa news.)

The Lisa glasses come with a collectible charm, one of 14 types. They’re also decorated with stars on the arms. Lisa fans and collectors might be excited by this. I’m not.

But Meta’s also releasing a bunch more frame designs and colors, including some new Meta Glasses looks. Meta says there are over 100 designs and colors across all types now, and it felt that way when I browsed a bunch of new frames at Meta’s campus.

A new Aviator line of Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 smart glasses. Scott Stein/CNET

Gen 3 Meta Ray-Bans have new designs, slightly better battery

There are also new third-gen Meta Ray-Bans, but they’re not nearly as notable as the second-gen ones I wore last year. The battery boost on third-gen models is just an hour more than with Gen 2 — 9 hours total at best. That matches the claims for Google and Samsung’s imminent smart glasses, which is likely no coincidence.

There are a few frame designs, mostly variations on familiar looks. One pops, though: an aviator design that I tried out without my prescription added. They’re bold, kinda interesting, and…I felt a bit sinister wearing them.

The third-gen glasses are also more expensive, ranging from $449 to $529 without a prescription. Meta’s self-branded glasses, released in June, start at $299 and have nearly identical features, except for that tiny battery bump.

This is actually a virtual version of me in Meta’s new Hologram avatar. I animated it by talking on Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays. Scott Stein/CNET

Meta Ray-Ban Displays haven’t evolved much at all (except for Holograms)

Last year, Meta made a big deal with its display-enabled Ray-Bans and innovative neural band interface, a setup that seemed to push toward a future where full AR glasses lurk.

And yet, a year later, Meta has no significant improvements for Displays. They’ll be available in more countries this year, and may be easier to buy. But they still don’t work for a larger range of prescriptions, limited to just a -4 maximum. My eyes still won’t work with them.

Meta has been opening up more app development for its glasses and rolling out more features for Displays over the last year. Still, I expected Meta might find a way to blend its neural band with a smartwatch, perhaps one of Garmin’s models, since Meta and Garmin already have a partnership. But that didn’t happen either. The prices of the glasses are also still the same.

The most interesting thing about the Displays is the addition of Holograms, a hyper-realistic video chat avatar system that I tested out at Meta’s campus and was wowed by. It scans your face with a phone app and then projects your presence to the phone screen (or glasses, or VR headset) of whoever you’re calling, to surprisingly realistic effect. It’ll only be available to a limited test group at first in beta and will work on WhatsApp, but deliver the sort of simulated video chat on glasses that has been promised by Meta for years.

Besides camera-free Meta glasses (left), the design of Meta’s new glasses and camera design (right) remains the same. Scott Stein/CNET

Sorry, no watch, new fitness modes or major privacy improvements yet

Meanwhile, I was also surprised that Meta had no fitness updates at Connect, despite introducing Oakley-branded Vanguard visors last year and Garmin-connected workout features.

The Muse agent can connect to fitness and health functions, but a lack of new dedicated fitness features leaves a gap that Google might fill quickly with possibilities for Fitbit integration on its upcoming glasses, and an interconnection between WearOS watches and its glasses to act as a mini control dashboard and even preview photos.

Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth hinted to me last year that the neural band could evolve into a watch, but those plans haven’t yet materialized. Unlike Google and Apple’s wearables, Meta’s glasses are limited in how they connect to phones, using an app and, in the future, agentic hooks via Muse’s AI.

And also, biggest of all, Meta’s privacy issues feel barely addressed. It’s still as easy to take a photo in public as before, and nothing’s changed with how the glasses present themselves to others: They’re easy to confuse with regular glasses (to Meta’s credit, design-wise) and still just show a small LED light when recording.

And while Meta has promises of a private compute layer in the cloud for its future features, can they be trusted, and will third-party observers get access in any way? Will any of these new agentic features misfire unpredictably, as we’ve already seen with AI agents? The answer there feels like a “when” rather than an “if.”

But Meta won’t be alone in the pursuit of agentic AI wearables. It’s just the biggest and first in the door. There’s a lot of potential lurking in wearable AI, and lots of concerns. And Meta’s continuing to roll forward through all of it.

Tech.title: Black Workers Allege Systemic Racism at Tesla as Landmark California Trial Begins
Tech.content:
Tesla is facing a major civil rights lawsuit due to years of alleged rampant racist behavior against dozens of Black employees at its flagship Fremont assembly factory in California.

During opening statements on Monday, California Civil Rights Department attorney Brett Watson presented evidence of severe workplace harassment at Tesla, as reported by The Guardian. Photos and court documents revealed swastikas carved into factory surfaces, widespread use of the N-word, images of Confederate flags and other white supremacist symbols across the Fremont plant.

Black employees reported receiving harassing messages, such as: “Go back to Africa,” and “You want to hang from a tree?”

The allegations extend beyond harassment, as several Black workers say Elon Musk’s company subjected them to unequal pay and were given inferior job assignments and fewer opportunities for career advancement than other employees. Complaints of unchecked systemic racism at Tesla’s Fremont plant date back to 2012. The current lawsuit was filed 10 years later, in 2022.

This isn’t the first time Tesla has been involved in a legal battle over racial discrimination. Also in 2022, a former Tesla worker at the Fremont plant, Owen Diaz, was awarded over $3 million in damages for similar racial discrimination accusations.

Tesla has denied any wrongdoing, calling the lawsuit “misguided” and suggesting the company is the real victim.

Tesla’s lead attorney, Tyree Jones, countered the state’s claims during opening arguments by repeatedly uttering the racial slur to illustrate his defense. Jones argued that in the context of the factory floor, the N-word was frequently used as a casual greeting among Black workers rather than a derogatory insult.

Because this is a bench trial, no jury will be present throughout the case. Judge Peter Borkon will determine whether Tesla violated California’s civil rights laws. If the state wins, it’s very possible Borkon could force Tesla to overhaul its labor policies and HR practices.

Given that this is one of Tesla’s most prominent factories, the judge’s ruling could have ripple effects throughout Silicon Valley, impacting workplace equity policies, while also serving as a test of the state’s strict antidiscrimination laws. The trial is expected to conclude in late October.

Tesla and the California Civil Rights Department didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

Tech.title: Discord Introduces Alternative Age Verification Tools After Pushback
Tech.content:
After Discord users pushed back on ID requirements for age verification, the social platform announced in a blog post on Tuesday that it would implement age verification for teens — but not in the way people expected.

“Discord is introducing a new approach to age assurance, strengthening teen safety without requiring everyone to prove their age,” the company said in an email to CNET. “More than 90% of users won’t be asked to confirm their age. Most will either be placed into an age group automatically or will be able to continue using Discord without confirming their age unless they want to access age-restricted content, spaces, or settings.”

For those who do need to verify, Discord focuses on measuring “age signals” for teens rather than actual IDs, and it tells users it will not receive any direct data about them except their age signal results. The platform will work with a variety of vendors who will examine different types of data to assess a person’s age. Discord says those vendors won’t use any of this data for ad targeting or AI model training.

This follows a Discord-related data breach in 2025, which exposed 70,000 government ID photos of users, among with other information, on a vendor website.

The good news is that young Discord users can now choose how to verify their age, including options that don’t show their faces or IDs. Some of Discord’s options look fairly privacy-friendly, such as the ability to use documentation already in Google Wallet or the Apple App Store to verify age. If you’ve been using Apple’s store long enough, you may not have to send any further documentation at all. They can also use a site called AgeKey to create a reusable age credential. This allows teens to verify their age across multiple platforms without sharing their personal data directly with Discord.

Some troubling choices

However, some of Discord’s verification options raise serious privacy concerns.

“While estimating age based on user behavior is less invasive than requiring users to upload photos, credit card information or a state-issued ID, age-gating the internet creates dangerous new forms of surveillance, censorship, and exclusion,” Electronic Frontier Foundation senior counsel David Greene told CNET.

Discord includes a facial age-estimation option that requires a video selfie. Although the site says all facial analysis happens locally on the device, this use of AI still gives us pause. Experts point to ongoing accuracy challenges and inherent data risks, raising concerns over how corporate policies and algorithmic parameters might evolve in the future.

We’re also not fans of the credit-card check option, which not only costs money but sends credit card details to a third party, which may increase financial security risks.

Inaccurate age estimates can always happen, and they complicate the process. While Discord notes that users can initially switch to alternative confirmation methods, manual review serves as the fallback if those options fail. However, this manual route is a last resort and requires a human representative to personally verify both a government ID and a photograph.

Tech.title: Trove of Stolen Sensitive FBI Employee Data Is Significant Intelligence Risk
Tech.content:
Hackers from the group ShinyHunters claim to have stolen personal data of “all” FBI employees and applicants, according to a report published Tuesday by 404 Media.

The group, which was also behind a breach that disrupted software used by 9,000 schools during final exams in May, reportedly gained access to the FBI’s recruitment site via an exploit in Oracle’s PeopleSoft product. ShinyHunters says it now has sensitive data on individuals who applied for FBI jobs as well as current employees, according to 404 Media. ShinyHunters couldn’t be reached for comment.

As of Wednesday afternoon, the apply.fbijobs.gov site shows a maintenance page reading, “We’re sniffing out site updates for you!” The main FBI Jobs home page serves up a “503 Service Temporarily Unavailable” error page. The bureau’s page highlighting eligibility for new applicants is live with a “System Unavailable” banner reading, “Apply.fbijobs.gov and the Special Agent Application Portal are currently unavailable.”

The FBI’s jobs website shows a maintenance page following a breach by hackers who claim to have stolen sensitive personnel records. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

“The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information,” a spokesperson for the FBI told CNET via email. “While the point of breach is still undetermined — whether a third-party or the FBI’s enterprise — we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”

ShinyHunters has been linked to numerous ransomware attacks, including a breach of 4.4 million TransUnion credit records and access to servers belonging to Rockstar Games, the developer of the Grand Theft Auto series. The group usually demands extortion payments to prevent it from leaking the stolen information.

However, the attack on the FBI’s data is different and has potentially much more serious implications.

The group reportedly wants the FBI to correct what it calls false allegations in a Public Service Announcement that the FBI issued about it. The report notes that ShinyHunter “actors commonly use harassment strategies, sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members, and in some cases swatting.”

In an email to The New York Times, a representative of ShinyHunters wrote, “We reiterate we are not extorting the FBI and this is not financially motivated… Our intention, goal and motive is to solely set the record straight.”

But the nature of the stolen data elevates this breach beyond corporate extortion.

Joseph Cox, who broke the story at 404 Media, wrote via email, “This data presents significant national security and counterintelligence risks, and isn’t in the hands of a foreign intelligence agency, but a group of likely younger, English-speaking hackers.”

A security analyst who asked to remain anonymous to avoid retaliation from the hacking group reiterated that this is a serious national security issue. “Remember, the FBI is tasked with both counterespionage and counterterrorism,” they said. “This could destroy [FBI employees’ ability] to go undercover, travel to other countries and more,” including threats to individuals and families.

Asked about the group’s claim that it has nothing to do with extortion, the analyst said, “Never trust anything they say. Ever.”

They said that advice also comes directly from colleagues who advise companies on how to handle the extortions. Gaining access to such sensitive data could be monetarily valuable to a state-level intelligence agency.

The FBI has seen other notable cyberattacks this year, including “suspicious activities” on the system the bureau uses to manage wiretapping and surveillance and claims by an Iran-backed group said to breach the personal email of FBI Director Kash Patel.

Tech.title: A Patent Filed by Microsoft Would Let Games Use AI to Rewrite Themselves
Tech.content:
