Most narratively driven computer games don’t change much once they’re released to the public. But what if AI could change a game based on how a player interacts with it? A patent filed by Microsoft in June might allow future Xbox games to do just that.

The patent outlines a system that would allow generative AI to intelligently change the game based on what players do. In modern games, changes are usually dictated by dialog branches, which are the game’s different pathways of choices and responses, and player decisions, resulting in unique endings or character interactions. Some games handle change very well, but there’s always a limit.

This new system would go beyond that, taking into account how players explore the game world, what they interact with and the characters they meet regularly. The generative AI would then rewrite or rework the game to favor those interactions, giving the player more of what they enjoy. Microsoft even outlines a system in which players’ facial expressions and reactions would be measured to further tune the experience.

“Players have the potential to become co-creators of the game as a result of their exploration of and interaction with the game,” Microsoft says in the patent filing. “The game may allow for very different gameplay per player and session.”

For example, if a player spends a lot of time in a specific area of the game, generative AI would create new quests, lore and in-game assets, such as monsters or NPCs, to give players more to do in that area. Similarly, Microsoft says that unengaging content may be removed to further prune the experience. This new content is then observed by the AI, which can decide whether to incorporate it into the game’s main narrative.

All of this would be done on the fly and be user-specific. The game would essentially adapt to what it thinks the player wants and create a wholly unique experience, separate from other gamers.

Could this be a fun idea?

A diagram showing that the generative AI would be controllable by the game designer. Microsoft

The use of generative AI in games has elicited mixed reactions. Gamers tend to shy away from games that use it, but Baldur’s Gate 3 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — both of which have won game of the year awards and are very highly rated by both reviewers and players — used generative AI to some extent. It’s tough to estimate how well a game would be received if it could automatically rewrite itself at the whims of its players.

Such games would still require developers and writers, so this may not be an example of replacing humans. The AI needs a game world, rules, stories and existing characters to learn how to create more of them. So while the key phrase in Microsoft’s patent is generative AI, it’s actually more reminiscent of an existing game development tool: procedural generation.

You’re most likely familiar with procedural generation in Minecraft, where each new map is procedurally generated using a “seed” code consisting of numbers and text. That seed is fed into the game’s procedural generation algorithm to determine where mountains, caves, resources and biomes appear as the map is built. Each seed generates an entirely different map.

No Man’s Sky is another example, with each new solar system and planet being the work of procedural generation. Some smaller modern games have even taken it a step further. Titles like RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress, and Wildermyth use procedural generation in character creation, world-building and storytelling.

Procedural generation is generally preemptive, creating these parts of the game before the player can interact with them. Microsoft’s idea would theoretically generate content only after the player interacts with it, making it reactive rather than preemptive.

That would make it more like Pandemic Legacy. This story-based version of the board game requires players to permanently alter the game board and player cards as they play through the story, resulting in a one-of-a-kind version of the game once players complete it.

Don’t expect to see games using this concept any time soon. The patent remains pending, and it could be years before the patent application is approved. Additionally, Microsoft has declined to comment on whether any current Xbox titles in development utilize this technology, suggesting a lengthy timeline before the system is seen in active operation.

Tech.title: I Wore Meta’s New $1,299 VR Glasses: A Tiny Quest, or Vision Pro to Go?
Tech.content:
I could see the whole room in front of me in surprisingly crisp color video detail, while looking at a grid of apps in front of me. Selecting an app with my eyes and a pinch of my fingers, I launched a 3D Billie Eilish concert video. Then I watched an immersive NBA game that stretched all around me. Was I on the Apple Vision Pro? No, I was wearing a pair of Meta VR Glasses, Meta’s $1,299 reimagining of its VR ecosystem coming next spring that feels like one part Apple, one part Meta Quest and one part AR glasses that haven’t been built yet.

Despite releasing waves of smart glasses over the last few years and ditching games studios, software initiatives and fitness apps, including Supernatural earlier this year, Meta’s not done with VR. But the Meta VR Glasses are a very different proposition than the Quest: in price, in design, in portability and in ambition. They’re not AR glasses, like Meta’s Orion prototype I tried two years ago. But they are a VR headset in glasses form, and share a lot in common with the Orion.

I felt echoes of other products as I slipped Meta’s new visor-like pair of VR glasses over my head. An Apple Vision Pro that’s been put onto folding glasses. No: a Meta Quest Pro shrunken down. Or, the Xreal Aura I tried earlier this year. The Meta VR Glasses – yes, that’s their real name – feel like they’re straddling gadget categories. And they’re pushing a price Meta hasn’t tried for in years.

Meta unveiled the VR Glasses on Wednesday at its Connect developer conference, along with camera-free Meta Ray-Bans and an FDA-cleared hearing enhancement feature and plans to install its Muse AI agent across its lineup of smart glasses.

Meta VR Glasses, when folded, are seriously compact. Scott Stein/CNET

Ultraportable VR

The best point of comparison for the Meta VR Glasses might be the now-discontinued Quest Pro, from their small size to their vivid displays and eye- and hand-tracking controls. But they’re also oddly evolutionary, like many other recent VR/AR products I’ve tried.

The magnesium frame glasses-like visor looks minimal compared to any other VR headset, but I’ve seen this form before. I wore another “VR glasses” device called the URXR One back in June.

Meta’s VR Glasses wired to the processor puck. They work as a team. Scott Stein/CNET

I felt like I was wearing a smaller, like a sliced-off front end of an Apple Vision Pro, bonded to a pair of glasses’ arms. The curved front visor is studded with cameras and sensors that can sense movement in front of and well below my field of view: I could gently pinch my fingers while resting them on the table, the sort of lazy interactions I can do on the Vision Pro. Volume buttons and another control button are embedded in the arms.

The processor puck is where the one USB-C passthrough port is located, and devices that input through it can stream that device into the VR environment, something I didn’t get to try. The puck comes with 128GB of storage, but also has a MicroSD card slot for expandable storage, which requires higher-speed cards. Still, it’s a first for Meta’s VR headsets.

The color passthrough video quality, which makes virtual experiences look projected into the room like augmented reality, was a big notch up from the Quest 3. It felt close to where Samsung and Apple are with their more expensive headsets.

Meta scanned my eyeglasses to provide prescription lens inserts that matched my vision. The inserts fit into the clear pancake lenses in the visor, which were covered in a soft mesh much like the inside of the Vision Pro headset. The Meta VR glasses fit well on my face, too, and they’re far lighter than wearing a Quest 3. They’re 100 grams, which is heavy for glasses but very, very light for a VR headset. They come in two different sizes, but I’m not sure which one I tried.

The lenses in Meta VR Glasses are small, but the viewing experience is impressive. Scott Stein/CNET

My hands-on time with the Meta VR Glasses

I controlled everything with my hands and eyes, because the Meta VR Glasses don’t come with any controllers at all. They’ll work with Meta Quest controllers, and new controllers will be sold separately, but the whole device is designed to work controller-free. Meta’s promising a series of new optimized games for the headset that will be eye and hand-tracking controlled, too.

I played one of them: a new version of Meta’s classic VR-lightsaber fitness game Beat Saber called Beat Saber Flux, which is arriving next year to time with the glasses. Flux has no sabers at all, actually. Instead, the game tracked my hands as I formed energy fields to punch and slice through oncoming waves of targets. It reminded me more of rhythm games like Synth Riders and Supernatural, but also was a good demo of the headset’s hand tracking chops.

Meta’s VR Glasses wowed me with their size. Scott Stein/CNET

I also tried casting multiple virtual monitors in front of me from a wirelessly connected laptop, something you can already do on the Quest and headsets like the Vision Pro and Samsung’s Galaxy XR. But it’s the smaller size of the Meta VR Glasses that makes this achievement seem particularly impressive.

I typed on a virtual keyboard projected directly onto the table in front of me, a trick Quest headsets can already do but which looked more impressive on Meta’s VR Glasses, particularly since the keyboard really looked as though it had been projected onto the table. It was properly positioned over my hands with realistic occlusion effects. But I don’t know how well it would work beyond my rapid hunt and pecking.

Another look at the glasses and their processor puck. Celso Bugatti/CNET

Navigating Meta’s hand and eye tracking interfaces felt fine, and again, very Apple Vision-esque. But also like Meta’s neural band hand gestures for its Ray-Ban Display glasses. Taps and thumb-swipes on my closed fist handled scrolling around, but I found that pinch-and-pull gestures in the air worked for scrolling too. It wasn’t always that easy to make out on-screen indicators of where my eyes were looking, though: Sometimes icons got a little bigger or wiggled, but not always.

Meta promises a 3-hour battery life with the included processor puck, which can fast recharge at 45W. It runs off a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset, the same one that’s in Xreal’s upcoming processor puck-tethered, VR-like pair of Android XR glasses, Xreal Aura.

Meta’s VR Glasses are small but they pack impressive micro OLED displays inside. Scott Stein/CNET

A clear display upgrade

In a half-hour demo session at Meta’s Connect developer conference, I watched a series of movie clips and videos meant to show off the quality of the headset as a portable cinema. The twin micro OLED displays with a combined effective 5K resolution felt as vivid as that of a Vision Pro, to my memory, but with a smaller 84-degree field of view. They’re 2,412×2,288 pixels per eye.

Watching a few movies on the Meta VR Glasses looked better than anything I’ve seen on Quest headsets, and clearly offers a step-up to approach the good-enough-for-home-cinema feel I get in the Vision Pro.

Beat Saber Flux is a hand tracking-focused game update for Meta VR Glasses (and coming to Quest too). Meta

Meta’s promising lots of streaming video app support. I viewed a series of brief Disney interactive environments for some of its streaming movies, which tried to give me a taste of something more immersive than what’s already on the Vision Pro and Quest’s Disney Plus app. As I watched Avengers: Infinity War, my room was engulfed by parts of the stellar forge Nidavellir while a scene between Thor and Peter Dinklage’s dwarf king Eitri played on a big virtual movie screen. At one point, Groot also popped out in 3D beyond the screen’s dimensions.

The displays and spatial audio are Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision capable, and Meta’s touting that the headset is certified for Imax film viewing in the proper aspect ratio. Meta’s launching its own movie store with these VR glasses, and it’ll also be available on Quest headsets.

In a sense, the Meta VR Glasses almost remind me of smaller micro OLED-equipped display glasses like the ones made by Viture and Xreal. They especially resemble Xreal’s upcoming Aura glasses, which I’ve tried several times and run Google’s Android XR operating system and connect to a processing puck. Aura’s field of view is even smaller at 70 degrees, but it’s more like a pair of display glasses that are remarkably VR-like. Meta’s headset feels like a VR headset that’s remarkably glasses-like. The two sort of meet in the middle.

This is how my early version of Hologram looks on a phone screen. It’s even more impressive in VR. Scott Stein/CNET

Holograms for chat, at last

A demo I tried in a separate session showed me something Meta’s been promising for years: realistic 3D avatars for video chat, much like what Apple already has in its Vision Pro Personas. Meta showed me early prototypes of its “Codec Avatar” vision for hyper-real avatar embodiment back in 2022 at its research labs, but the new Holograms feel like a slice of that, aimed at working on both VR Glasses, Quest headsets, and even Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays in its smaller 2D screen.

I was actually blown away by my Holograms demo, because what I saw didn’t look like uncannily real people: they looked exactly like real people, as if appearing in a video chat in front of me. A quick head scan and recording of my voice and expressions (mostly with smiling or positive emotions expressed) on a phone app led to a 3D scan of myself that then appeared inside VR Glasses when I made a WhatsApp call to a Meta team member. I couldn’t see myself, but I did see them appear in front of me, first as a 3D torso in a window, then opening out to stand in the room with me, legs and all, when I tapped an icon in my chat window.

It looked like a volumetric video capture of someone, not an artificial scan. And while Holograms currently animate body movement using AI to interpret voice tone, they’ll eventually have body tracking using the VR Glasses’ downward-facing cameras, which track both face and body movements. It seemed like they were in the room, right by a table in front of me…but turning in a ghostly manner to keep facing me no matter which way I turned.

Holograms are going to launch alongside Meta VR Glasses, but also get tested as a Met Ray-Ban Display feature in beta later this year for WhatsApp calling. The technology leans heavily on cloud compute, using stable diffusion versus Gaussian splatting like Apple’s Personas uses. I’ve never seen a more realistic deepfaked version of myself before.

The Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses (left) next to Meta VR Glasses (right). They’re getting closer in size than ever. Scott Stein/CNET

The start of a new phase for VR and AR?

My time with the Meta VR Glasses impressed me, especially compared to other recent VR devices and display glasses I’ve tried, and I immediately thought about what it would be like to travel with them. But their unusual design and higher price, clearly aimed at making a premium experience for movie-watching, immersive HD video and wearable displays, is a risk. It’s a play that Meta hasn’t made since the Quest Pro was released back in 2022.

Would I use the Meta VR Glasses for work? Maybe. I like that they can also connect directly to a laptop, phone or any other UBS-C device with video out to turn them into a portable display, but Xreal Aura will do that too. I also like that they’ll run all the Quest apps I already use, but Meta’s still facing an uphill battle over all the Android and iOS apps Google and Apple’s XR devices can tap into.

How long will it be until Meta’s VR and glasses lines converge? Scott Stein/CNET

I feel more comfortable with Meta as a wear-sometimes device maker in the VR space. I’m much less happy with Meta as a broker of some sort of always-on glasses-based personal assistant (which is where all the AI glasses are headed). But, clearly, those categories are merging, slowly. The VR Glasses feel like an early herald of the attempted merge.

Which raises my final question: Are the Meta VR Glasses a premium upgrade for Quest owners, a portable upsell or a pitch to reach people who’ve never tried VR or AR before? I definitely found them more wearable than any Quest headset, with no pressure on my face and a more casual comfort.

I kept thinking about Valve’s recently released Steam Frame, a headset that costs a similar amount but has a more traditional but modular VR headset design. Valve’s Frame wants to push Steam into new forms. Meta’s VR Glasses are aiming to push the Quest library into new forms, too. And then there are Xreal’s similar Aura glasses coming this fall, and even Snap Specs, which are full augmented reality glasses with clear lenses but have no processor puck tether at all.

They all want to come with me on a trip. Which would I actually take? Or afford? Meta VR Glasses aren’t even on sale until next spring, but I’m already wondering if they’ll be something I’d pick over alternatives, or whether Meta’s VR glasses flex is more of a stepping stone to AR glasses the company can’t quite make happen yet. But I want another go in them, for sure. And I’d love to travel with them next year.

Tech.title: Some of Samsung’s AI Fridges Became Giant, Cool Bricks After Bad Update
Tech.content:
A SmartThings software update went sour for some owners of Samsung smart fridges in Korea when their devices became unresponsive, as reported by outlets such as ZDNet Korea. Reports found owners complaining about spoiled food due to their refrigerators shutting down and being unable to cool.

Samsung said it’s addressing the problem, but the timing of the bug could not have been worse, happening just days before Thursday’s start of Chuseok, a major Korean fall harvest holiday.

A representative for Samsung didn’t respond to a request for comment.

A Samsung community page for its SmartThings products said that the company accidentally sent internal test software to customers on Tuesday, resulting in “abnormal symptoms regarding the power and screen of some customers’ refrigerators.” The post said the company was prioritizing emergency measures through its Samsung Electronics service centers.

Some users on the forum complained that they were not promised service until Sept. 29, after Chuseok, or even into October. “You’re saying you’ll come and check on the food after it’s all rotten?” wrote one (translated from Korean).

Most reports seem to focus on the company’s newer models of the Bespoke AI four-door refrigerator. Since debuting at CES in 2021, Samsung’s Bespoke product line has been pitched as a way to shift home appliances from anonymous metal boxes to customizable, intelligent lifestyle items. So far, there haven’t been any reports of Samsung fridges experiencing this problem outside Korea.

The internet of (broken) things

A bricked phone is an inconvenience. A bricked fridge is a biohazard. Welcome to the internet of broken things.

Smart home devices can make life much easier, but when software on internet-connected appliances goes wrong, it can lead to frustration and lost time. Smart appliances with Wi-Fi and AI are also susceptible to privacy violations, such as the sale of private data, and to outright danger from hackers. Simply being online makes them easy targets, and because they lack the constant security updates that smartphones and PCs receive, they’re often more exposed.

Advanced internet-based features can add convenient capabilities to appliances, such as downloading recipes or gathering information about what’s inside your smart fridge. But app and internet connectivity requirements add a level of complexity and vulnerability that wouldn’t be an issue with traditional, non-connected gadgets or appliances.

Last month, owners of Petlibro pet feeders expressed outrage when an app outage left their devices inoperable for longer than the company promised. Some who were traveling found their pets left at home hungry. The company issued a public update but faced even greater backlash when customers continued to have problems days after a reported fix was rolled out.

Smart tech has gotten more efficient and reliable in recent years, but diagnosing a failure is still a massive headache. After all, it could be your Wi-Fi, a software or firmware update, or simply the age of the device itself.

Tech.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo: Comparing Apple’s New Pro Phone Against Its First Foldable
Tech.content:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro is now on sale, but the foldable iPhone Duo is still awaiting its big debut on Oct. 23. While both phones are premium showstoppers, they’re also very different.

The 18 Pro features the company’s best camera yet on an iPhone, including a variable aperture for the first time. That feature helps you control light exposure, which can improve low-light photography, and you can use the new Pro Controls for additional features, like adjusting shutter speed. And while the outside is similar to the iPhone 17 Pro, the inside has been redesigned to accommodate a larger vapor chamber that helps keep the phone cool during intensive use.

But it’s the iPhone Duo that really captured people’s attention. It’s Apple’s first foldable phone, with a passport-style design that’s made to fit in your hand when closed. Then you can unfold it like a book to reveal a wide screen that’s almost the size of an iPad Mini (an open iPhone Duo has a 7.6-inch screen while an iPad Mini measures 8.3 inches). Yet, it only has two rear cameras rather than the three that the 18 Pro has, so it won’t have a telephoto lens for zooming into a subject as far as the Pro and Pro Max can. It also doesn’t have the aforementioned variable aperture.

On top of that, the iPhone Duo is extremely expensive: It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB version. The iPhone 18 Pro isn’t cheap either, but it is less of a stretch, with a starting price of $1,199 for the 256GB version.

Here are the top highlights for each phone, and you can use our specs chart to compare them further.

The Duo’s inner selfie camera is geared toward FaceTime videos. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Design and display

The primary difference between the two phones lies in their designs. The iPhone 18 Pro has the usual slab iPhone design that we’ve come to know over the years. It even has the same dimensions as its predecessor, measuring 5.9 by 2.3 by 0.3 inches. This means you can use the same phone cases whether they were designed for the iPhone 17 Pro or the 18 Pro. The 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design with a triple camera array on the back. On the front is a 6.3-inch OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. The display also includes a slimmer Dynamic Island cutout for the front-facing camera and Face ID, which can now display three Live Activities at once.

The iPhone Duo, on the other hand, is quite the departure from Apple as the company’s first foldable. Closed, it has rounded corners on the upper and lower right along with flat titanium sides. Due to its passport size, it has a rather squat 5.4-inch cover display on the front. When it’s closed, it measures 4.6 by 3.3 by 0.4 inches.

The iPhone Duo when closed. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Open the Duo up, and you will see a 7.6-inch OLED display. While the cover screen has the usual glossy glass display of other iPhones, the main internal display of the iPhone Duo has a matte nano-textured finish designed to reduce reflections and minimize the appearance of the crease. Also, when the Duo is open, it’s just 0.2 inches thick, which is even thinner than last year’s iPhone Air (0.22 inches). Both displays support a 120Hz refresh rate, and the phone can use StandBy mode widgets when folded into a tent-like position. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have Face ID and instead uses a side fingerprint sensor for Touch ID unlocking.

Both phones are IP68-rated for dust and water resistance. That’s particularly notable for the Duo, as it’s one of the few book-style foldable phones to carry that rating. (Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold and 11 Pro Fold are also rated IP68.)

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max on display at Apple’s store on Fifth Avenue in New York for the phones’ launch. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Cameras

The iPhone 18 Pro has the best camera features that Apple has to offer. It has a triple rear camera array: a 48-megapixel wide, ultrawide and telephoto. Its new variable aperture, lets you control how much light hits the sensor, allowing for improved low-light photography, greater depth-of-field for close-up shots and overall a lot more flexibility for creative photography.

While the iPhone Duo has a compact foldable design as its spotlight feature, its camera system harkens more to what’s included on the iPhone 17. Despite being substantially more expensive than the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo has a 48-megapixel wide camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. It does not have a telephoto camera, but its camera system does allow for a 2x optical quality zoom along with a digital zoom to 10x. It also does not have the variable aperture that’s included on the 18 Pro.

Both phones have selfie cameras; the 18 Pro has a 18-megapixel front-facing camera, while the Duo has a 12-megapixel Center Stage selfie camera on the cover display as well as a hidden under-display FaceTime camera on the main display. The benefit of the Duo, however, is that you can actually use the 48-megapixel rear camera as your “selfie” camera when the phone is open as the cover display becomes a viewfinder.

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Performance and battery

Both phones ship with Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, which is the company’s first to be made with a 2-nanometer process. The processor is therefore denser and should result in a 20% faster CPU and a 40% faster GPU than last year’s A19 Pro. It should also help keep the phone cool even during intensive use.

As for battery life, Apple doesn’t give the specific capacity for both phones, but it does say that the 18 Pro should last up to 24 hours, while the iPhone Duo will last up to 44 hours while watching videos when closed, and up to 31 hours when open.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is able to show three Live Activities at once. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

In our preliminary test with the 18 Pro, we found that it lasted almost a full day before needing to be charged. It’s also one of the fastest-charging phones CNET has tested, charging from 0% to 82% in just 30 minutes. According to Apple, the iPhone Duo will charge to 50% in about 15 minutes with a 60-watt charger, or to 50% in 30 minutes with a 35-watt wireless MagSafe charger. We’ll have to perform further tests to be sure.

Check out the specs chart to further compare the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo.
